entry.title: Before the event: what United Western Bank's filings did and did not reveal
entry.summary: A construction-PIT replay of United Western Bank: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
entry.content:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It opens the public United Western Bank record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is 2006-09-02. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated 2001-03-31, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of 2001-05-30. Its status is threshold_2, its breached fields are NNPA, and its recorded lead is 63 months.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: True. Its first signal is dated not observed, with knowledge-time proxy not available, index unavailable, band not observed, flags none published, and lead unavailable months.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

What the lenses saw

The public replay page preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains 15 failed institutions and 5 first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of 41 months. The funding replay contains 10 institutions with liability disclosures and 4 first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For United Western Bank, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is ****. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

What today's board shares

Today's board contains 0 red, 0 orange, 1 yellow and 2 green rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next United Western Bank.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes 35 stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

Follow the pressure chain

Seiche asks whether system funding capacity is tightening. LiquiLens asks which institution balance sheet would transmit that pressure. Undertow asks whether the risk can be exited in traded markets. The three layers may disagree, and that disagreement is often the finding.

Readers who need the rule tested on their own counterparties can use the six-week proof pilot. The public replay, including this case's misses and voids, stays open.

Sources, method, and limits

  • - LiquiLens historical validation record, the structured source for every case value quoted above.
  • - The United Western Bank replay, a human-readable case file generated from that record.
  • - Three-market evidence index, which states why India, US and Europe evidence has different status.
  • - Current Failure Radar board, used only for today's tier counts and coverage boundary.
  • - Seiche overview and Undertow public board, sibling layers not used to score this case.
  • - LiquiLens research record and reviewed investigations.

This article reports a construction-PIT historical diagnostic. It is not a validated backtest, a publication-vintage reconstruction or real-money evidence. It is not a credit rating or a prediction. Where an exact publication timestamp is absent, the record uses a filing-availability proxy. Fraud-masked cases expose a hard limit of honest-disclosure models. Similar mechanisms do not imply a repeated outcome. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Sambandh Finserve’s funding flag was an early disclosure signal, not a forecast
entry.summary: A historical replay places Sambandh Finserve’s first fragile funding signal before its recorded default. The evidence identifies a disclosed wholesale-leverage vulnerability, while fraud masking and construction-PIT timing limit what that chronology can establish.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news. It is not a forecast, a credit rating, or investment advice. The filing period discussed below ended on 2016-03-31; the knowledge-time proxy is 2016-05-30. Sambandh Finserve’s recorded default date is 2020-10-13.*

The narrow answer to LiquiLens’s desk question is that Sambandh Finserve was the balance sheet that warranted earlier scrutiny because a disclosed funding measure crossed the published fragile threshold. That is not a claim that the filing predicted default, identified its cause, or created a tradeable warning. It is a claim about what the disclosed liability structure showed under a stated rule before the recorded event.

The funding lens placed Sambandh Finserve at 78.7, in the fragile band, for the period ending 2016-03-31. Its recorded flag was wholesale leverage of 8.51x against a 7x threshold. The replay calculates a 52-month lead to the recorded default. That interval is a reconstructed filing-period chronology using a knowledge-time proxy. It is neither a market-price signal nor a model-derived probability of failure.

The record before the event

The first funding signal belongs to the 2016-03-31 reporting period and is treated as known on 2016-05-30. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. That is more cautious than assuming a balance-sheet date was instantly available, but it remains a proxy rather than a verified contemporaneous information set.

The record is classified as PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not eligible for validated backtesting, is not eligible for real-money use, and has no bitemporal input contract. Potential lead times may therefore be optimistic. The 52-month result is best read as a reconstructed chronology of a disclosed ratio, not evidence that a lender or investor could have acted with the same timing, information, or confidence.

A more serious limitation is that Sambandh Finserve is fraud-masked. The dossier warns that institutions whose filings were later shown to be falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. A mechanical screen cannot retrieve undisclosed facts or correct untruthful disclosures. This makes the case useful for testing the limits of a visible funding flag, but unsuitable for claiming that the flag explained, detected, or forecast the eventual outcome.

The underlying materials are available through the failure-radar board, the dedicated Sambandh Finserve replay, and the broader replay archive.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw wholesale leverage above its published threshold. That is a filing-period observation: a rule applied to a disclosed liability-side measure. It is not evidence of observed lender behaviour, refinancing prices, or market consensus. It also is not a model derivation of a calibrated failure likelihood.

The PCA lens does not provide an earlier action-zone finding for Sambandh Finserve. No first action zone or related lead period is recorded. That absence cannot be converted into evidence that the institution was safe, that supervisory thresholds cleared it, or that the funding lens was sufficient on its own.

Across the replay, the PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions; 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also covers 15 failed institutions, but liability disclosures exist for only 10. The funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. These are descriptive results from a restricted disclosure record, not prospective validation. The historical validation record retains those restrictions.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. It carries the same construction-PIT, non-real-money, and non-validated limitations. Sambandh’s fraud-masked status matters especially because the headline excludes the category in which disclosure-based thresholds can be most misleading.

Why the warning mattered

Wholesale leverage matters because it raises a balance-sheet question about refinancing dependence. If asset performance weakens, earnings and capital capacity may be less able to absorb losses. Where wholesale liabilities are important, funding terms and rollover willingness may become more consequential. That is a plausible pressure chain, not an established account of what happened at Sambandh.

The flag therefore mattered as a prompt for harder investigation of funding concentration, maturity structure, liquidity resilience, lender diversity, and loss-absorption capacity. The fragile label does not demonstrate that a lender withdrew, repriced, shortened, or refused funding. The dossier supplies a threshold flag, not lender-by-lender rollover evidence, cash-flow history, or a verified transmission sequence.

This distinction is essential. A filing signal can reveal a disclosed structural exposure. A market-price signal would require authorized evidence of repricing or drawdown. Neither establishes causation. A model derivation would require an eligible prospective framework able to translate inputs into a validated probability. This record explicitly does not meet that standard.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat an overconfident thesis. Wholesale funding is not inherently fatal. An institution can carry substantial wholesale liabilities while asset quality, capital capacity, liquidity buffers, maturities, funding diversity, and lender relationships remain resilient. A ratio threshold is a coarse representation of a more complex balance sheet.

The historical model evidence is not decisive either. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with a 95% interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic comparator reports 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only.

A sceptic can reasonably conclude that the flag marked a broad vulnerability rather than a dependable countdown. Fraud masking intensifies the objection: incomplete or false disclosures can make the relationship between reported leverage and actual condition unknowable. The defensible conclusion is limited to this: Sambandh’s disclosed funding profile justified more investigation than a comparable profile without the flag.

What today's board shares

The current board is separately dated 2026-10-20 and does not present Sambandh as a current scored row. It contains 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8; Annapurna Finance Private Limited is green at 96.5; Arohan Financial Services Limited is green at 97.1. Each row is as of 2026-03-31 and aged 7 months.

The board excludes 35 stale institutions. It does not present quarterly filings older than 183 days or annual filings older than 400 days as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design rather than scored from memory. Those eligibility rules matter as much as the visible rows.

The market pack is fresh as of 2026-10-16, but it has no admission, publication, signal, or tier authority. Rights and display approvals are absent, and admitted canonical records are 0/25. It cannot supply market-price confirmation for this article. See the market-evidence endpoint.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if prospectively timestamped, vetted disclosures show flagged institutions retaining refinancing access, liquidity resilience, and loss-absorption capacity through stress while comparable unflagged institutions deteriorate first. It strengthens only if original filing vintages, explicit publication clocks, liability composition, and later outcomes are preserved before results are known.

That test cannot be satisfied by extending a retrospective replay. It requires a pre-specified prospective cohort and evaluation that does not inherit revised knowledge from later filings or outcomes.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct analytical objects, not interchangeable confirmations.

The LiquiLens research archive provides institution-focused context. The Seiche overview is system context only here. The Undertow board addresses exit capacity, not Sambandh’s historical funding flag. System strain or market illiquidity cannot replace missing institutional disclosures or turn a filing replay into a forecast.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the supplied LiquiLens record only: the failure-radar board, historical validation, market evidence, and Sambandh replay.

The decisive limitations are the period-end-plus-60-days availability proxy, absent bitemporal input control, potentially optimistic lead times, missing liability disclosures, fraud masking, and the absence of authorized market-derived display or tier evidence. The finding is not that Sambandh’s end was forecast. It is that a disclosed funding vulnerability appeared early enough to warrant harder questions, while the record remains too constrained to claim more.

Research and market data, not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: At New India Co-operative Bank, the first disclosed stress was asset quality—not funding
entry.summary: The replay places an NNPA action-zone breach at the FY2021 filing period, ahead of the 2025-02-13 event date. That is a filing-period signal under a construction-PIT proxy, not a market-price warning, a validated forecast, or proof that the record revealed fraud.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines New India Co-operative Bank around its 2025-02-13 event date. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is New India Co-operative Bank: disclosed balance-sheet stress appeared first in the asset-quality lens. The replay records an RBI action-zone breach for NNPA in FY2021, for the period ending 2021-03-31. Its assigned knowledge-time proxy is 2021-05-30, and the recorded lead is 44 months.

That finding requires careful classification. It is a filing-period signal: a breach derived from a reported period, with availability assigned by an explicit publication clock when available or by period end plus 60 days otherwise. It is not a market-price signal, and it is not a model-derived probability of failure. The record is fraud-masked and labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT; it is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. The dossier says its lead times are optimistic.

The record before the event

The first action-zone observation was FY2021. The listed breach was NNPA. The replay links the 2021-05-30 knowledge-time proxy to the 2021-03-31 period end, before the 2025-02-13 event. This supports a limited sequencing claim: the disclosed asset-quality screen fired before the recorded event.

The funding lens did not provide an earlier result. New India’s funding record is scoreable, but no first funding signal or funding lead is reported. This is missing signal evidence, not affirmative evidence of calm funding. The funding lens can assess only institutions that disclose a liability series. The absence of an earlier disclosed funding flag does not establish that deposits, liquidity, or other liabilities were free from pressure.

The fraud-masked designation is material. A threshold engine sees reported inputs rather than concealed conditions. The dossier notes that filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine, with the forensic screen owning that limitation. A public-disclosure replay cannot convert a reported ratio into proof of institutional condition, solvency, or safety.

What the lenses saw

The regulatory lens observed an NNPA breach. The funding lens did not establish an earlier disclosed signal. That is the complete supported ordering. It permits the conclusion that asset-quality deterioration was the earliest visible warning in this replay. It does not support the stronger claim that funding was sound, irrelevant, or later in the institution’s underlying condition.

Across the historical summaries, lenses do not have a universal order. Of 15 failed institutions in the PCA/SAF summary, 5 entered the action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. Of those 15, 10 had liability disclosures in the funding summary; funding fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. These are descriptive public-disclosure replays, not an ordering rule for all lenders.

The PCA/SAF exercise replays RBI tripwires using public disclosures. Timing begins at an exact publication time where available and otherwise uses the period-end-plus-60-days proxy. The Failure Radar board and historical validation record should be read before treating any lead-time statistic as investable evidence.

Why the warning mattered

NNPA is a filing-period indicator of disclosed asset-quality stress. The warning mattered because it raised a balance-sheet question before the event: whether reported problem assets were eroding the institution’s capacity to absorb further deterioration. That is an investigative question, not a demonstrated causal history.

Any fuller chain is a model derivation rather than an observed fact in this dossier. Impaired-asset pressure may require greater loss absorption; reduced capacity may make confidence or funding pressure more consequential. But the supplied evidence contains no series for capital, provisions, depositor behaviour, cash flows, or a causal explanation for the event. It supports an earlier NNPA screen, not a complete postmortem.

The New India replay and the wider replay archive are therefore best used as historical investigation tools, not as current institution dossiers.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis: the reported NNPA ratio may not have reliably represented the balance sheet. The fraud-masked label makes that possibility central. If disclosures were incomplete or distorted, an apparently early ratio breach may not describe the true onset, scale, or mechanism of stress.

Timing is a further objection. The 44-month lead uses a knowledge-time proxy, not a fully verified vintage archive. The period-end-plus-60-days convention is more conservative than dating information to the reporting period, but remains a construction assumption where no exact publication clock exists. It is consequently an optimistic historical lead, not a tradable timestamp.

Model diagnostics do not rescue the claim. The temporal hazard test reported AUC of 0.645 against a diagnostic gate of 0.65 and did not pass. Historical tier wiring for the conformal alarm is suspended pending prospective revalidation; it has no score or tier authority. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC was 0.799 against hazard AUC of 0.752. None validates this case as a forecast.

The thesis also weakens if complete, timely liability data repeatedly provides earlier verified funding warnings in comparable institutions. A missing funding signal is not a clean liquidity bill of health.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this replay. As of 2026-10-19, it has 0 red, 0 orange, 1 yellow, and 2 green comparison rows. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow; Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green. Their listed filing date is 2026-03-31 and their listed age is 7 months.

New India is not a current score. Failed institutions are replayed on the Evidence tab. The board excludes 35 stale institutions and presents nothing older than 183 days for quarterly filings or 400 days for annual filings as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design.

The market layer is available as of 2026-10-16 and was retrieved on 2026-10-19. It is fresh and clock-authorized, but it has no publication, model-gate, or tier authority. Rights and approvals are incomplete, with admitted canonical records at 0/25. It cannot support a current tier inference. See the market evidence endpoint.

The next falsifiable test

A proper test would preserve actual publication timestamps, retain missing-data states, isolate forensic exceptions, and assess a prospective cohort only after its outcome window closes. The thesis fails if vintage-controlled evidence shows that NNPA action-zone breaches do not precede later balance-sheet stress more often than competing lenses after fraud masking and liability-disclosure gaps are handled.

It also fails if a complete liability dataset repeatedly supplies earlier verified funding signals for comparable institutions. Until then, 44 months is an investigative replay result—not a calibrated probability, a failure forecast, or evidence for a trading decision.

Follow the pressure chain

The disciplined chain is disclosed NNPA pressure, evidence of capacity to absorb further loss, then independently evidenced funding strain. Each link needs its own record. A missing funding signal is not reassuring, and system context cannot fill an institution-level disclosure gap.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct products and evidence domains. Seiche’s 2026-10-19 composite is EROSION with value 43.8, while its confidence is guarded because slow-moving or modelled structure has not broadly been confirmed by current market plumbing. Undertow labels UST STRAINED while other segments are PARTIAL or NORMAL. Neither is used in the institution score. Consult Seiche’s overview and the Undertow board as separate context, not manufactured corroboration.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied dossier and permitted sources: the Failure Radar board, validation record, market evidence, New India replay, replay archive, research archive, and US NDFI monitor.

The clocks are not interchangeable: the filing period ended 2021-03-31; the replay proxy is 2021-05-30; the event date is 2025-02-13; the board date is 2026-10-19; and the market date is 2026-10-16. Construction-PIT status, optimistic leads, fraud masking, missing liability evidence, and the absence of a bitemporal input contract are material limits, not footnotes.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Nedungadi Bank’s capital breach came first—but it was not a failure forecast
entry.summary: The replay records a CRAR action-zone breach before Nedungadi Bank’s default and no scoreable funding signal. That ordering identifies a balance-sheet pressure point, not a causal timetable or a live prediction.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Nedungadi Bank through reconstructed public-disclosure timing before its default. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution.*

The answer to the desk question is narrow. In this replay, Nedungadi Bank’s capital position produced the first identified warning: an RBI action-zone breach in CRAR at the period ended 1999-03-31. The bank defaulted on 2002-11-02. The funding lens did not produce an earlier competing signal because the institution was not scoreable under that lens.

That is a sequence, not a complete explanation of failure. A filing-period signal says that a disclosed condition was recorded for a reporting period. A knowledge-time proxy estimates when that condition could have been known. A market-price signal, by contrast, is a contemporaneous repricing measure. A model derivation turns available inputs into a rule, score, or tier. Confusing those categories can make a historical replay sound more predictive than the evidence permits.

The relevant research boundary is explicit: PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT evidence is not a validated backtest and is not real-money-eligible. The institution-risk boundary is equally explicit: LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. It does not turn a historical action-zone observation into a default probability, a credit rating, or a trade instruction.

The record before the event

Nedungadi Bank’s first recorded PCA action-zone observation was FY1999, for the period ended 1999-03-31. The status was threshold_1 and the breach was CRAR. The reconstruction assigns 1999-05-30 as the knowledge-time proxy, using the stated period-end-plus-60-day convention where no explicit publication clock is available. The reported lead to default is 41 months.

These dates serve different purposes. 1999-03-31 is a filing-period endpoint, not proof that market participants knew the result that day. 1999-05-30 is a conservative availability proxy, not a verified publication timestamp. 2002-11-02 is the default date. The distinction is material: the reported lead depends on the availability convention, and the dossier says lead times are optimistic.

The Nedungadi Bank replay and the Failure Radar board support only the narrow finding that CRAR was the first action-zone breach captured in this reconstruction. They do not establish the full path of asset deterioration, management action, supervisory intervention, depositor behavior, or funding conditions between the observation and default.

The record does not mark Nedungadi as fraud-masked. Still, the framework cautions that filings later shown to be falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. That is why a forensic screen owns disclosure deception rather than the threshold logic. No filing-based system can observe what disclosed data omit.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens fired first because CRAR crossed an action-zone threshold. The funding lens was not scoreable: it has no first signal and no funding lead-time result. This is missing-data disclosure, not evidence that funding was healthy, stable, or irrelevant.

That difference matters. The PCA lens is a filing-based supervisory-threshold signal. The funding lens requires a usable disclosed liability series. In the historical funding summary, 10 of 15 failed institutions had liability disclosures; a funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures suggest that funding disclosures can add warning where they exist. They do not make absent disclosures reassuring.

The PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions, of which 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. It is a public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA/SAF tripwires, not a causal study. Timing begins at an exact publication time when present, or the period-end-plus-60-day proxy otherwise. The historical validation record preserves that condition.

The broader India diagnostic includes 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. But it carries the same construction-PIT limitation: no bitemporal input contract, no validated-backtest eligibility, and no real-money eligibility. A useful historical pattern is not automatically a live, tradable signal.

Why the warning mattered

A capital breach matters because it identifies reduced loss-absorbing room under a supervisory framework. In mechanism terms, less capital capacity can constrain management options, sharpen supervisory attention, and make confidence more consequential. Funding pressure may then follow, or may become observable only later.

Nedungadi supports that conditional mechanism only in a limited sense. The capital breach is observed. The funding lens is unavailable. The record therefore permits: capital weakness was the first captured warning. It does not permit: capital weakness caused every subsequent development, or funding stress was absent.

This is also why the absence of a funding alert cannot be read as an all-clear. “Unscoreable” is not “safe.” It means there is no eligible funding inference from the disclosed series. The distinction is the core editorial lesson of the case.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case is strong enough to defeat any deterministic thesis. A CRAR threshold can identify supervisory concern without measuring severity, persistence, recoverability, or the route to eventual default. A 41-month interval weakens claims of imminence. And the availability date is partly derived from a filing-period proxy, so even the apparent lead may be optimistic.

The model evidence is also insufficient for a failure-forecast claim. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score reached 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only.

The counter-case wins whenever the replay is presented as a dependable prediction engine. The evidence supports an observed warning order, not a reliable timetable, causal proof, or investable forecast.

What today's board shares

The current Failure Radar is dated 2026-10-18. Its displayed institution filings are as of 2026-03-31 and aged 7 months. It shows 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions, with no red or orange names; 35 institutions were excluded as stale. These are published screening outputs, not credit ratings.

The market layer is separately as of 2026-10-16 and retrieved on 2026-10-18. Its clock is fresh, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25, and display rights are not approved for every expected record. Thus no market-price signal may validate or alter a LiquiLens tier here. The market evidence index is evidence of a separate layer, not authority to publish derived institution-level market conclusions.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if prospectively time-stamped filings show that capital action-zone breaches add no earlier or more useful warning than eligible funding disclosures, forensic evidence, or other published components. It also fails if exact publication timestamps erase the apparent advantage created by the period-end proxy.

A credible test requires a bitemporal input contract, prospectively frozen inputs and outcomes, and missing liability series retained as missing. It must test the signal after applying the forensic boundary, rather than treating disclosure-based compliance as a complete account of risk.

Follow the pressure chain

The products answer distinct questions. LiquiLens addresses institution and lender balance-sheet risk through LiquiLens investigations. Seiche addresses system dollar-funding capacity through the Seiche overview. Undertow addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity through the Undertow board.

They are not interchangeable scores. Seiche’s current context is low confidence because a source or engine fault reduced its evidence set. Undertow labels UST STRAINED while other segments are NORMAL or PARTIAL. Neither is used in LiquiLens institution scoring. The US NDFI watch is likewise a separate disclosure-based watch, not evidence about Nedungadi.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies only on the Failure Radar board, historical validation, Nedungadi replay, market evidence index, Seiche overview, Undertow board, and US NDFI watch.

The historical record is construction-PIT, lacks a bitemporal input contract, and may overstate lead times. Missing funding evidence is not reassurance. A filing-period observation is not a market-price signal; a model derivation is not an observed fact. Nedungadi’s capital breach is therefore a meaningful historical warning sequence, not a current forecast.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Madhavpura replay: the warning a disclosure screen could not honestly give
entry.summary: Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank is classified as fraud-masked. Its record does not establish an early warning from either the PCA-style or funding lens; it establishes a boundary between reported filings, market prices, and model output.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank’s recorded default date is 2012-06-04; this article was published on 2026-10-17.*

Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank presents the hardest version of LiquiLens’s desk question: which institution balance sheet should feel financial stress first, and why? The honest answer cannot be manufactured from an incomplete record. The dossier classifies Madhavpura as fraud-masked, records no PCA first action-zone date or lead-month measure, and says the funding lens is not scoreable.

That does not mean the institution was sound before its recorded default. Nor does it show that a public disclosure model detected the problem late. It means the supplied evidence does not support either claim. A filing-period signal describes what an eligible disclosed record produced. A market-price signal describes repricing in a market series. A model derivation combines admitted inputs under stated rules. None can repair a compromised or unavailable institution-level disclosure record.

The record before the event

Madhavpura is classified as an urban co-operative bank, with a recorded default date of 2012-06-04. The dossier marks it fraud-masked. No institution-specific filing as-of date is supplied. That absence matters: a missing publication or filing date cannot be converted into proof that the reported position was stable, timely, or representative of the economic position.

The PCA replay records no first action-zone breach and no measured lead for Madhavpura. The funding lens is explicitly not scoreable, with no first signal and no lead time. Those are eligibility and observability results, not negative findings on financial stress.

The framework’s method note identifies the central problem directly: an institution whose filings were later shown to have been falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. In that circumstance, the apparent filing result concerns the disclosed record, not necessarily the underlying balance sheet. The forensic screen, rather than a ratio threshold, owns that limitation.

The Madhavpura replay and the failure-radar board retain the classification without inventing a pre-event chronology. That restraint is the point. Nothing in the dossier permits an assertion that Madhavpura cleared a stress test, escaped a warning, or had no funding pressure.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens supplies no usable first-warning sequence for this institution. It is a filing-period lens: its relevant observation is whether disclosed and eligible inputs meet an action-zone rule. For Madhavpura, the dossier does not report the first action-zone date or a lead-month measure. There is therefore no institution-specific PCA timing claim to make.

The funding lens is even more limited. It is not scoreable because the required liability disclosure series was unavailable to that lens. An unscoreable funding result is not evidence of secure funding. It says that the model’s required input was not available in a form that made the institution eligible for the calculation.

Neither result is a market-price signal. The record supplies no admitted Madhavpura market-price measure, drawdown, or market-derived tier. A market price, where properly authorized, could show investor repricing; it would not by itself verify the balance-sheet condition. Here, it is absent as institution-specific evidence.

The wider historical summaries are useful context but cannot be used to fill Madhavpura’s missing fields. In the PCA summary, 15 failed institutions are included, 5 entered the action zone first, and median lead is 41 months. In the funding summary, 15 failed institutions are included, 10 have liability disclosures, 4 had the funding signal fire first, and median lead is 38 months. Those are replay summaries for their eligible samples, not proof that either lens warned on this fraud-masked case. The historical validation record is the appropriate source for that distinction.

Why the warning mattered

The warning in this replay is methodological rather than predictive. A reported capital, asset-quality, liquidity, or funding measure is an observation from a filing-period record. It is not automatically a verified statement about the economic balance sheet. Where the disclosed record is compromised, a threshold result can be accurately calculated and still fail to describe the underlying condition.

A model derivation has a separate boundary. It may fuse eligible components for presentation, but it cannot infer reassurance from unavailable inputs. It cannot transform an unscoreable funding series into a calm funding finding, and it cannot interpret an unreported PCA event date as evidence that no stress existed.

That is why fraud masking must remain visible. Folding such cases into a simple success or failure count would exaggerate what the screen observed. Madhavpura is not evidence that the PCA lens warned first, that funding warned first, or that either lens had a measured lead. It is evidence that disclosure integrity comes before any model claim.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat an overbroad thesis: disclosure screens should not be expected to reveal information that was concealed, unavailable, or not eligible for their rules. Their performance should be judged on the disclosed records they can actually observe.

There is supportive, but bounded, evidence for usefulness in observable cases. The India evidence index covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet the same evidence is identified as a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and does not have a bitemporal input contract.

Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic. That qualification can defeat any claim that the reported lead is equivalent to a tradable or contemporaneously knowable warning. The PCA and funding summaries therefore demonstrate conditional historical signal behavior, not a clean real-time record and not a Madhavpura-specific detection.

The counter-case is stronger than a disclaimer: public disclosures may be useful when disclosures are credible and eligible, while being unable to penetrate a fraud-masked record. Madhavpura does not disprove the lenses. It does disprove the claim that their non-signal was reassuring.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this historical replay. As of 2026-10-17, it shows 0 red institutions, 0 orange institutions, 1 yellow institution, and 2 green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow with a score of 77.8. Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green with scores of 96.5 and 97.1. Their filing as-of date is 2026-03-31, and each is 7 months old on the board date.

The board excludes 35 stale institutions. Exclusion is not a safety finding. The method does not present quarterly filings older than 183 days or annual filings older than 400 days as current, and institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design.

The market layer is fresh on its own clock, with an as-of date of 2026-10-15, but it has no publication authority and no tier authority. It has 0 admitted canonical records out of 25. Yahoo Finance daily closes may be available as market data, but this package is not approved to create or support a displayed tier. The market evidence index documents that boundary.

The next falsifiable test

This interpretation would weaken if preserved pre-default disclosures established that Madhavpura crossed the PCA-style action zone before 2012-06-04. It would also weaken if a qualifying liability series produced an earlier funding signal under the stated rule. Either result would create a measured institution-specific lead that the current dossier does not provide.

The opposite result would also be informative. If the historical record continued to contain no usable eligible disclosures for either lens, fraud masking and missing eligibility would remain the better explanation for the non-signal. That would not establish that every fraud-masked institution behaves alike. It would preserve the narrower claim about this case and this record.

Follow the pressure chain

The required sequence is disclosure integrity, lens eligibility, filing-period signal, model derivation, authority, and only then an institution-risk conclusion. Madhavpura breaks that chain at disclosure integrity and funding eligibility. A non-reported PCA timing field and an unscoreable funding field cannot be recast as a calm balance sheet.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. Those are distinct research boundaries, not interchangeable evidence categories. The Seiche overview and the Undertow board can provide separate system or exit context, but cannot substitute for Madhavpura’s missing institution-level evidence.

Sources, method, and limits

The principal sources are the Madhavpura replay, failure-radar board, validation record, and market evidence index. Readers can also consult LiquiLens research and the replay archive.

The tier framework is a screen, not a credit rating or a prediction of failure. Its conformal alarm is diagnostic only and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Construction-PIT lead times use a 60-day filing-lag convention where no explicit publication time is present and are labelled optimistic. Missing evidence is not calm. Fraud masking is not a model pass. This is research, not investment advice.

entry.title: First Leasing’s replay marks the boundary where a balance-sheet warning can fail
entry.summary: The case does not identify current default risk or establish a timely historical signal. It shows why a threshold screen cannot treat apparently compliant disclosures as proof of safety when the underlying record is fraud-masked.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. First Leasing Company Of India defaulted on 2013-12-02; the current Failure Radar board is dated 2026-10-16, the market layer is as of 2026-10-15, and publication is dated 2026-10-16.*

The answer to the desk question is deliberately uncomfortable. This record does not show that First Leasing’s balance sheet should have felt financial stress first. It shows a harder proposition: a disclosure-driven balance-sheet screen can appear reassuring when its source disclosures fail to represent the condition the screen is meant to measure.

First Leasing is marked fraud-masked. Its PCA replay has no first action-zone entry and no lead-time observation. Its scoreable funding lens has no first signal and no lead-time observation. Those absences are not evidence of resilience. They establish only that these mechanical lenses did not document an earlier warning in the supplied replay.

The record before the event

First Leasing Company Of India is classified as an NBFC, with a recorded default date of 2013-12-02. The fraud-masked designation is central to interpretation, but it should not be inflated into a complete reconstruction of the event. The validation material says filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that problem.

This historical evidence is classified as PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not eligible for validated backtesting or real-money use, has no bitemporal input contract, and uses a 60-day filing-lag assumption when an explicit publication clock is unavailable. Availability is assigned using an explicit publication clock when present, otherwise period end plus 60 days. Lead times are explicitly optimistic.

The dossier provides neither a separate filing as-of date nor a line-by-line First Leasing filing history. That missing evidence must remain missing. It cannot be converted into a claim that an unobserved disclosure was timely, complete, or benign. Readers can examine the First Leasing replay alongside the wider LiquiLens replay archive.

What the lenses saw

Neither the PCA lens nor the funding lens produced a documented first signal for First Leasing. In a conventional screen, no breach might be treated as benign. Here it cannot carry that meaning. A PCA or supervisory-action lens responds to disclosed tripwires. A funding lens sees only institutions that disclose a liability series. Neither independently verifies the truthfulness of its inputs.

The funding limitation is observable in the historical summary: 10 of 15 failed institutions had liability disclosures. The PCA summary reports that 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary reports 4 first funding signals, with a median lead of 38 months. These are descriptive replay results, not promises that either lens will warn on every institution or every failure.

Their timing also inherits the explicit publication-clock rule or the 60-day proxy. These are filing-period signals under a construction-PIT framework. They are not market-price signals, and they do not prove tradable advance knowledge. The historical validation record preserves those eligibility limits.

Why the warning mattered

The analytical chain is narrow. A threshold model can classify only disclosed balance-sheet conditions. If disclosed asset quality, capital, liquidity, or liabilities do not represent underlying claims, the model may not fire. A clean result can mean no disclosed breach; it cannot prove no economic breach.

That distinction separates observation from derivation. A filing-period signal is constrained by what was published and when it was available. A market-price signal reflects a separate repricing process, where such data are authorized for use. A model tier is a derivation from published components: a published rule over published components, not an independent observation. It is not a credit rating, a finding of fraud, or a prediction of default.

The India construction record covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. First Leasing belongs at the boundary of that result, not inside a comforting reading of it. The case is fraud-masked, while the headline result specifically concerns non-fraud failures. The market evidence index retains the construction label and the eligibility limitations.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat an inflated thesis. A fraud-masked label does not prove that ordinary balance-sheet thresholds were useless, nor that a forensic overlay would have supplied a timely and usable warning. The dossier does not provide the First Leasing filing series needed to reconstruct a discrepancy line by line. It also does not establish a causal sequence beyond the default date, the fraud-masked classification, and the absence of documented first signals in these lenses.

The broader model evidence does not cure that gap. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The comparator heuristic records 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only.

The counter-case therefore lands: this replay cannot validate a timely warning for First Leasing. It may be no more than an example of a screen lacking the inputs needed to see a hidden problem. But that conclusion does not establish calm. Missing mechanical signals cannot validate the absence of underlying stress where disclosure integrity is itself at issue.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a live verdict on First Leasing. As of 2026-10-16, it contains 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions, with no red or orange institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow with a score of 77.8. Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green with scores of 96.5 and 97.1. Their as-of date is 2026-03-31 and their age is 7 months. The board excludes 35 stale institutions.

Those are filing-period disclosures presented under current board rules, not market-price confirmation. The Failure Radar board carries a critical exclusion: institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. Nothing there is scored from memory.

The market layer is fresh in clock terms, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority. Rights approval, display-use approval, model-gate approval, and tier-use approval are absent; admitted canonical records are 0/25. Fresh data without authorization is not an authorized tier input. A market reading may be visible as knowledge, yet remain unavailable for publication or model use.

The next falsifiable test

This thesis fails if prospective, independently verified records show that forensic exceptions add no useful warning beyond action-zone and funding measures. It also fails if reconciled disclosures show that the fraud-masked designation does not distinguish cases in which threshold inputs were materially misleading.

A meaningful test requires publication-time source capture rather than period-end proxies, auditable asset and liability series, explicit missing-data treatment, and a prospectively frozen forensic rule. It must preserve the distinction between a filing-period observation, a market-price observation, and a model derivation. Until then, the responsible output is uncertainty, not a claim of detection skill.

Follow the pressure chain

The research boundary is explicit. Seiche: system dollar-funding capacity. LiquiLens: institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Undertow: market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are different observations with different failure modes.

Seiche’s system view is context only for this purpose; it is not used in the institution score. Undertow’s market-liquidity board concerns executable exit capacity, not whether a lender’s disclosed balance sheet is accurate. Plumbing pressure, institution risk, and exit conditions may interact, but none substitutes for another.

Sources, method, and limits

The supplied sources are the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, the First Leasing case file, and LiquiLens research.

The methodology does not present quarterly filings older than 183 days or annual filings older than 400 days as current. Failed institutions are replayed on the Evidence tab instead. Components are replayed independently on the 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings can remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. In this case, market-derived display is not approved for every expected canonical record. Those safeguards limit what the system claims to know; they do not repair falsified inputs. That is the durable lesson of First Leasing’s replay. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: IL&FS replay: a funding warning preceded the event, but fraud limits what the screen could know
entry.summary: IL&FS’s disclosed funding lens registered before the recorded default, while no PCA action-zone entry appears in the replay. That is a filing-period signal under a proxy clock—not a market-price signal, a forecast, or proof of causation.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

This is a historical replay, not current news, a forecast, or investment advice. IL&FS’s recorded default date is 2018-08-28. The contested proposition is narrow: within the disclosed data used here, IL&FS’s funding lens registered before any recorded formal action-zone entry. It does not follow that default was inevitable, that the signal revealed the full cause, or that an investor had a tradable warning.

The record carries an overriding qualification: IL&FS is fraud-masked. A balance-sheet screen can process disclosed series; it cannot recover facts absent from, or distorted in, those disclosures. The distinction between a filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and a model derivation is therefore central rather than semantic.

The record before the event

IL&FS is classified as an NBFC. Its funding lens first registered a watch-band reading at the 2015-03-31 period end, with an index of 45.4 and no listed flags. The replay assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2015-05-30, yielding a recorded lead of 38 months to default.

That date is not a verified observation timestamp. The construction rule uses an explicit publication clock where one exists; otherwise it applies period end plus 60 days. This makes 2015-05-30 an availability convention, not evidence that every observer received, interpreted, or could have acted on the disclosure then. The historical evidence is explicitly labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, lacks a bitemporal input contract, and warns that lead times are optimistic.

The PCA record is different: IL&FS has no recorded first action zone and no PCA lead time. That absence cannot establish that supervisory measures were irrelevant. It may mean that no public action-zone event was captured; it may also reflect missing or misleading public evidence. Fraud masking makes both explanations live possibilities.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a filing-derived vulnerability: a watch-band index in a disclosed liability series. It did not see a market-price confirmation. The market layer is a separate data product, sourced from Yahoo Finance daily closes, and its readings are not authorised for publication, model gates, signals, or tiers in this dossier. Freshness alone is not authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25, while display and tier use remain unapproved. See the market evidence record.

Nor is the filing reading itself a calibrated failure probability. The dossier says PD levels are corpus-fitted and prior-corrected to a 0.25%/yr population base rate, while the Merton PD is a market repricing signal rather than a calibrated failure frequency. The IL&FS watch reading is therefore neither a quoted market judgment nor a claim that a specified probability of failure was known.

Across the historical funding summary, 15 institutions failed, 10 had usable liability disclosures, and the funding signal fired first in 4 cases. Median lead was 38 months. Those results support investigation of disclosed funding structures, but not universal coverage: the lens can only operate where a liability series is available. The historical validation record retains that eligibility boundary.

A broader India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. But it is also construction-PIT, not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and not bitemporal. Those are limits on the result, not boilerplate beneath it.

Why the warning mattered

A funding warning matters because liabilities can require continuing confidence and refinancing while assets may not convert into cash on matching terms. A disclosed liability pattern can therefore merit scrutiny before a formal action-zone measure appears in a public record.

For IL&FS, the defensible conclusion is limited: the funding lens identified its earliest designated disclosed stress evidence at the 2015-03-31 period end, using the 2015-05-30 proxy clock. It was earlier than any recorded PCA action-zone entry because the record contains none. That does not prove the funding signal caused the subsequent default or that it was sufficient to diagnose the institution.

Fraud masking is decisive to interpretation. The PCA summary states that filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine, and that the forensic screen owns those cases. A compliant-looking disclosed ratio is not proof of a sound underlying balance sheet. Equally, a visible funding warning can be partial, distorted, or incidental to facts the disclosed series could not show.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. The apparent 38-month lead may largely be a construction artefact. A period-end plus 60-day proxy is not a complete historical information set, and the dossier explicitly calls lead times optimistic. A full bitemporal archive could shift the availability date, alter the observed sequence, or remove the apparent advantage.

Coverage is a second challenge. Only 10 of 15 failed institutions had usable liability disclosures. A lens that excludes institutions without that series cannot establish that funding risk ranks reliably across all institutions. Missing data must remain missing; it cannot be recoded as a healthy balance sheet.

Third, IL&FS is fraud-masked. The screen may have detected a real disclosed vulnerability, but it cannot establish whether that vulnerability was the dominant mechanism, nor reconstruct unavailable facts. The missing PCA lead is likewise not evidence that PCA-type conditions were absent. The thesis survives only as a prompt to examine disclosed funding, not as a model victory.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an IL&FS call. As of 2026-10-15, it shows 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions, with no red or orange names. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8; Annapurna Finance Private Limited is green at 96.5; Arohan Financial Services Limited is green at 97.1. Their filing as-of date is 2026-03-31 and their age is 7 months. The board excluded 35 stale institutions rather than presenting them as current. Consult the Failure Radar board.

These are published-rule screens, not ratings or predictions. A tier can reflect level, deterioration, a funding flag, a forensic indicator, or an authoritative market drawdown. But market-derived tier authority is absent here. A market price may be fresh and still be unusable for a published institution tier when admission and display rights are not approved.

The next falsifiable test

The proposition fails if prospectively clocked disclosures show that funding-watch readings do not precede independently established stress more reliably than no such reading, after fraud-masked cases and missing liability series are handled explicitly. It also fails if a complete bitemporal record materially changes the IL&FS ordering.

A credible test would retain exact publication times, preserve unavailable liability series as missing, and test the funding lens against formal action-zone and forensic screens rather than blending them. The existing hazard exercise is insufficient for promotion: its temporal AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate, and construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote.

Follow the pressure chain

The chain begins with disclosed liabilities, then asks whether refinancing and liquidity-management capacity become vulnerable, and only then considers whether mismatched asset and liability timing could constrain payment capacity. IL&FS supplies an early filing-period link in that chain. It does not supply every intervening fact, and fraud masking prevents a complete causal reconstruction.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are adjacent questions, not interchangeable evidence. The IL&FS replay, research archive, and investigations archive provide the appropriate institution-level handoff; the Seiche overview and Undertow board are context, not substitutes for it.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the Failure Radar board, validation endpoint, and market evidence endpoint, alongside the LiquiLens replay archive. The relevant historical signal period end is 2015-03-31; its availability proxy is 2015-05-30.

The historical replay is construction-PIT, not a validated backtest or real-money evidence. The market layer is fresh by its own clock but lacks admission, publication, and tier authority. Fraud-masked, missing, stale, future-dated, and unclocked evidence are limitations—not reassurance. The appropriate conclusion is disciplined: IL&FS makes disclosed funding worth investigating early, while showing why public balance-sheet screens cannot claim to see what the records do not reveal.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Religare Finvest’s replay shows a funding warning before default—and why it was not enough
entry.summary: A watch-band funding signal preceded Religare Finvest’s default in a historical replay. Fraud masking and proxy timing make the case an investigative prompt, not a validated forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines information around Religare Finvest’s default on 2018-01-18; similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

Religare Finvest is the balance sheet that should have felt financial stress first in this replay only in a limited sense: its disclosed funding profile entered a watch band before the event. The first signal was for 2016-03-31, with an index of 44.3 and a proxy knowledge date of 2016-05-30. The recorded lead is 19 months.

That is a filing-period signal, not a market-price signal and not proof that a model derived a tradable failure forecast. It is also not a claim about the institution’s concealed condition. Religare Finvest is marked fraud-masked. Filings later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; disclosures can reveal pressure while failing to reveal the facts that matter most.

A tier is a screen, not a credit rating. This is research, not investment advice.

The record before the event

The replay records a watch-band funding signal with no additional listed flags. Where no explicit publication clock exists, the construction treats information as available at period-end plus 60 days. The 2016-05-30 date is therefore a knowledge-time proxy, not evidence that every participant had the information then.

The historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Its lead times are explicitly described as optimistic. The 19-month interval is a reconstructed filing-timeline result, not an investable timestamp.

The PCA record supplies neither a first action-zone entry nor a PCA lead time. Funding, rather than a documented PCA action-zone signal, is the lens that fires first in this case. Readers can inspect the Religare Finvest replay and the wider failure-radar board.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens can see only institutions that disclose a liability series. Among 15 failed institutions in the historical summary, 10 had usable liability disclosures. The funding signal fired first in 4, with a median lead of 38 months. That is limited evidence of a potentially useful lens, not universal coverage.

The PCA or SAF-style replay also covers 15 failed institutions. It records 5 action-zone-first cases and a median lead of 41 months. Its own note identifies the crucial limitation: falsified filings can look compliant to a threshold engine, leaving forensic work to address what disclosed ratios cannot see.

The hazard results reinforce restraint. Leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752 across 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. A heuristic scored 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC was 0.645, below its 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only. The validation record does not support calling this a validated predictive machine.

Why the warning mattered

A funding warning can matter before failure because liabilities must be rolled, renewed or replaced while asset outcomes remain uncertain. That is a balance-sheet mechanism, not an assertion that a watch reading establishes insolvency. A weaker disclosed funding position may leave less room for refinancing strain, delayed recoveries or loss of confidence.

The signal therefore justified investigation of funding resilience. It does not identify the relevant instruments, counterparties, asset losses, transactions or causal sequence behind the default; the dossier does not provide them. Fraud masking is decisive here: the visible balance sheet may not have been the actual balance sheet.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case defeats any broad predictive thesis. This is retrospective pattern recognition around a known default, timed with a period-end plus 60-day proxy when an explicit publication time is absent. The resulting lead may be optimistic.

The usable funding sample is narrow, the hazard interval is wide, and the temporal diagnostic missed its stated gate. A reasonable sceptic can conclude that 44.3 was an observation worth investigating, not sufficiently specific evidence that Religare Finvest would default.

Fraud masking strengthens that objection. A filing-based threshold cannot measure concealed facts merely because it later appears near a failure. The defensible conclusion is narrower: a disclosed funding concern preceded the event, while the full causal explanation lay beyond this screen’s observable information.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this replay. As of 2026-10-14, it has 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions, with no red or orange names. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8; Annapurna Finance Private Limited is green at 96.5; Arohan Financial Services Limited is green at 97.1. Their listed filings are as of 2026-03-31 and 7 months old.

The board excludes 35 stale institutions. Quarterly filings older than 183 days and annual filings older than 400 days are not presented as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. Missing evidence is not evidence of calm.

A market layer exists, dated 2026-10-13 and retrieved on 2026-10-14, but it has no publication or tier authority. Admitted canonical records are 0/25, and display rights are not approved for every expected record. The market-evidence endpoint may document market-derived observations, but cannot support a published market tier here.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if a prospective, explicitly time-stamped filing record finds that liability warnings do not precede independently observable funding deterioration or later distress more often than comparable institutions without warnings. It also fails if accepted forensic evidence finds no relationship between disclosed funding measures and actual funding capacity in fraud-masked cases.

A meaningful test needs explicit publication clocks, a bitemporal input contract and prospectively frozen rules. It must distinguish missing liability data from stable disclosed funding. Until then, this is diagnostic evidence, not a tradable forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

The pressure chain is plausible but not deterministic: liability disclosures may indicate funding vulnerability; vulnerability may reduce balance-sheet room; reduced room may amplify asset-side uncertainty; fraud masking may make every visible link incomplete. The replay supports the first link, not every later one.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; its overview is context, not an institution score. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity; its board is likewise a separate market-price and exit-capacity diagnostic. These boundaries prevent system context or market structure from being presented as proof of institution-level failure.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the supplied dossier and permitted sources, including the failure-radar board, validation material, Religare Finvest replay, LiquiLens research, and the NDFI watch endpoint.

The relevant filing period is 2016-03-31; its proxy knowledge date is 2016-05-30; the default date is 2018-01-18. These are distinct from current-board and market dates. The record preserves period-end proxy timing, the 60-day filing lag, optimistic lead times, missing liability disclosures, fraud masking, stale-data exclusions, and absent market publication and tier authority. It is a framework for harder questions, not a claim that an unflagged institution, missing data or a green tier is safe.

entry.title: Global Trust Bank’s earliest disclosed warning was capital and asset quality, not funding
entry.summary: The replay finds CRAR and NNPA action-zone breaches before Global Trust Bank’s default. That is a filing-period signal, not market confirmation or a validated model forecast; fraud masking limits what the disclosures can establish.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Global Trust Bank before its default date of 2004-07-24. This is research, not investment advice, and it is not a credit rating.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is Global Trust Bank. Its disclosed record first showed stress through CRAR and NNPA, which jointly breached the PCA action-zone criteria for the period ended 2002-03-31. The funding lens was not scoreable and produced no first signal.

That finding needs strict limits. It is a filing-period signal reconstructed from reported information. It is not a market-price signal, because no authorized market reading supports the conclusion. Nor is it a model derivation that forecasts default. Global Trust Bank is fraud-masked, meaning a threshold engine can only process the reported record; it cannot establish that reported figures were truthful or complete.

The record before the event

The PCA replay places Global Trust Bank in an action zone at the 2002-03-31 period end, on CRAR and NNPA breaches. Its knowledge-time proxy is 2002-05-30, and the recorded lead to the 2004-07-24 default date is 25 months.

That lead is not a tradable timetable or a claim that every action-zone breach ends in failure. The underlying construction is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. The subject record is available in the Global Trust Bank replay and the broader screen is available on the Failure Radar board.

Where no explicit publication time exists, the record uses period end plus 60 days. That is an availability convention, not evidence that an investor, creditor, depositor, or supervisor knew the information at the reporting date. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic. An economic condition, a report date, and an observer’s usable knowledge are different clocks; collapsing them would overstate what this replay demonstrates.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens supplied the first usable disclosed warning: simultaneous CRAR and NNPA breaches. The funding lens did not. It was not scoreable, had no first signal, and has no reported funding lead-month measure for this institution.

That absence is an eligibility disclosure, not reassurance. The funding framework only sees institutions that disclose a liability series. It cannot establish stable liabilities, easy refinancing, or the absence of liquidity pressure when the required disclosed series is unavailable. In this case, capital and asset-quality disclosures were usable; funding evidence was not.

Fraud masking makes that distinction more important. The validation record says that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine, with the forensic screen owning that problem. Here the reported ratios nevertheless breached the PCA lens. But the result is not a forensic reconstruction of the bank, nor proof that the disclosed record captured all relevant stress.

The broader historical summaries are similarly constrained. Of 15 failed institutions in the PCA summary, 5 entered the action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary covers 10 failed institutions with liability disclosures; 4 had the funding signal fire first, with a median lead of 38 months. These are descriptions of a limited construction record, not probabilities for a current lender. The historical validation record retains the eligibility conditions behind those figures.

Why the warning mattered

The significance of the paired breach is modest but useful. The disclosed record showed both asset-quality pressure and a capital-related supervisory tripwire. That combination provided a usable balance-sheet warning before the funding lens could be scored.

It does not establish a complete causal chain to default. The replay does not identify unreported funding conditions, prove the timing of off-record pressures, or demonstrate that a different intervention would have changed the outcome. Nor does it show that capital and asset quality always lead funding stress. It only shows which disclosed lens produced the earlier recorded warning for this subject.

The appropriate conclusion is therefore comparative, not absolute: on this record, the PCA lens warned before the available funding lens because the latter was unavailable for scoring. Funding was not cleared; it was unobserved by this framework.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat any stronger thesis. The record relies on a period-end proxy and, where needed, a 60-day filing-lag convention. It lacks a bitemporal input contract, is ineligible for validated-backtest and real-money use, and labels lead times optimistic. A real-time observer may have possessed later, less complete, or less reliable information than the replay implies.

Fraud masking is a still deeper objection. If filings were later shown falsified, reported ratios cannot be treated as a complete account of the economic balance sheet. The bank may have been weaker or stronger than the disclosures suggested. The replay identifies where the disclosed record raised concern, not when every relevant fact became knowable.

Model results do not repair this limitation. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, after 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and remains diagnostic only; the heuristic comparison is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Those results cannot promote this construction replay into live predictive authority.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from the Global Trust Bank replay. It has 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions, with no red or orange names. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8. Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green at 96.5 and 97.1. Their filing as-of date is 2026-03-31, their age is 7 months, and no signals fired are listed.

Those rows are not solvency judgments, forecasts, or credit ratings. The board excludes 35 stale institutions rather than presenting old filings as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory.

The market layer is present but has no tier authority. It is as of 2026-10-09 and was retrieved on 2026-10-13, yet it has 0 admitted canonical records out of 25. Display, model-gate, and tier-use approvals are not granted. The market evidence endpoint is context rather than an authorized live-tier input. A market-price signal is distinct from a filing-period signal, and none is used to support the historical conclusion here.

The next falsifiable test
