Its display and rights approvals are absent, and it has no tier authority. A current market-price context cannot be retrofitted into the IL&FS filing replay.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate current snapshot as of 2026-10-04: 0 red, 0 orange, 1 yellow, and 2 green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with a score of 77.8, using a filing as of 2026-03-31 that is 7 months old. Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green, at 96.5 and 97.1. No displayed institution has fired signals listed.

These are published-rule outcomes over published components, not inherited lessons from IL&FS. The board excludes 35 stale institutions. Nothing older than 183 days for quarterly filings or 400 days for annual filings is presented as current. Institutions without vetted public dossiers are absent by design; absence is not a calm signal.

The market evidence index remains context only. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings can remain visible but have no signal or tier authority; here, even fresh market records are not authorized for publication or tier use.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if prospectively collected, properly time-stamped filings show that funding-watch conditions do not precede subsequent institution-specific pressure more often than comparable institutions without those conditions. It also fails if actual publication timestamps erase the lead attributed to period-end proxies.

A credible test needs fresh vetted liability disclosures, a predefined observation horizon, and prespecified handling of missing, stale, future-dated, and unclocked inputs. It should compare funding warnings with PCA or SAF signals and with the disclosure-score heuristic. If funding adds no timely, reproducible information under that design, IL&FS should remain a historical anecdote rather than an operating thesis.

Follow the pressure chain

Begin with the liability disclosure: a funding watch may indicate reduced flexibility. Then seek corroboration in prudential or forensic evidence. Only after that should a reader consider an authorized market-price input. The sequence prevents a filing-period observation from being mistaken for either a current price verdict or a model-derived certainty.

The product boundaries are deliberate. LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. System or exit conditions may provide context, but they are not institution-specific verdicts and are not used in the Failure Radar score.

Sources, method, and limits

The relevant materials are the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence index, IL&FS replay, LiquiLens research, and LiquiLens investigations.

Components are replayed independently on the construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation. The conformal alarm is diagnostic; its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Missing evidence, fraud masking, stale inputs, and unclocked inputs require restraint. They do not justify an inference of calm.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Religare Finvest’s funding watch was early—but fraud masking limits what the replay can prove
entry.summary: The historical replay records a liability-side watch before Religare Finvest’s default. It also shows why a filing-period signal is neither a market-price signal nor proof that a disclosure-based model can see concealed facts.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

*This is a historical replay, not current news or a forecast. This is research, not investment advice, a credit rating, or a recommendation. It examines disclosed information before Religare Finvest’s default; similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.*

Religare Finvest is a useful test of a narrow proposition: a funding-related disclosure signal can arrive before a default. It is not evidence that a model diagnosed the whole cause of failure. The subject is marked fraud-masked, which is the central constraint on this replay rather than a footnote. A threshold engine working from public disclosures can register a visible condition while missing concealed facts that later change the interpretation of those disclosures.

The case therefore separates three things that are too easily blended. A filing-period signal is an observation derived from reported information at a reporting date, assigned an availability time by an explicit publication clock where available or by a filing-lag proxy. A market-price signal is a separate repricing observation. A model derivation is the rule that transforms admitted inputs into an index, score, or tier. None is, by itself, proof of causality or a failure forecast.

The record before the event

Religare Finvest defaulted on 2018-01-18. The funding lens first signalled for the period ending 2016-03-31, when its index was 44.3 in the watch band. The replay assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2016-05-30, using the stated period-end plus 60-day convention where no explicit publication clock is present. The resulting historical lead is 19 months.

That chronology should not be rewritten as a claim about an investor’s actual information set. The filing-period observation is dated 2016-03-31; the model’s availability convention dates its usable proxy to 2016-05-30. The default date is an event date. These are construction points in a replay, not a real-time trading record.

There is no first action-zone result for Religare Finvest in the PCA replay. The Religare Finvest replay and the Failure Radar board preserve that absence rather than filling it with inference. The fraud-masked designation matters because filings later shown to have been falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. The dossier assigns that blind spot to the forensic screen, not to a capital or funding threshold.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens recorded a watch condition from a relevant liability disclosure series. It did not establish why that condition existed, identify concealed facts, or demonstrate that default was inevitable. Its result is a filing-period signal: an index reading derived from a disclosed liability series and made available under the replay’s timing convention.

The PCA lens did not provide a first action-zone signal in this case. That contrast permits only a modest inference: these lenses are not interchangeable. A funding lens and a regulatory-trigger replay use different inputs and test different conditions. The absence of a PCA first signal does not prove that funding was universally earlier, or that PCA was incorrect.

Across the historical validation summary, 15 failed institutions are listed. Of those, 10 had liability disclosures, the funding signal fired first for 4, and median lead was 38 months. The PCA summary also covers 15 failed institutions; 5 entered the action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. These are descriptive replay results, not validated trading or real-money results. The underlying validation record is more useful than a simplified win-rate claim.

The broader India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it is explicitly a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Its lead times may be optimistic.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it was visible before the event under the stated replay convention. That is the entire defensible historical result. It identifies a pre-default liability-side condition that deserves review; it does not establish the economic mechanism behind it.

The stronger but unsupported formulation would be that the model “called” the failure. The dossier does not support that. Fraud masking means the public record may not have represented the underlying state accurately. A model can be early about a disclosed condition and still be incomplete about the institution’s actual condition.

Nor should this filing-period signal be conflated with a market-price signal. The current market layer is sourced from Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, but has no admission, publication, or tier authority. It is not evidence about Religare Finvest’s historical signal, and it cannot repair a disclosure-based forensic blind spot.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. Religare Finvest may show that a reported funding condition preceded default without showing that the condition was the principal cause, the cleanest early warning, or a usable prospective indicator. If disclosures were compromised, the observed watch could be a partial symptom of deeper concealed problems rather than a reliable causal signal.

The missing PCA first action-zone result strengthens that challenge. A skeptic can reasonably conclude that the funding flag was incomplete and that the replay cannot rank it above every other lens. The historical hazard work adds a separate restraint: temporal AUC was 0.645 against a 0.65 diagnostic gate, which it did not pass. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote into authoritative tiering.

This is the appropriate conclusion: the replay shows an early disclosed funding watch in a fraud-masked case. It does not validate a general prediction rule, establish causality, or demonstrate forensic detection.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this historical replay. As of 2026-10-03, the filing-based board has 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow; Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green. Their filings are as of 2026-03-31 and aged 7 months. The board excludes 35 stale institutions rather than presenting old disclosures as current.

The market pack is as of 2026-10-01 and was retrieved on 2026-10-03. It is fresh by its clock, but admitted canonical records are 0/25. Rights, display, model-gate, and tier approvals are not present for every expected record. Accordingly, market-derived readings have no admission, publication, signal, or tier authority. Missing, stale, future-dated, or unclocked data are not evidence of calm.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche’s overview covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow’s board covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. Those are distinct research boundaries, not substitutes for one another.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis would weaken in a prospective cohort with a bitemporal input contract if funding-watch conditions did not precede subsequent balance-sheet stress more often than comparable no-signal cases. It would weaken if exact publication times erased the apparent lead created by the period-end plus 60-day proxy.

A forensic test is harder and more important. If later-established falsification repeatedly leaves funding and regulatory lenses apparently calm until the event, that would confirm the disclosed limitation: threshold engines cannot infer facts absent from trustworthy inputs. That outcome would not vindicate the screen.

Follow the pressure chain

The appropriate handoff begins with the disclosed funding watch, then asks whether the filing record is fresh, vetted, and sufficiently trustworthy for the reported condition to bear interpretation. It then keeps the institution record separate from system funding and exit-liquidity context.

Readers can inspect historical mechanisms in the replay library, examine current institution work in LiquiLens investigations, and consult the research archive. The sequence is diagnostic, not promotional.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies on the Failure Radar board, the historical validation record, the market evidence index, and the Religare Finvest replay.

Historical evidence is period-end-proxy construction PIT. Explicit publication time is used when present; otherwise availability is period end plus 60 days. Lead times may therefore be optimistic. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic only and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design and are not scored from memory.

The conclusion is deliberately narrow: Religare Finvest’s disclosed funding signal was historically early under the replay convention. Fraud masking means that result was insufficient to penetrate concealed facts, and it must not be treated as a forecast, rating, market-price signal, or proof of causality.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Global Trust Bank’s earliest disclosed warning was a balance-sheet breach, not a market signal
entry.summary: The replay finds a PCA action-zone entry before Global Trust Bank’s default, led by CRAR and NNPA breaches. But fraud masking, proxy timing, and missing funding data make this a triage lesson—not a validated forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Global Trust Bank’s pre-event disclosures and does not infer that similar mechanisms will produce the same outcome elsewhere. The historical record is construction-PIT, not a validated backtest or a real-money signal.*

The narrow thesis is that Global Trust Bank’s first disclosed institutional warning appeared in its balance-sheet record: an RBI PCA action-zone entry associated with breaches in CRAR and NNPA. That is a filing-period signal. It is not evidence that a market price warned first, because this case has no scoreable funding signal and the current market layer cannot be used to support an institutional claim. Nor is it proof that a model predicted failure. The replay uses a period-end availability proxy and explicitly labels its lead times optimistic.

The decisive limitation is fraud masking. A threshold engine can identify pressure in reported measures, but cannot establish that the reports were complete or truthful. This is therefore a useful case for separating disclosed stress, price-based evidence, and model construction from hindsight.

The record before the event

Global Trust Bank defaulted on 2004-07-24. The record places its first PCA action-zone entry at the 2002-03-31 period end, identified as FY2002. The status was threshold_2; the recorded breaches were CRAR and NNPA. Using the dossier’s knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30, the replay reports a 25-month lead to default.

That lead is not an observed trading-time advantage. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the framework uses period end plus 60 days. The relevant historical status is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT; there is no bitemporal input contract, no validated-backtest eligibility, and no real-money eligibility. The record says directly that lead times are optimistic.

Still, the filing-period result has analytical content. The PCA lens recorded a joint capital and asset-quality breach before the event. It says the disclosed balance sheet had crossed a supervisory-style threshold, not that every investor, depositor, creditor, or market participant possessed the same information at the same instant. The Global Trust Bank replay and Failure Radar board preserve that distinction.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens is the only lens that produces a first signal in this case. Its action-zone record combines CRAR and NNPA breaches. Within the replay, that is the basis for saying that disclosed balance-sheet stress arrived before the default.

The funding lens does not offer a rival chronology. Global Trust Bank is marked unscoreable for funding, with no first signal and no lead time. That should not be translated into evidence that funding conditions were benign. It means the liability-disclosure series did not permit scoring. Missing data is neither a clean negative signal nor permission to fill the gap with narrative.

The forensic limitation is more important still. Global Trust Bank is explicitly fraud-masked. The validation record states that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine, and that the forensic screen owns that problem. In this instance, the PCA signal can show what the disclosed measures indicated; it cannot certify the integrity of those measures.

The broader summaries are descriptive context, not a probability model. The PCA replay covers 15 failed institutions, with five entering an action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also covers 15 failed institutions, but only 10 had liability disclosures; four saw the funding signal fire first, with a median lead of 38 months. The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. It retains the same construction-PIT, proxy-availability, and optimistic-lead-time warnings. See the validation record and market evidence index.

Why the warning mattered

The significance of the joint breach is not that a threshold mechanically causes default. It is that the reported record placed asset quality and capital resilience under simultaneous scrutiny. A CRAR breach concerns the disclosed capital cushion; an NNPA breach concerns disclosed net non-performing assets. Together, they identify a balance-sheet condition that warranted closer examination before the event.

That is a triage conclusion. The signal directs attention to the reported loan book, provisioning, capital capacity, supervisory thresholds, disclosure credibility, and the unavailable funding lens. It does not supply an event chronology, assign causality, or establish that the reported breach alone determined the outcome.

The proper hierarchy is therefore clear. The filing-period signal is the PCA entry. A market-price signal would require authorized market evidence and a separate price-based interpretation. A model derivation is the replay’s application of rules and timing conventions to its historical inputs. Treating any one of those as the other would overstate the record.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat a stronger version of the thesis. The apparent 25-month lead may exaggerate usable foresight because it begins with a period-end proxy and a 60-day filing-lag convention where an explicit publication clock is absent. Without immutable historical vintages and a bitemporal contract, the replay cannot prove the information set available on each decision date.

The diagnostics do not rescue that claim. The leave-one-institution-out hazard result reports row AUC of 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. Its heuristic comparator has AUC of 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reports AUC of 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only. These outputs may be informative construction checks, but they are not a promotion path to validated prediction.

Fraud masking is the deeper objection. A disclosure-driven engine cannot see through false, incomplete, stale, or unavailable inputs merely because its thresholds are well specified. The case can support the modest statement that disclosed PCA stress preceded the event in this replay. It cannot support a claim that the system would reliably uncover concealed weakness or issue a tradable failure call.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this replay. As of 2026-10-02, it shows no red institutions, no orange institutions, one yellow institution, and two green institutions. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with a score of 77.8 and a 2026-03-31 as-of date. Annapurna Finance Private Limited and Arohan Financial Services Limited are green, with scores of 96.5 and 97.1. The displayed filings are seven months old, and 35 stale institutions are excluded.

Those rows are not analogues of Global Trust Bank. Belstar has no listed fired signals and no market drawdown in its comparison row. The current market layer is fresh and clock-authorized, but lacks display, admission, publication, model-gate, and tier approval. It has admitted canonical records of 0/25. It therefore cannot substantiate a present institutional-risk claim.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct products, evidence types, and authority boundaries.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis should fail if a prospective record with actual publication timestamps and immutable vintages finds that joint PCA-style CRAR and NNPA breaches do not precede independently observed institutional stress after fraud-masked cases, unavailable liability series, and stale filings are separated. It should also weaken if verified disclosures show that such breaches routinely resolve without subsequent pressure over the applicable observation horizon.

The reverse is not a rerun of this replay. Credibility would require prospective evidence, explicit publication clocks, complete eligibility rules, preserved missing-data treatment, and a clear distinction between disclosure signals and market signals. Replacing the period-end proxy with auditable availability is the test.

Follow the pressure chain

Begin with the reported assets and asset-quality measures. Then ask whether the reported capital measure has crossed the relevant action-zone threshold. Next, determine whether liability disclosures actually support a funding assessment; for Global Trust Bank, they do not. Finally, test whether the disclosures themselves deserve confidence. In a fraud-masked case, apparent calm in a reported component is not a clean bill of health.

The handoff should remain disciplined: use LiquiLens for balance-sheet review, Seiche for broad dollar-funding context, and Undertow for market exit conditions. Do not fuse their outputs into one failure verdict.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only recorded dossier outputs: the Global Trust Bank replay, Failure Radar board, historical validation output, market evidence record, Seiche overview, and Undertow board. Further desk material is available through LiquiLens research.

The historical evidence remains PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, not validated-backtest eligible and not real-money eligible. The funding lens is unscoreable for Global Trust Bank. Fraud masking limits every disclosure-based inference. Current market data may be visible in the underlying system, but its authority gates prohibit its use here as institutional proof. These limits are central to the conclusion, not footnotes to it.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Altico’s funding warning arrived before the event—but the replay is a diagnostic, not a forecast
entry.summary: Altico’s disclosed commercial-paper reliance appeared well before its default. The chronology supports a funding-risk hypothesis, but the construction-PIT record cannot validate a real-time forecast.
entry.content:
*This is not current news and is not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Altico, which defaulted on 2019-09-12. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution or in another market.*

The balance sheet likely to feel stress first is not necessarily the lender with the weakest-looking assets. It may be one that must repeatedly refinance when confidence changes. Altico is a bounded example. Its earliest recorded funding signal was commercial-paper reliance of 29% at 2017-03-31, labelled rollover-freeze exposure. The funding index was 23.7, while the band was stable. That is a filing-period signal about disclosed liability structure—not evidence that a crisis had begun, and not a market-price signal.

The replay assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2017-05-30, using period end plus 60 days, and records a 27-month lead to default. That sequence is informative but not investable proof. The historical record is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, lacks a bitemporal input contract, is not eligible as a validated backtest or real-money record, and explicitly says lead times are optimistic.

The record before the event

Altico’s scoreable funding lens, rather than its PCA field, supplies the earliest recorded warning. The PCA record has no first action zone and no PCA lead-month value. The funding flag says only that commercial-paper reliance created rollover-freeze exposure. Its stable band is an important restraint: a visible vulnerability is not equivalent to an imminent failure call.

The wider summaries establish possibility, not a universal ordering. Of 15 failed institutions in the PCA summary, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. Of the same 15, 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months.

Those results are reconstructions under filing-availability assumptions. They cannot establish that every relevant disclosure was available to a decision-maker at the reconstructed time. The Failure Radar board and historical validation record retain that eligibility boundary.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a disclosed liability mix: commercial paper represented 29% at the cited period end. A lender dependent on repeated issuance has a specific vulnerability if refinancing becomes unavailable. It may need replacement cash or other balance-sheet actions under time pressure.

But the dossier does not identify a particular creditor, failed issuance, liquidity reserve, asset-quality trend, management action, or contemporaneous market repricing. It does not establish that every proposed step in a pressure chain occurred at Altico. The correct reading is narrower: disclosed funding dependence preceded a recorded default.

The PCA lens did not offer an earlier action-zone signal here. That does not prove funding measures are superior to supervisory-style tripwires. It shows that the lenses address different failure pathways and can disagree in timing.

Nor should disclosed-data screening be mistaken for forensic detection. The validation note says filings later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine, with the forensic screen owning those cases. Altico is not fraud-masked in this dossier. That classification does not turn absent evidence into evidence of calm.

Why the warning mattered

Commercial paper can be efficient in ordinary conditions. Its distinctive risk is not simply cost; it is the need to obtain market consent again and again. A refusal or delay can compress the time available for balance-sheet decisions before assets run off or other funding is secured.

That creates a plausible chain: refinancing reliance can create rollover risk; rollover risk can force defensive liquidity or asset actions; those actions can affect confidence; weaker confidence can make subsequent refinancing harder. This is a model derivation from a disclosed liability structure, not a demonstrated causal narrative of Altico’s final months.

The distinction is essential. A filing-period signal identifies what accounts disclosed. A market-price signal would describe repricing in traded instruments. The dossier supplies the former for Altico, not the latter. A model derivation explains why the disclosed feature might matter; it must not be presented as an observed event.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case defeats any simple thesis. A 29% commercial-paper share may be a manageable funding choice rather than a precursor to distress. A lender may roll paper reliably, hold liquidity, use alternative funding, or manage asset and liability timing in ways this observation cannot see. Altico’s stable band supports that caution.

The aggregate evidence is also limited. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with an interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic AUC was 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC was 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only.

The counter-case is therefore central: Altico may be an intelligible historical chronology without being reliable evidence that comparable commercial-paper reliance predicts failure elsewhere. The construction-PIT diagnostic cannot promote into a forecast claim.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from the Altico replay. As of 2026-10-01, it contains 1 yellow institution and 2 green institutions: Belstar Microfinance Limited, Annapurna Finance Private Limited, and Arohan Financial Services Limited. Their cited filing date is 2026-03-31 and their age is 7 months. Their scores are 77.8, 96.5, and 97.1, respectively; no signals fired are listed.

Yellow is not a credit rating or a prediction of failure. Under the published rule, it may reflect deterioration, a level threshold, a funding flag, a forensic indicator, or a fresh authoritative market drawdown condition. The board excludes 36 stale institutions. Its method does not present quarterly filings older than 183 days or annual filings older than 400 days as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing is scored from memory.

Market data were as of 2026-09-30 and retrieved on 2026-10-01. The market layer is fresh and clock-authoritative, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority. Admitted canonical records are 0/25, while display rights and expected-record approvals are absent. It cannot upgrade the current tier story. See the market evidence record.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if future vetted disclosures show comparable refinancing reliance commonly persisting without liquidity strain, or if stressed institutions more often lack prior disclosed funding vulnerability. It also fails as a useful model if a prospective bitemporal dataset finds no discrimination beyond simpler disclosed-data heuristics.

A credible test needs actual publication times rather than the period-end-plus-60-days proxy, preserved missing disclosures, and outcomes unavailable when a signal was formed. It must not assign model or tier authority to unapproved market data. Until that work exists, historical lead times remain reconstructions rather than promises.

Follow the pressure chain

The product boundaries are deliberately separate. LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity.

These questions can move together without becoming interchangeable. System funding conditions are not an institution filing signal. An institution’s disclosed liability structure is not a traded-market price. Exit capacity is not proof of either balance-sheet solvency or refinancing access. The LiquiLens research archive is a research record, not a substitute for those distinctions.

Sources, method, and limits

This article draws on the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, Altico replay, and replay archive. Publication date: 2026-10-01.

Altico’s filing observation is 2017-03-31; its availability proxy is 2017-05-30; its default date is 2019-09-12. Current institution filings cited here are as of 2026-03-31, while the market layer is as of 2026-09-30. This is a bounded historical interpretation of disclosed-data diagnostics. Its construction-PIT, missing-data, staleness, fraud-masking, rights, and authority limits are part of the finding, not footnotes to it. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Abhyudaya’s replay: an asset-quality breach arrived before the recorded event
entry.summary: Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank entered an RBI action zone on disclosed NNPA before its recorded default date. The replay is a filing-period signal, not a market-price call or a live forecast—and its proxy clocks materially limit the claim.
entry.content:
This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank’s recorded default date is 2023-11-24. The narrow proposition is that its first disclosed RBI action-zone breach was an asset-quality signal that appeared before that event. It is not proof that the breach caused the outcome, that the signal was tradable, or that another institution with a similar disclosure will fail.

Three categories must remain separate. A filing-period signal records what a disclosed balance-sheet measure showed for a reporting period. A market-price signal records repricing in traded instruments. A model derivation turns inputs into a score, tier or diagnostic. They may point in the same direction, but they do not share an observation clock, an evidentiary status or a causal meaning. This article concerns the first category: a disclosure-based replay.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. It is not a credit rating and this is not investment advice. The supporting record is available at the Abhyudaya replay and the Failure Radar board.

The record before the event

The first recorded action-zone entry was for the period ending 2021-03-31, identified as FY2021. The recorded breach was NNPA. The replay applies a knowledge-time proxy of 2021-05-30: an explicit publication clock when present, otherwise period end plus a 60-day filing-lag proxy. On that convention, the interval to the recorded default date is 29 months.

That is a constructed chronology, not a preserved contemporaneous market record. The historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and does not have a bitemporal input contract. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic. A period-end measure can be economically relevant before it is publicly available; conversely, a proxy availability date cannot demonstrate when every creditor, depositor or market participant understood its significance.

Abhyudaya is not fraud-masked in this record. Its funding lens was scoreable, but it has no first funding signal. That leaves the NNPA breach as the earliest recorded signal in this replay, not as confirmation that funding conditions were calm or that the asset-quality measure contained the entire explanation.

What the lenses saw

The PCA/SAF lens saw an NNPA breach. The funding lens did not fire first. That asymmetry is the case’s usable observation: this disclosure framework identified stress first on the asset side.

The broader PCA summary includes 15 failed institutions. Five entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also includes 15 failed institutions, but liability disclosures exist for 10; a funding signal fired first for four, with median lead of 38 months. These are replay descriptions, not failure probabilities, and they do not establish that one lens should always lead another.

The India evidence index covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. That headline carries the same construction-PIT qualification. The validation record reports a temporal AUC of 0.645 against a 0.65 gate. The gate did not pass; construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote.

A model derivation adds another layer of restraint. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, nine events and 27 institutions, after 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, while the heuristic comparison is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Those figures describe a limited diagnostic exercise. They do not validate a live ranking, and they do not improve the evidentiary status of Abhyudaya’s filing-period breach.

Why the warning mattered

An NNPA breach can matter because asset impairment may reduce a lender’s tolerance for further deterioration. It can make earnings, capital, funding confidence and management options more consequential. But the ratio itself is not a mechanism that mechanically causes default. The replay supports a sequence—disclosed asset-quality stress before the recorded event—not a complete causal account.

The published quadrant rule treats any RBI action-zone breach as red. That is a rule-based response to a supervisory threshold, rather than a claim that a fused score is more authoritative than the underlying breach. In Abhyudaya’s case, the rule directs attention to a disclosed constraint on the balance sheet.

The warning therefore mattered as a scrutiny trigger. It said the institution’s asset side had crossed a stated threshold. It did not say when a final event would occur, whether a market instrument should reprice, or whether the liability side would become the immediate source of pressure.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis: the apparent lead may be largely a hindsight artefact created by proxy dating. Where no explicit publication clock exists, the record uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier calls the resulting lead times optimistic. A later adverse event can make an earlier ratio look more decisive and more actionable than it was in real time.

There is also no independent market-price confirmation available for publication. The market layer is fresh and clocked, but admitted canonical records are 0/25. Rights, display, model-gate and tier-use approvals are absent, and the layer has no admission, publication or tier authority. It must not be used to infer whether securities markets confirmed, anticipated or rejected the filing-period signal.

Nor does the absence of a funding signal resolve that uncertainty. The funding lens sees only institutions with liability disclosures. Missingness is not reassurance. The dossier also warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases.

What today’s board shares

The current board is not an Abhyudaya forecast analogue. As of 2026-09-30, it shows zero red, one orange, three yellow and 15 green institutions among fresh vetted public dossiers. A further 21 institutions were excluded as stale. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory.

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, using a filing as of 2025-03-31, aged 18 months, with score 74.9 and no signals fired. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, using 2026-03-31, aged six months, with score 77.8 and no signals fired. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, using 2025-09-30, aged 12 months, with score 66.0 and no signals fired. These are board entries under published rules, not ratings, predictions or evidence that any named institution resembles Abhyudaya’s path.

The available market layer is as of 2026-09-29 and was retrieved on 2026-09-30. Its lack of publication and tier authority prevents it from decorating those institutional observations with market-price claims.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if prospectively preserved filings with actual publication times show that comparable asset-quality action-zone entries do not provide earlier or more informative warning than other lenses. It weakens as well if timely liability disclosures reliably lead such breaches in the relevant population.

The necessary test is prospective rather than reconstructed: retain original filing vintages, record actual availability times, preserve missingness, and compare the first signal with later stress without letting amended history rewrite the information set. Until that record exists, Abhyudaya is a disciplined historical clue, not a validated forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with the institution replay, then compare the current board and validation file. Keep system dollar-funding capacity separate through Seiche’s overview. Keep market liquidity and executable exit capacity separate through the Undertow board.

That separation prevents a filing-period balance-sheet observation from being mistaken for a system-funding measure or a market-exit measure. A market repricing signal, where authorized and observable, would be a different input. A tier remains a published rule over published components.

Sources, method, and limits

The relevant materials are the Failure Radar board, historical validation file, market evidence index, Abhyudaya replay, Seiche overview, Undertow board, and the LiquiLens research archive.

Abhyudaya’s relevant clocks are 2021-03-31 for the filing period, 2021-05-30 for the knowledge-time proxy, and 2023-11-24 for the recorded default date. Those clocks are not interchangeable. Historical results remain construction-PIT rather than validated-backtest or real-money evidence. The market layer remains visible but unauthorized for publication or tier use. Those constraints are not footnotes; they define the claim that can responsibly be made.

entry.title: United Western Bank’s first disclosed fault line was asset quality, not funding
entry.summary: The replay places an NNPA action-zone breach before United Western Bank’s recorded default, while the scoreable funding lens produced no first signal. That sequence is informative, but its timing is a construction-PIT availability proxy, not a tradable forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines disclosures associated with United Western Bank before its recorded default on 2006-09-02. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution.*

United Western Bank offers a narrow answer to the desk question: the earliest disclosed pressure point in this replay was asset quality. The record identifies an NNPA breach in the PCA action zone for the period ended 2001-03-31, assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2001-05-30, and measures a 63-month lead to default. The funding module was scoreable, yet it produced no first signal.

That is a sequencing observation, not a claim that an NNPA threshold determines failure. A filing-period signal says what a reported balance-sheet measure showed at period end. An availability proxy estimates when that disclosure may have been knowable. A market-price signal would show separate contemporaneous repricing. A model derivation summarizes a rule or statistical relationship built from a dataset. This case supplies the first, proxies the second, does not supply the third, and should not be enlarged into the fourth.

The record before the event

The public-disclosure replay identifies United Western Bank’s first PCA action-zone entry in FY2001, for the period ending 2001-03-31. The stated breach is NNPA. The case is not marked fraud-masked. The replay assigns its knowledge-time proxy to 2001-05-30 and measures 63 months to the default date of 2006-09-02.

Those facts establish an observed order, not inevitability or a complete causal history. The record does not show every later management decision, creditor response, liability movement, recovery path, or shock. Nor does it establish that outside users possessed the same information at the proxy date. A reporting date is not itself a public-knowledge date.

The funding result is limited rather than reassuring. The module was scoreable, but no first signal is recorded. That means the available liability-disclosure lens did not provide the first recorded alert. It does not certify stable funding, exclude later funding stress, or demonstrate calm. The funding lens only sees institutions that disclose a liability series, so missing liability disclosure remains a material boundary rather than a benign result.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw the asset-quality action-zone breach first. In the historical validation summary, 15 failed institutions are included; 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. This is a public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA/SAF tripwires, not a complete account of information available to a lender, depositor, supervisor, or market participant. The underlying framework can be inspected through the failure-radar board and historical validation record.

The funding lens did not fire first here. Across the same summary, 10 of 15 failed institutions have liability disclosures; a funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Funding can therefore lead in observable cases. But the result does not show that funding should have led in this case, because observation depends on disclosure and the available series is not a complete map of all funding channels.

A broader India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports that 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. Its evidence is period-end-proxy construction PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. The evidence index is useful for inspection, but a construction diagnostic is not evidence of executable performance.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it located disclosed pressure in asset quality before the replay recorded a funding alert. That differs sharply from saying funding was already broken. An asset-quality tripwire can identify a balance-sheet area requiring scrutiny before losses, capital pressure, earnings weakness, funding sensitivity, or confidence effects are fully visible in the available record.

The case supports only a modest proposition: the balance sheet that feels disclosed stress first may be the one whose asset-quality threshold has already been crossed, even if another lens is silent. It does not establish a universal ordering among assets, capital, funding, and market pricing. It also does not turn NNPA into a calibrated probability of default.

A market-price signal remains a separate category of evidence. The current market layer uses Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, and is fresh as of 2026-09-28. But market-derived display, admission, model-gate, and tier use lack approval; admitted canonical records are 0/25. Clock and knowledge fields do not authorize publication or tier use. Those governance limits prevent current market data from being retrofitted into this historical case.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. This may be retrospective pattern recognition: because United Western Bank later defaulted, an earlier breach can appear more decisive after the fact than it was when disclosed. The replay uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. Its evidence states that lead times are optimistic. Actual availability could differ from the assigned proxy.

The threshold may also not have been the most informative signal in a fully reconstructed record. Funding could have deteriorated through channels not captured by the disclosed liability series. Other facts may have been known to creditors or supervisors. The absence of a first funding signal is therefore missing explanatory power, not affirmative evidence of resilience.

The model record adds restraint. The temporal diagnostic reports an AUC of 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and does not pass. The hazard result reports AUC of 0.752, while the comparison heuristic reports 0.799 on the same held-out rows. These are model derivations and diagnostics, not grounds to promote the replay into a validated prediction engine.

Threshold systems also cannot uncover concealed facts. The PCA note says filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. United Western Bank is not fraud-masked, but that limitation still constrains the inference.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate screen, not an extension of the United Western replay. As of 2026-09-29 it has 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 are excluded as stale. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on 2025-03-31 and aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, based on 2026-03-31 and aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, based on 2025-09-30 and aged 12 months.

These classifications are published rules over components, not forecasts. The rule can incorporate level, deterioration, funding, forensic, market, or RBI action-zone conditions. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design rather than scored from memory. Current board context is available from the failure-radar board.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis should fail if prospectively clocked filings show that action-zone asset-quality breaches do not precede later balance-sheet stress more reliably than competing signals after disclosure becomes available. It should also fail if usable liability disclosures show funding signals consistently arriving first in comparable cases, or if bitemporal validation removes the apparent lead.

A meaningful test needs explicit publication times, preserved revisions, rules fixed before outcomes are known, and retained missing-data exclusions. Until then, the 63-month lead is an informative replay measure, not an estimate of what an investor could have earned or avoided.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct research boundaries, not interchangeable labels.

For this case, begin with the disclosed asset-quality threshold; then ask what the record can and cannot say about capital, earnings, and funding; then separate institutional facts from market exit conditions. The United Western replay belongs to the first task. The Seiche overview and Undertow board address different questions and cannot be fused into one unsupported verdict.

Sources, method, and limits

Sources include the validation record, evidence index, United Western replay, LiquiLens research, and LiquiLens investigations.

The historical evidence is period-end-proxy construction PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise period end plus 60 days. Lead times are optimistic. Those limitations are the boundary of what this replay can claim.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Sambandh Finserve’s funding signal arrived early—but could not see through fraud
entry.summary: The historical replay identifies wholesale leverage as Sambandh Finserve’s first disclosed funding warning. It is a liability-side clue, not a market verdict, a causal proof, or a validated prediction of default.
entry.content:
*This is not current news and is not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Sambandh Finserve, which defaulted on 2020-10-13. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The balance sheet that should have felt pressure first was Sambandh Finserve’s funding structure. The evidence does not show that a model foresaw default, or that a market price confirmed an approaching event. It shows something narrower: on 2016-03-31, disclosed wholesale leverage was 8.51x, above the funding lens’s 7x flag, and the lens classified the institution as fragile.

Under the replay’s availability convention, that filing-period observation became knowable on 2016-05-30, using period end plus a 60-day proxy where an explicit publication clock is unavailable. That is 52 months before the default date. It is an early filing-derived signal. It is not evidence that creditors repriced Sambandh on that date, nor proof that the disclosed leverage caused the eventual failure.

The crucial complication is that Sambandh is fraud-masked. Where filings were later shown to be falsified, threshold engines can make an institution look compliant. A leverage flag can identify vulnerability in what was disclosed; it cannot recover risks concealed from disclosure. The forensic screen owns that blind spot.

The record before the event

Three clocks must remain separate. The reporting period ended on 2016-03-31. The construction-PIT proxy places public availability on 2016-05-30. The institution defaulted on 2020-10-13. Treating the first date as immediate public knowledge would overstate what an outside creditor, investor, or analyst could have known.

The funding record supplies one stated first flag: wholesale leverage 8.51x >= 7x. The band is fragile. The PCA record has no first action-zone entry and no recorded lead months. That absence is not a clean bill of health. It means only that this replay does not identify a PCA action-zone signal before the event.

The historical evidence is explicitly PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and does not have a bitemporal input contract. Its availability basis is an explicit publication clock when present, otherwise period end plus 60 days. Lead times are therefore optimistic. This is a disciplined reconstruction of a possible information set, not a verified record of every participant’s information set.

The Sambandh replay is consequently more useful as a question for due diligence than as a retrospective claim of foresight.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a liability-side exposure: reliance implied by elevated wholesale leverage. The economic proposition is conditional. A lender with greater refinancing dependence can be more sensitive to creditor confidence and rollover conditions. If refinancing capacity contracts, liquidity preservation or balance-sheet adjustment can become more urgent. The dossier does not establish the specific creditor actions, liquidity movements, or operational sequence between the flag and default.

The PCA lens did not provide a recorded action-zone lead. The funding signal therefore stands alone as the first visible balance-sheet warning in this case. It should not be inflated into confirmation from a second lens.

Nor does the broader model stack repair that gap. The conformal alarm remains a diagnostic, while its historical tier wiring is suspended pending prospective revalidation; it has no score or tier authority. The hazard temporal test recorded AUC of 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and did not pass. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote.

Those are model-derivation facts, not market facts. They describe how the analytical apparatus performed on its limited record. They do not report a traded price, a creditor withdrawal, or an independently observed funding squeeze.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because funding fragility can be visible before a public case for failure is established. Reported asset stress may emerge slowly, while a wholesale-funded institution can remain exposed to a change in creditors’ willingness to extend or renew financing.

Yet “mattered” must not become “predicted.” Wholesale leverage above a threshold identifies a reason to investigate the funding stack, its maturity profile, creditor concentration, refinancing options, and the quality of the underlying disclosures. It does not establish an imminent event. The 52-month interval is especially important: the record supports an early vulnerability signal, not a timing tool.

The wider funding summary reinforces that restraint. Among 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures usable by the funding lens. The funding signal fired first in 4 cases, with median lead of 38 months. Those are descriptive results from disclosed series, not a calibrated probability of default. The historical validation record preserves those eligibility limits.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. Wholesale leverage may be too broad and too slow-moving to support a decision beyond additional investigation. It fired first in only 4 cases in the disclosed-liability record, and Sambandh’s fraud-masked status makes the reported balance sheet an unusually weak basis for a complete diagnosis. If the core condition was concealed, the signal may have described only a peripheral vulnerability.

The long gap to default further weakens any claim of near-term usefulness. A flag that precedes an event by 52 months may distinguish fragility from resilience, but it may also impose years of false urgency. The period-end proxy can also manufacture apparent lead: a fully bitemporal record could materially change when information was actually available.

A sceptical reader can therefore conclude that the replay offers no verified causal chain, no validated trading or credit signal, and no proof that public disclosures revealed the institution’s true condition. That conclusion is compatible with the narrower thesis: the disclosed liability structure was worth examining earlier than the eventual default alone would suggest.

What today's board shares

Today’s Failure Radar is dated 2026-09-28 and should not be merged with Sambandh’s historical filing record. It reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange as of 2025-03-31; Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of 2026-03-31; ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow as of 2025-09-30. A further 21 institutions are excluded as stale.

The current board presents one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier; nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Its tiers are published rules over published components, not credit ratings or failure forecasts. See the Failure Radar board.

Market data were fresh as of 2026-09-25, but their display, admission, model-gate, tier-use, and publication permissions were not approved for every expected canonical record. Admitted canonical records were 0/25. Market-derived display therefore has no tier authority. Absence of an authorized market signal is not evidence of calm.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if a prospective, fully clocked record shows that wholesale-leverage flags do not precede independently evidenced refinancing pressure, liquidity constraint, or balance-sheet stress more often than comparable institutions without a flag. It also fails if verified publication timestamps erase the apparent lead produced by the 60-day proxy.

A meaningful test needs prospective validation, liability disclosures, publication-time evidence, and separate forensic treatment for fraud-masked institutions. Until then, Sambandh supports an investigative workflow rather than confidence in a predictive model.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are boundary phrases, not interchangeable labels.

Seiche’s overview reports a guarded EROSION read and says divergence is a warning to investigate, not proof of a squeeze; consult the Seiche overview. Undertow marks UST STRAINED, while other segments are NORMAL or PARTIAL; consult the Undertow board. Neither system plumbing nor exit conditions proves Sambandh’s historical mechanism, and neither should be used to retrofit a market-price confirmation that the dossier does not contain.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the Sambandh evidence page, the Failure Radar board, the validation file, and the market-evidence index. Further methodology is available through LiquiLens research and related casework through LiquiLens investigations.

The hard limits are timing and observability. Period-end observations are mapped to explicit publication time when available, otherwise to period end plus 60 days. Fraud masking remains a boundary that a threshold screen cannot overcome. Missing, delayed, stale, future-dated, unclocked, or unauthorized evidence is not evidence of calm. The replay is valuable only if those limits travel with the signal.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: New India Co-operative Bank showed a disclosed stress breach before the event — and the fraud boundary is the point
entry.summary: A historical replay finds an NNPA action-zone breach at the FY2021 period end, ahead of the later default date. It supports investigation of disclosed balance-sheet pressure, not confidence that a threshold screen can see through false accounts.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines the public record before New India Co-operative Bank’s default date of 2025-02-13. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The desk question has a conditional answer. On the disclosed record, New India Co-operative Bank should have drawn attention through an asset-quality signal: an NNPA breach placing it in the RBI PCA/SAF action zone for the period ended 2021-03-31, labelled FY2021. The replay uses 2021-05-30 as its knowledge-time proxy and records a 44-month lead to default.

That is a filing-period signal. It is not proof that the published balance sheet described the institution’s actual condition, and it is not a market-price signal or a model result. The dossier marks this case fraud-masked. That qualification is decisive: a reported threshold crossing warrants investigation, but cannot deliver a forensic account of a bank whose filings may have been unreliable.

The record before the event

Three clocks must remain separate. The filing period ended on 2021-03-31. Where no explicit publication clock is available, the replay uses period end plus 60 days, producing the 2021-05-30 knowledge-time proxy. The default occurred on 2025-02-13. None is a current-market timestamp, or evidence of what management, supervisors, depositors, or counterparties knew privately.

The PCA/SAF lens replays public disclosure against the RBI’s action-zone tripwires. It can identify a reported threshold breach, not establish causation, reconstruct undisclosed cash movements, assess intent, or verify that the reported inputs were true. The New India replay is evidence of what a disclosure screen could flag from the available record.

Fraud-masked is not a footnote. Institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. Even this early visible breach cannot establish whether reported deterioration captured the full problem, its first stage, or only part of it. A disclosure warning can be useful and materially incomplete at once.

What the lenses saw

The PCA/SAF lens saw the NNPA breach. The funding lens produced no first signal for New India. That is missing evidence, not evidence of stable funding: the funding lens only sees institutions that disclose a liability series. No funding signal cannot become a funding all-clear.

Across 15 failed institutions, 5 entered the PCA/SAF action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary has liability disclosures for 10 of those 15 institutions; its signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. These are replay descriptions, not prospective accuracy claims.

The wider India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and says 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it is explicitly PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT: not eligible as a validated backtest or real-money test, without a bitemporal input contract, and with optimistic lead times. The validation record and market evidence index retain those limits.

A model derivation is separate again. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, while the heuristic reaches 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Its temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only. Those results describe a constrained construction exercise; they do not show that New India was predictably destined to fail.

Why the warning mattered

A disclosed action-zone breach changes the question from whether an institution looks routine to whether reported asset quality, loss absorption, disclosure quality, and possible funding vulnerability warrant deeper scrutiny.

If reported condition is genuine, pressure may move from asset quality into loss absorption, confidence, funding, and resilience to further losses. But that is a pressure chain, not a demonstrated causal sequence here. New India has an asset-side warning and no funding first signal. Its fraud-masked designation means disclosures may not have measured the actual condition fully. Investigation, rather than a tidy narrative of linear deterioration, is the warranted inference.

The 44-month lead is both meaningful and hazardous. It identifies an early public point at which the disclosed record crossed a regulatory threshold. But a long replay lead can make a threshold engine appear to have seen more than historical filings could reveal.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat any broad thesis. New India does not establish that disclosed thresholds reliably forecast institutional failure. An NNPA breach is not proof of insolvency, liquidity failure, misconduct, or an impending default. Fraud-masked cases sharpen the objection: a system built from public disclosures cannot claim forensic sight when the disclosures themselves may be unreliable.

Timing is another objection. The replay uses explicit publication time when present and otherwise a period-end-plus-60-days proxy. That can make lead times optimistic. Without a bitemporal input contract, the record cannot prove what a live user could access on each historical date. The conformal alarm is diagnostic, with no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

A later event also does not retroactively prove decision usefulness. The heuristic’s stronger held-out AUC and the failed temporal gate limit the model conclusion. The defensible thesis is narrower: disclosed action-zone pressure is a reason to investigate earlier, while fraud and missing disclosures limit what the investigation can infer.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this replay. As of 2026-09-27, the Failure Radar shows 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months, with a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, based on 2026-03-31 and aged 6 months, with a score of 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, based on 2025-09-30 and aged 12 months, with a score of 66.0.

These are published-rule screen outputs, not credit ratings or forecasts. The board excludes 21 stale institutions. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; absence is not a clean bill of health. The Failure Radar board is not a current extension of the New India case.

The market layer was available as of 2026-09-25 and retrieved on 2026-09-27, but has no admission, publication, or tier authority. Approval checks were incomplete for every expected canonical record. Thus a market-price signal cannot upgrade or downgrade institutional tiers. Fresh prices are not authority to publish a risk classification.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if institutions crossing disclosed action-zone thresholds do not later show persistent, independently disclosed balance-sheet pressure more often than comparable institutions that do not cross them. It also weakens if prospective testing with actual publication timestamps, rather than period-end proxies, fails to retain useful separation.

A persuasive test must distinguish a filing-period signal from a market-price signal and from a model derivation. It must establish what was public, when it was public, whether it was accurate, and whether it added information beyond simpler disclosure rules. A later event alone cannot satisfy those tests.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity.

Those boundaries matter. Seiche’s composite is 41.5 and labelled EROSION, with guarded confidence; its note says slow-moving or modelled structure leads current market confirmation. Undertow contains partial segments. Neither a system-plumbing reading nor an executable-exit reading proves New India’s historical balance-sheet condition, fills an unavailable liability disclosure, or overcomes a fraud-masked filing record.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied evidence dossier and permitted sources, including the New India replay, historical validation, market evidence, LiquiLens research, and the Failure Radar board.

The method is a public-disclosure historical replay. Its construction-PIT status, 60-day filing-lag convention, missing-data limits, fraud-masked designation, and optimistic lead-time warning remain in force. The conclusion is deliberately limited: New India’s disclosed NNPA breach was an early investigative signal in the public record. It was not market-price confirmation, not a validated prospective model result, and not a substitute for forensic verification of the accounts.

Research and market data, not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Nedungadi Bank’s capital breach was the first observable link in a long pressure chain
entry.summary: A historical replay places Nedungadi Bank in an RBI action zone on its FY1999 CRAR disclosure before default. It is a filing-period signal under a proxy clock, not a market-price warning or a calibrated forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. The relevant filing period ended on 1999-03-31; the replay uses 1999-05-30 as its knowledge-time proxy. The separate market-data pack is as of 2026-09-25.*

Nedungadi Bank should have appeared under pressure first through disclosed capital, not through a scored funding signal. The narrow thesis is that its CRAR entry into the first RBI action zone in FY1999 was the earliest observable warning in this replay. It preceded the bank’s 2002-11-02 default by 41 months. That does not prove capital caused the default, establish what market participants knew, or show that an investor could have traded a known outcome.

The distinction is central. The CRAR breach is a filing-period signal, subject to an availability proxy. A market-price signal would require authorised market evidence, and none establishes Nedungadi’s historical pathway. A model derivation is a rule or diagnostic built over observed records; it is not itself an observed event. Conflating these categories would turn a limited replay into a claim it cannot support.

This historical replay is not investment advice and not a credit rating.

The record before the event

The Nedungadi Bank replay records its first PCA/SAF action-zone entry at the 1999-03-31 period end, labelled FY1999. The breach was CRAR and its status was threshold_1. The knowledge-time proxy is 1999-05-30, using the stated 60-day filing lag. The replay’s 41-month lead runs from that proxy date to the recorded default.

That chronology is less certain than its precision may suggest. Historical evidence is classified as PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It has no bitemporal input contract, is not eligible as a validated backtest, and is not eligible for real-money use. When an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the convention is period end plus 60 days. The dossier explicitly warns that lead times may be optimistic.

Thus, 1999-03-31 is an accounting reference date, while 1999-05-30 is an imposed availability convention. Neither proves every participant received the information simultaneously. The Failure Radar board preserves that separation rather than silently treating period-end information as immediately known.

Nedungadi is marked as not fraud-masked. That means this replay does not assign it to the group in which filings later shown to be falsified can make an institution appear compliant to a threshold engine. It does not establish that disclosed information was complete.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw the CRAR breach. The funding lens was not scoreable and produced no first signal. This is a missing-data outcome, not a conclusion that funding was calm, stable, or irrelevant. The funding framework can observe only institutions disclosing a liability series; Nedungadi’s record does not support that lens.

The broader summaries remain bounded. Of 15 failed institutions in the PCA summary, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. In the funding summary, 10 of 15 failed institutions had liability disclosures, 4 had the funding signal fire first, and the median lead was 38 months. These are constrained replay descriptions, not competing failure probabilities or proof that one lens is always earlier.

The hazard work cannot repair this gap. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, and its temporal AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate. The temporal result is diagnostic only; construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote. The validation record documents limitation rather than a performance warrant.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it was a disclosed regulatory tripwire before default, attached to a named measure, period, and availability convention. The replay can say Nedungadi’s CRAR entered an RBI action zone before the outcome. It can also say the funding lens supplied no competing dated signal because that lens was unscoreable.

It cannot complete a causal transmission story. The dossier provides no historical market repricing measure for Nedungadi, no scored funding event, and no evidence identifying the intervening route from CRAR weakness to default. “Capital was first” therefore means first observable within these disclosed and scoreable inputs, not first in the bank’s economic reality.

The rule-based threshold_1 classification is also not a market price. The 41-month lead is a model derivation from a proxy knowledge date and a recorded default date. Neither converts an action-zone breach into a calibrated failure frequency.

The strongest counter-case

A stronger version of this thesis can fail. One action-zone breach in a construction-PIT record may identify regulatory vulnerability while revealing little about timing, severity, or the eventual failure mechanism. A 41-month lead itself argues against interpreting the result as an imminent-event alarm.

The availability convention may flatter apparent warning time. The record lacks a bitemporal input contract and substitutes period end plus 60 days where no explicit publication clock exists. Even that proxy leaves lead times labelled optimistic. Missing funding evidence is equally ambiguous: absent liability disclosure is not absent funding pressure.

If fully timestamped, contemporaneous liability information had generated an earlier warning, the claim that capital should feel stress first would fail. If a market-price measure had repriced before the filing became knowable, it would answer a different question and also defeat any claim that the filing was the first observable warning overall. The defensible conclusion is narrower: capital was the earliest recorded signal in this replay.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a live continuation of Nedungadi. As of 2026-09-26, it contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions, while excluding 21 stale institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 dossier. Belstar Microfinance Limited and ESAF Small Finance Bank are yellow.

These are published-rule screens over vetted public dossiers, not ratings. Yet the current market layer has 0 of 25 admitted canonical records and has no tier or publication authority. It is fresh and clocked, but display and tier use are not approved. The market evidence endpoint records that boundary.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if a prospective, fully timestamped filing record shows that action-zone entry does not precede meaningful balance-sheet stress more reliably than available alternatives when disclosure timing is held constant. It also weakens if institutions with disclosed liability series repeatedly generate earlier usable funding warnings and CRAR adds no incremental diagnostic value.

That test must use actual publication timestamps rather than period-end proxies, preserve missing disclosures as missing, and separate forensic cases in which filings can mask weakness. Until then, this remains a historically grounded mechanism claim, not a calibrated forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

The pressure chain supported here stops at disclosed CRAR weakness, RBI action-zone entry, and eventual default. The funding link is unobserved, not absent. No market-price link is established.

The product boundaries matter: Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk; Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. Seiche’s composite is 41.2 and labelled EROSION, with guarded confidence because slow-moving or modelled structure has not been broadly confirmed by current market plumbing. Undertow reports partial coverage across segments. Neither is evidence about Nedungadi’s historical route. See the Seiche overview and Undertow board.

Sources, method, and limits

Primary material is the Nedungadi replay, the Failure Radar board, and the historical validation endpoint. Further method material is in the LiquiLens research archive.

The decisive limits are construction-PIT historical status, no real-money eligibility, no bitemporal input contract, proxy timing that can leave lead times optimistic, no authorised market-derived tier evidence, and unscoreable funding evidence for Nedungadi. Missing evidence is not calm. It is a boundary on what this replay can claim.

entry.title: First Leasing replay: when a public balance-sheet radar cannot see through the record
entry.summary: First Leasing Company Of India’s fraud-masked default is not an early-warning success. It is a boundary case showing why a filing-period signal, a market-price signal and a model derivation must not be treated as the same evidence.
entry.content:
*Historical replay — not current news and not a forecast.* First Leasing Company Of India defaulted on 2013-12-02. The useful lesson is not that a public screen called the event. The supplied record does not establish that it did. Rather, it shows a harder limitation: an institution can be under severe economic pressure while its reported balance sheet fails to transmit that pressure to a threshold-based public-data system.

The distinction matters for the desk question: which balance sheet should feel stress first, and why? A filing-period signal describes what disclosed reports showed at an available reporting point. A market-price signal describes repricing in tradable instruments, when the market data are authorized for that use. A model derivation combines permitted inputs under a stated rule. None can be silently substituted for another; none proves the underlying economic condition by itself.
