First Leasing is marked fraud_masked in this replay. Its case therefore tests the boundary of disclosed-data surveillance, rather than supplying evidence that an ordinary balance-sheet deterioration was identified in time.

The record before the event

First Leasing Company Of India is classified as an NBFC, with default date 2013-12-02. Its PCA record contains no first action-zone date and no lead-month figure. Its funding record is scoreable, but contains no first signal and no lead-month figure. These are missing replay results, not affirmative findings that funding was calm, capital was adequate or the institution was safe.

The historical framework explicitly warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. That warning is central here. The dossier does not provide underlying accounting particulars that would establish the route from misstatement to default. It does establish that the reported public record did not produce an earlier PCA action-zone entry or funding signal in this replay.

The India evidence is broader but tightly qualified. It covers 48 institutions across two decades, with a headline finding that 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged and median lead was 21.5 months. Yet its status is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT: it is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible and has no bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier says lead times are optimistic. These are diagnostic construction results, not tradable performance evidence. See the Failure Radar board, validation record and First Leasing replay.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens is a public-disclosure replay of the RBI’s PCA/SAF tripwires. Among 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. That is evidence that disclosed supervisory-style thresholds can be informative in some cases. It is not evidence that they identified First Leasing: its supplied PCA fields show no action-zone date and no lead time.

The funding lens is narrower because it requires a disclosed liability series. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. First Leasing is marked scoreable, yet no first funding signal is recorded. That is a non-result in the replay, not a clean bill of health.

A filing-period signal must also be separated from a model derivation. The published rule can fuse disclosed levels, deterioration, a funding flag, a forensic indicator and an authoritative market drawdown into a presentation tier. PD levels are corpus-fitted and prior-corrected to a ~0.25%/yr population base rate using King-Zeng. That makes them model outputs, not direct observations. The conformal alarm is retained only as a diagnostic: its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

A market-price signal is different again. The dossier describes Merton PD as a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. For the current market layer, data are fresh and clocked, but display, model-gate and tier use are not approved; admitted canonical records are 0/25. Market information therefore cannot authorize a current tier in this record.

Why the warning mattered

A reported balance sheet is supposed to connect asset quality, loss absorption and creditor confidence. If losses, impairment or other relevant conditions are not truthfully represented, reported capital and risk measures can remain clear of a threshold. If disclosure does not reveal why liability providers should reassess the institution, a funding lens may not fire either.

That is an inference about the limits of observable inputs, not a reconstructed account of First Leasing’s finances. The dossier supports the narrower conclusion: in a fraud-masked case, apparent compliance in disclosed data may be an artefact of the record rather than evidence of resilience. A missed signal in an honest, timely disclosure regime could challenge the threshold. A missed signal where filings were later shown falsified can instead show that the measured balance sheet was not a reliable map of the institution.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any inflated version of this thesis. Perhaps the framework is simply too weak to identify stress reliably. First Leasing has no recorded PCA or funding lead. Historical availability is sometimes proxied using period end plus 60 days, and the dossier expressly calls the lead times optimistic.

The hazard evidence is also limited. The panel has 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with an interval of 0.338 to 1.0. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC is 0.799, above the hazard AUC. The temporal test has AUC of 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate, and cannot promote construction-PIT diagnostics.

That critique means this replay cannot demonstrate that the radar would have protected a creditor, investor or supervisor. Nor can a fraud_masked label solve forensic identification after the fact. The defensible claim is smaller: the system reports the absence and limits of disclosed signals rather than converting unavailable or compromised evidence into reassurance.

What today's board shares

The board as of 2026-09-25 has 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green; 21 stale institutions are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on a 2025-03-31 filing as-of date aged 18 months, with score 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of 2026-03-31, aged 6 months, score 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow as of 2025-09-30, aged 12 months, score 66.0. Each supplied comparison row lists no fired signals and no market drawdown.

These are current screen observations, not analogues of First Leasing and not predictions. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current, while institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. The current market layer is as of 2026-09-24, but lacks publication and tier authority. Read the market evidence index and LiquiLens research with those restrictions intact.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if a genuinely bitemporal, prospectively audited sample finds that disclosed PCA, funding and forensic signals do not identify pressure before adverse outcomes better than chance. It also weakens if exact publication clocks erase the diagnostic lead, or if fraud-masked cases cannot be distinguished through a documented process independent of the outcome.

It gains credibility only if prospective records preserve what was knowable when, retain missing and stale observations instead of filling them with calm, and separately test filing signals, market-price signals and model derivations. This is not investment advice and not a credit rating.

Follow the pressure chain

The disciplined sequence is reported assets and capital; disclosed liability structure; supervisory-style thresholds; forensic indicators; then market and exit conditions where authority permits. A break should prompt investigation, not automatic certainty.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. Those are product boundaries, not mutual confirmation. The handoff is diagnostic: institution records locate disclosed balance-sheet pressure; system and exit tools ask whether funding conditions or execution conditions corroborate it.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied dossier and linked records: the board, historical validation, replay archive and investigations archive.

The controlling limitation is construction-PIT status. Explicit publication time is used when available; otherwise the replay uses period end plus 60 days. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible and has no bitemporal input contract. Missing evidence is not calm; historical lead times are optimistic; and First Leasing’s fraud-masked status prevents any inference that absent PCA or funding signals described its true condition.

entry.title: Rupee Co-operative Bank replay shows where a balance-sheet warning ends
entry.summary: The record supports a disciplined distinction: a filing-period screen can organize disclosed pressure, but it cannot turn unavailable data, an unapproved market layer, or a modelled diagnostic into proof of the path to failure.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. Rupee Co-operative Bank’s recorded default date is 2022-09-22. The Failure Radar board is as of 2026-09-24; the available market layer is as of 2026-09-23. This article is published on 2026-09-24.*

Rupee Co-operative Bank is a useful test of editorial discipline precisely because it is a failure case with an incomplete replay record. The question is not whether the institution later failed. That is recorded. The question is whether the available evidence establishes which disclosed balance-sheet pressure appeared first, when it became knowable, and whether a market-price or model signal independently confirmed it.

The answer is constrained. The supplied record does not show a first action-zone date, a lead time, a scoreable funding series, or a first funding signal for this institution. Those absences do not amount to evidence of resilience. They also do not license a retrospective claim that the screen warned clearly and early. A historical endpoint cannot repair a missing pre-event chain.

LiquiLens concerns institution and lender balance-sheet risk. It is not a finding about system-wide dollar funding, nor an assertion that a security price supplied a tradable warning. The distinctions matter: filing-period evidence is what disclosures say at, or are proxied from, a reporting period; market-price evidence is a separate repricing observation; and model output is a derivation from its specified inputs and rules.

The record before the event

Rupee Co-operative Bank is classified as a UCB. Its default date is 2022-09-22, and the case is not marked fraud-masked. Yet the PCA record has no first action-zone field and no lead-month measure. The funding lens is explicitly unscoreable, with no first signal and no lead-month measure.

These are not interchangeable non-results. “No recorded first action-zone” means the supplied replay does not establish the first relevant supervisory-threshold entry. “Unscoreable” means the funding lens lacked the liability-series input needed to make its assessment. The latter is missing eligibility, not a negative funding finding.

Nor can the absence of a fraud-masking flag settle why the record is incomplete. It says only that this classification is not present in the dossier. It does not establish fraud, rule it out, or explain any silent lens. The proper conclusion is narrower: the evidence supports inclusion in a historical replay, but not a reconstructed sequence in which a particular disclosed signal led the event.

The timing construction imposes another limit. Historical evidence is designated PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. When an explicit publication clock is absent, the availability rule uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier therefore labels lead times optimistic. That makes this a filing-availability proxy, not proof of what a depositor, investor, or supervisor could have acted upon at every point in real time.

What the lenses saw

For Rupee Co-operative Bank, the action-zone lens does not provide a recorded first breach. The funding lens cannot be scored because the required liability disclosure series is unavailable. The case consequently cannot demonstrate that supervisory thresholds beat funding pressure, or that funding pressure beat supervisory thresholds.

The broader validation record gives useful but limited context. Among 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary covers 10 institutions with liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures describe eligible subsets, not Rupee Co-operative Bank.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. But it carries the same period-end proxy construction and optimistic-lead warning. Its role is to show that disclosed indicators may contain historical information, not to certify prospective performance or convert a named failure into a clean advance call. Readers can inspect the Failure Radar board, validation record, and Rupee Co-operative Bank replay.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because a screen should preserve the difference between pressure detected and evidence unavailable. A filing-based rule can identify disclosed deterioration, threshold conditions, funding flags, or forensic indicators where the relevant inputs exist. It can then direct an analyst to ask whether the institution has a coherent pressure chain rather than treating a tier as a conclusion.

Rupee Co-operative Bank demonstrates the inverse discipline. No scoreable liability series cannot be translated into stable funding. No recorded first action-zone date cannot be translated into an absence of stress. And a later default cannot be translated backward into a proven warning sequence.

That restraint is especially important because the published tier is a rule over published components, not a credit rating and not a failure prediction. The rule defines red, orange, yellow, and green conditions using level, deterioration, RBI action-zone breaches, funding flags, forensic indicators, and authoritative market drawdowns. But the rule cannot manufacture an eligible funding observation for a case that lacks one.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is that a structured replay remains more useful than an unstructured archive. The PCA and funding summaries show substantial median leads in their eligible subsets. The hazard model reports a leave-one-institution-out AUC of 0.752; the stated heuristic comparison is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. That is evidence that the disclosed corpus may carry signal.

The case deserves respect. A repeatable rule can force comparability across filings, distinguish an observed condition from narrative confidence, and make omissions visible. It may be better at generating investigative priorities than retrospective storytelling.

But it can also defeat the thesis if held to its own limits. The panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows are excluded. The temporal diagnostic has an AUC of 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and is diagnostic only. Its construction-PIT status cannot promote it to a validated or real-money result. The counter-case therefore supports continued testing and investigation, not certainty about Rupee Co-operative Bank or a general claim of investability.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate current-screening artifact, not evidence about the historical Rupee event. As of 2026-09-24, it has 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, while Belstar Microfinance Limited and ESAF Small Finance Bank are yellow. The board also excludes 21 stale institutions.

The listed rows must be read with their eligibility disclosures. Utkarsh’s filing is as of 2025-03-31 and is 18 months old. Belstar’s is as of 2026-03-31, and ESAF’s is as of 2025-09-30. Institutions without vetted public dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory. Empty signal lists do not prove calm, and a tier does not settle creditworthiness.

The market layer is fresh on its own clock, but it has no publication, display, model-gate, or tier authority. Although it covers 25 names, admitted canonical records are 0/25 because rights and identity approvals are incomplete. Market-derived display is not approved for every expected canonical record. The market evidence index can establish provenance, not upgrade an institution tier or supply a market-price conclusion for Rupee Co-operative Bank.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if a genuinely prospective dataset with publication timestamps finds that these screens do not identify later pressure within their stated limits, or if apparent leads disappear after replacing the period-end-plus-60-day proxy with actual availability. It also fails for this replay if newly eligible primary disclosures establish a materially different chronology.

The test should freeze rules before outcomes, preserve publication times, retain unavailable fields as unavailable, and assess signals only after the forward observation horizon closes. Until then, historical leads remain diagnostic. This is not investment advice.

Follow the pressure chain

The research boundary is explicit. LiquiLens addresses institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche addresses system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity.

Those are different questions. Seiche’s current read can describe a divergence that warrants investigation without proving an institution squeeze. Undertow can describe partial market coverage without determining a lender’s disclosed capital condition. Conversely, an institution filing screen can justify further work even when market-derived data lack tier authority. The Undertow board and LiquiLens investigations should be treated as distinct analytical handoffs, not confirming votes.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied evidence universe: the board, historical validation, market evidence, Rupee replay, and LiquiLens research.

The central limitation is substantive: this is a period-end-proxy construction with a 60-day fallback filing lag and optimistic historical lead times. Missing liability data are not evidence of stable funding. A missing action-zone date is not evidence that pressure was absent. A visible market layer can still lack admission, publication, and tier authority. Rupee Co-operative Bank is therefore a warning about evidentiary boundaries: a balance-sheet screen can sharpen an investigation, but it cannot create the missing proof of sequence.

entry.title: IL&FS replay: funding signalled early, but disclosure limits defeat any clean verdict
entry.summary: The IL&FS record supports a narrow proposition: a disclosed funding signal can precede default, while fraud masking and proxy timing prevent that signal from becoming proof.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

*This is a historical replay, not current news or a forecast. The relevant filing period ended on 2015-03-31; its knowledge-time proxy is 2015-05-30. IL&FS defaulted on 2018-08-28. The replay is explicitly fraud-masked.*

The uncomfortable answer to LiquiLens’s question is not that one balance sheet was transparently doomed. It is narrower: IL&FS’s disclosed funding lens moved to watch before a recorded public action-zone signal, producing a stated 38-month lead to default. That is a filing-period signal. It is not a market-price signal, and it is not a model-derived probability of failure.

The difference matters. The filing record gives the funding index a value of 45.4 for 2015-03-31, with a watch band and no listed flags. The later default makes that observation worth studying. But the dossier also says the historical construction uses an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise a 60-day fallback; it lacks a bitemporal input contract; and its lead times are optimistic. Fraud masking is the decisive constraint: filings later shown to be falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. A warning may be early without being complete, actionable without being dispositive.

The record before the event

IL&FS is classified as an NBFC. Its funding lens is scoreable, and its first recorded signal belongs to the filing period ending 2015-03-31. The construction assigns 2015-05-30 as the knowledge-time proxy and records the watch index at 45.4. The reported lead to the 2018-08-28 default is 38 months.

That sequence is the historical fact pattern, not an assertion that contemporaneous observers held a full and verified view of the institution. The record has no PCA first-action-zone date and no PCA lead-month value for IL&FS. It therefore supports a comparison between what this funding lens recorded and what this PCA field did not record; it does not establish that supervisory information was absent, nor that a funding signal alone could identify the timing or cause of failure.

The replay is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not eligible for validated backtesting, not eligible for real-money use, and not based on a bitemporal input contract. Readers can inspect the published inputs through the Failure Radar board, the validation record, and the dedicated IL&FS replay.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw the first recorded signal in this case. That is meaningful precisely because it is limited. Across the historical funding summary, there are 15 failed institutions, yet only 10 have liability disclosures. The funding signal fired first for 4, and the reported median lead is 38 months. A lens restricted to institutions disclosing a liability series cannot infer safety from missing disclosure.

The PCA summary has a different pattern: 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. Its stated basis is a public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA/SAF tripwires. This is a different filing-based diagnostic, not private supervisory visibility.

The wider India evidence describes 48 institutions across two decades and reports that 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet the same evidence is construction-PIT and explicitly ineligible for validated backtesting and real-money use. IL&FS belongs to the exception that prevents a triumphalist reading: a fraud-masked institution can appear compliant to any threshold engine. The market evidence index preserves that historical-evidence label rather than converting it into a performance claim.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered as a prompt for investigation, not as a default forecast. The funding lens recorded a liability-side anomaly well before the default date, while the PCA field has no recorded first action-zone event for IL&FS. That divergence makes funding a plausible place to look first when assessing a lender’s disclosed pressure points.

But the chain of inference stops there. A filing-period index is a transformation of disclosed information. The dossier does not present it as a tradable price, a calibrated failure frequency, or a forensic finding. Its methodological note similarly distinguishes corpus-fitted, prior-corrected PD levels from the Merton PD, which is a market repricing signal rather than a calibrated failure frequency. IL&FS’s funding watch must not be relabelled as either.

The case therefore supports a discipline: a disclosed warning should alter questions asked of the balance sheet—whether the liability series exists, how it was timed, and what it cannot see. It cannot certify the truthfulness of disclosure or fill a forensic gap.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. This may be retrospective selection: IL&FS failed, so a prior movement can be made to appear predictive. The evidence itself supplies the reasons for restraint. Availability is sometimes proxied from period end plus 60 days. Original vintages are not preserved under a bitemporal contract. Lead times are labelled optimistic. The historical result has no validated-backtest or real-money eligibility.

Coverage compounds the objection. Only 10 of 15 failed institutions in the funding summary disclosed the relevant liability series, and the funding lens fired first for only 4. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and its promotion effect is none. On the same held-out rows, heuristic AUC is 0.799 and hazard AUC is 0.752; neither comparison repairs the construction-PIT boundary.

Most damaging to any clean thesis, fraud masking means apparent compliance is not evidence that disclosures were true. The defensible conclusion is not that funding screens reliably foresee default. It is that their signals may warrant scrutiny, while their silence and their apparent orderliness cannot establish calm.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an IL&FS forecast. As of 2026-09-23, the Failure Radar has 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on 2025-03-31 information aged 18 months, with a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow on 2026-03-31, aged 6 months, with 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow on 2025-09-30, aged 12 months, with 66.0.

These are published-rule screen tiers, not credit ratings or failure predictions. 21 stale institutions are excluded. The market layer was fresh and clock-authorized as of 2026-09-22, but it has no admission, publication, signal, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25, and display rights are not approved for every expected record. Market-derived display therefore cannot strengthen or weaken these tiers.

The next falsifiable test

The proposition fails if future stressed institutions with fresh, vetted liability disclosures do not show deterioration before independently observable distress or default once genuine availability times are preserved. It also fails if the apparent lead disappears after corrected disclosures, missing-data eligibility, and fraud-masked cases are handled prospectively.

A meaningful test would retain original filing publication times and vintages, declare the eligible liability-disclosure universe before outcomes, and avoid rewiring the tier after the event. Until then, this is a historical diagnostic, not a predictive result.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are connected questions, but they are not interchangeable signals.

Seiche’s composite is 41.5, EROSION, with 100.0% coverage; its editorial confidence is guarded because modelled or slow-moving structure leads current market confirmation. That is not proof of a lender-specific squeeze. Conversely, an institutional filing warning does not prove broad system stress or executable market exits. The appropriate handoff is investigative: use LiquiLens for the institution, Seiche for system capacity, and Undertow for exit conditions. Related work is available in LiquiLens research and investigations.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied dossier and its linked Failure Radar board, validation, market evidence, and IL&FS replay. It is neither investment advice nor a credit rating.

The research boundary is exact: India’s historical evidence is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, with an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise period-end plus 60 days; lead times are optimistic. The institution-risk boundary is equally exact: missing liability data limits the funding lens, fraud-masked institutions can look compliant, and institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. None of those omissions can be converted into reassurance.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Religare Finvest’s funding warning came first—but the replay cannot forecast
entry.summary: A disclosed-liability signal appeared before Religare Finvest’s default date under a conservative availability proxy. The result is a fraud-masked historical sequence, not causal proof, a market verdict, or a tradable forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. The thesis is narrow: on the supplied record, Religare Finvest’s disclosed-liability lens registered before the available action-zone lens. The evidence clock is the filing publication time when available, otherwise period end plus 60 days. The stakes are equally narrow: confusing that reconstructed sequence with a live market signal, a causal explanation, or a prediction would overstate what the evidence can bear.*

The record before the event

Religare Finvest is the desk’s answer only in a defined historical sense. Its funding side is the balance-sheet area that registered stress first in this reconstruction. The first funding signal is attached to the period ended 2016-03-31: an index of 44.3, in the watch band, with no recorded flags. No explicit publication clock is supplied for that observation, so the replay applies its stated fallback of period end plus 60 days. The resulting knowledge-time proxy is 2016-05-30.

The recorded default date is 2018-01-18. The construction therefore records a 19-month lead. The PCA record supplies neither a first action-zone entry nor a lead time. That supports a sequence claim, not a stronger one: among the supplied lenses, the disclosed-liability lens moved first.

The case is fraud-masked. That qualification is decisive. The dossier warns that filings later shown to be falsified can make an institution appear compliant to a threshold engine. Public disclosure can be incomplete or distorted; a visible warning does not establish the full mechanism of failure, and an apparently calm threshold does not demonstrate safety. The Religare Finvest replay is consequently an event reconstruction, while the failure-radar board is a current roster built from vetted public dossiers.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens is a filing-period signal. It uses disclosed liability information and can operate only where a liability series exists. In the historical summary, 10 of 15 failed institutions had such disclosures. The funding signal fired first in 4 cases, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures describe a selected historical disclosure subset. They are not a prospective hit rate and cannot speak for institutions without the relevant series.

The PCA/SAF lens is also filing-based, but it replays public-disclosure versions of the RBI’s own tripwires. Of 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. It measures a different condition from a liability signal. Its apparent ordering against funding cannot establish that one condition caused the other, particularly where fraud may have impaired the reported inputs.

The model derivation is a third category of evidence. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. A simpler heuristic reaches 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reports 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and fails. It remains diagnostic only.

A filing-period signal is an observation placed on an availability convention. A model statistic is a derived property of a limited historical panel. Neither is a market-price signal. The historical validation file and market-evidence index preserve that distinction rather than allowing a model result to be presented as observed market confirmation.

Why the warning mattered

A liability-side warning can matter because funding is a distinct balance-sheet channel. A lender must sustain assets while meeting obligations through its liability structure. Deterioration in disclosed funding conditions may therefore justify investigation before a public action-zone proxy shows a breach. That is a plausible investigative rationale, not a causal result established by this replay.

Religare Finvest fits the ordering but not the proof. Funding registered watch while the supplied PCA record has no first action-zone moment. The useful, limited implication is that a disclosed-liability deterioration can be a reason to inspect the balance sheet earlier than an action-zone lens alone would permit.

Fraud masking limits even that implication. Distorted reporting can delay, suppress or alter the measures being compared. The funding observation is not a calibrated failure probability, a determination of default risk, or a substitute for forensic work. The dossier assigns the problem of falsified filings to the forensic screen rather than claiming that disclosed thresholds can solve it.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. This is one fraud-masked institution reconstructed under PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. The historical evidence is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Its availability basis is an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise period end plus 60 days. Lead times are explicitly optimistic. The recorded 19-month advantage may exceed what a fully audited contemporaneous information set would have delivered.

Coverage is also selective. The funding lens only sees institutions disclosing a liability series. Five of the 15 failed institutions in the funding summary lack that observation. Missing data remain missing: they are neither evidence of sound funding nor a measured warning. A finding from the observable subset cannot automatically generalize to the unobserved subset.

The model does not rescue the story. Its temporal gate fails, while the conformal alarm is retained as a diagnostic with historical tier wiring suspended pending prospective revalidation. The strongest conclusion is therefore not that funding screens predict failure. It is that this replay makes liability disclosures a reasonable first place to investigate, while leaving open data availability, fraud masking and construction choices as explanations for the apparent order.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not evidence about the historical event. As of 2026-09-22, it contains 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange from a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow from 2026-03-31 and aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow from 2025-09-30 and aged 12 months.

These are published rules over published components, not failure predictions or credit ratings. The board excludes 21 stale records. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Institutions without vetted public dossiers are absent by design; absence is not a claim of safety.

The market layer is a separate market-price signal, not corroboration for those tiers. It is fresh as of 2026-09-18, but it has no admission, tier or publication authority. Rights and display approval are absent for every expected canonical record, and admitted canonical records are 0/25. Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, cannot validate or alter institution tiers here.

The next falsifiable test

This thesis should fail if prospective, fresh, vetted public dossiers show that disclosed-liability flags do not precede independently recorded stress more often than other available lenses once an auditable publication clock is applied. It should also fail if a bitemporal dataset removes the apparent lead in fraud-masked cases or shows that the relevant filings were not available when the reconstruction assumes they were known.

Credibility would require the ordering to persist prospectively, with liability-disclosure coverage specified in advance, fraud-masked cases identified separately, missing observations retained as missing, and stale, future-dated or unclocked readings denied signal and tier authority. Until then, this is an investigative hypothesis, not investment advice.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with the filing-period signal: identify the reporting date, the publication clock and whether a liability series is disclosed. Separate that from an action-zone signal and a forensic concern. Consult a market-price signal only afterward, and only where its use authorities permit it.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct research boundaries. A balance-sheet warning can justify checking the other domains; it cannot establish either one.

Seiche’s current editorial read is guarded: its composite is 39.6, EROSION, and its note says modelled or slow-moving structure leads while current market plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. Undertow reports partial coverage across several segments. Neither reading proves an institution-specific squeeze, and neither should be fused with Religare Finvest’s historical filing sequence.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies only on the failure-radar board, historical validation file, market-evidence index, Religare Finvest replay, Seiche overview and Undertow board. It is a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic, not a validated backtest or real-money record. Its availability convention can overstate lead times, fraud masking can make disclosures look compliant, and liability-series coverage is incomplete. Its appropriate use is disciplined investigation of published evidence, not prediction from a single historical replay.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Global Trust Bank’s replay: an early threshold warning, and the disclosure problem it could not solve
entry.summary: The recorded capital and asset-quality breaches arrived before Global Trust Bank’s default. But this fraud-masked case is stronger as a lesson in the limits of filing-based surveillance than as a claim that a model called the event.
entry.content:
*This is not current news and is not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Global Trust Bank, whose default date is 2004-07-24. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

Global Trust Bank presents a deliberately uncomfortable answer to the question of which balance sheet should feel stress first. Its recorded supervisory-threshold signal appeared in reported capital adequacy and non-performing assets, not in a scoreable funding series and not in a market-price signal. For the period ended 2002-03-31, the replay records CRAR and NNPA breaches, a threshold_2 action-zone status, and a knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30. That is a 25-month lead to default.

The finding matters, but only within its narrow evidential boundary. It is a filing-period signal reconstructed with a publication proxy where an explicit publication clock is unavailable. It is not proof that a tradable market anticipated the event, and it is not a model-derived probability of default. Most importantly, the institution is fraud-masked. The case says both that disclosed deterioration can warrant scrutiny and that reported disclosure can be the wrong object to trust.

The record before the event

The first recorded action-zone entry was FY2002, for the period ended 2002-03-31. The stated breaches were CRAR and NNPA. The system assigns the knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30, then measures the interval to the 2004-07-24 default date as 25 months.

That chronology is not a clean point-in-time record. Historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. The availability rule uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it assumes period end plus 60 days. There is no bitemporal input contract. The replay is not validated-backtest eligible and is not real-money eligible. Its lead times are explicitly described as optimistic.

A period end is not the same thing as public knowledge. A proxy can make disclosures appear more uniformly available than they were, and can overstate the practical time available to investigate, fund, sell, or hedge. The replay therefore supports an investigative observation: reported capital and reported asset quality entered a defined danger zone before the event. It does not establish an executable historical trade or a contemporaneous credit decision.

The broader PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions, of which 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. That is useful context for a threshold lens, not a universal failure clock. The underlying limitations are available in the historical validation record and the institution-specific Global Trust Bank replay.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw the first recorded warning: CRAR and NNPA crossed the stated action-zone framework. This is a filing-period signal. It concerns reported loss-absorption capacity and reported impaired assets. The economic logic is straightforward but conditional: worsening impaired assets can require provisions or generate losses; losses can reduce capital; a smaller capital buffer leaves less room for further deterioration.

That logic is balance-sheet arithmetic, not an assertion that every threshold breach ends in default. The dossier does not provide a complete sequence of losses, liabilities, counterparties, withdrawals, or interventions. It cannot establish a complete causal route from the reported period to the later default.

The funding lens did not deliver a competing signal. It is scoreable: false for Global Trust Bank, with no first signal and no lead time. This is missing-data information, not a positive finding on funding resilience. The funding lens can only observe institutions that disclose a liability series. No usable signal cannot be translated into stable funding.

Nor does this replay contain a market-price warning. A market-derived reading is conceptually different from a filing signal: it reflects price movement rather than reported balance-sheet information. The historical case offers no scoreable funding lead and no stated market lead. It should not be rewritten as evidence that markets confirmed the threshold breach.

Finally, fraud masking changes the hierarchy of evidence. The validation note states that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. Reported ratios can identify disclosed vulnerability. They cannot independently authenticate the reports from which those ratios are made.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it changed the right investigative question. Once reported capital and reported non-performing assets cross a supervisory threshold, the task is no longer simply to ask whether the institution looks healthy. It is to examine how much further asset deterioration the reported capital base can absorb, whether the disclosed asset-quality measure is credible, and what information is missing from the liability side.

This is not a claim that the threshold caused the outcome. It is a claim about triage. A defined breach creates a reason to intensify diligence on capital, assets, funding disclosures, and reporting integrity.

The distinction between a signal and a verdict is essential here. The recorded breach is a filing-period observation. The 25-month lead is a construction-PIT derivation from the selected availability rule and the default date. Neither is equivalent to a verified, real-time warning available on an exact market clock. The value of the replay lies in preserving that distinction rather than erasing it.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any claim that the threshold engine “called” Global Trust Bank. The institution is fraud-masked. A system based on reported CRAR and NNPA can be misled if reports are unreliable. Its historical availability also relies on period end plus 60 days where publication timing is absent, and the dossier says lead times are optimistic.

The aggregate diagnostics add restraint rather than rescue. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, with 179 censored or unusable rows excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score reaches 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only.

Those figures do not promote construction-PIT work into a validated forecast. The proper conclusion is narrower: the replay records a prior disclosed threshold breach, while simultaneously documenting why reported thresholds alone cannot settle a fraud-masked case.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a continuation of this historical case. As of 2026-09-21, it lists 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, as of 2025-03-31, with an age of 18 months and a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, as of 2026-03-31, age 6 months, score 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, as of 2025-09-30, age 12 months, score 66.0.

These are board tiers, not default predictions, credit ratings, or evidence that any named institution resembles Global Trust Bank. The board excludes 21 stale institutions. It presents one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier; institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design, not scored from memory.

The current market layer is fresh and knowledge-authorized, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. Market-derived display is not approved for every expected canonical record. Thus current market data cannot authorize board tiers. Read the Failure Radar board alongside the market evidence index, not as interchangeable evidence.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if prospectively collected, properly time-stamped disclosures show that action-zone capital and asset-quality breaches do not identify subsequent fragility after disclosure integrity is independently examined. It weakens further if exact publication times replace the 60-day proxy and the apparent lead time disappears.

The test is practical: preserve each filing’s exact availability time, validate reported inputs, retain missing liability disclosures as missing rather than benign, and evaluate threshold and forensic lenses prospectively. If that process does not improve on disclosed-ratio heuristics, the claimed early-warning value should be reduced rather than defended by retrospective reconstruction.

Follow the pressure chain

Begin with asset quality: NNPA points to reported impairment. Move to capital: CRAR points to the reported buffer against losses. Then ask whether liabilities are disclosed well enough for funding analysis; Global Trust Bank shows why no scoreable funding signal is not evidence of strength. Finally, test disclosure integrity, because fraud masking can make apparent ratio comfort unreliable.

LiquiLens addresses institution and lender balance-sheet risk. It should be paired, not confused, with Seiche’s system dollar-funding capacity view and Undertow’s market liquidity and executable exit capacity view. These are different questions: a lender’s reported resilience, the capacity of dollar-funding plumbing, and the ability to exit a position need not move together. See Seiche’s overview and Undertow’s board.

Sources, method, and limits

The relevant primary materials are the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, and the Global Trust Bank replay. Broader context is collected in LiquiLens research and LiquiLens investigations.

The historical record remains construction-PIT, not fully point-in-time. Its 60-day filing proxy applies where explicit publication clocks are absent; lead times are optimistic; it is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible. Missing liability disclosures constrain the funding lens. Fraud masking constrains every interpretation based on reported thresholds. The current board is a diagnostic screen, not investment advice, a credit rating, or a forecast of failure.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Altico’s historical warning was funding dependence, not a forecast of failure
entry.summary: A construction-period replay identifies commercial-paper reliance as Altico’s earliest documented vulnerability. That is a filing-period signal about rollover exposure, not proof that markets priced distress or that a model forecast default.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Altico before its 2019-09-12 default. The key filing period ended 2017-03-31; the conservative knowledge-time proxy is 2017-05-30. The market-layer date is 2026-09-18 and publication is 2026-09-20.*

The proposition is deliberately narrow: Altico’s balance sheet should have been investigated first through funding, because disclosed commercial-paper reliance created rollover-freeze exposure. That is neither a claim that the flag proved distress nor that it forecast a default. It distinguishes a filing-period signal from a market-price signal and from a model derivation. The former records a disclosed liability structure; the second would show repricing by market participants; the third converts inputs into a score or rule. None is interchangeable.

The record before the event

Altico was an NBFC, its funding lens was scoreable, and the dossier records no fraud-masking designation. Its first funding signal was a 23.7 index reading in the stable band at the 2017-03-31 period end. The accompanying flag was explicit: “CP reliance 29% (rollover-freeze exposure)”. The replay assigns a 27-month lead to the 2019-09-12 default.

That interval must not be mistaken for a tradable warning. The evidence status is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier says lead times are optimistic, the record has no bitemporal input contract, and it is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible. A period-end observation is therefore not proof that an outside creditor, investor, or counterparty possessed it on that date.

Readers can inspect the Altico replay alongside the Failure Radar board and validation record. The appropriate conclusion is that the liability structure merited investigation, not that the historical timestamp established actionable foresight.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a disclosed dependency on CP and labelled its relevant vulnerability: a possible rollover freeze. It did not document an actual freeze, identify the cause of the later default, or establish a complete causal chain. Its contribution was more limited: it isolated a liability channel through which refinancing conditions could become consequential while the asset side remained outstanding.

The historical funding record is small and selectively observable. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures, and the funding signal fired first for 4; median lead was 38 months. The lens can only assess institutions that disclose a liability series. Missing disclosure is missing data, not evidence of comfortable funding. Nor does a funding flag tell readers whether another lens supplied an earlier or more useful warning.

The broader model diagnostics reinforce restraint. The hazard panel had 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with an interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The temporal result was 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC was 0.799. These figures describe model derivations under constrained historical construction; they do not validate a live failure forecast.

Why the warning mattered

A liability requiring renewal can create pressure before a broad balance-sheet screen visibly changes. If renewal becomes less available or more costly, replacement liquidity becomes the immediate question. That mechanism explains why CP reliance is a sensible diligence prompt. It does not assert an unrecorded Altico event.

The stable band is central to the interpretation. A stable composite reading did not erase the documented funding flag; equally, the flag did not overrule the stable reading and pronounce distress. The useful lesson is about sequencing: an individual funding dependency can deserve scrutiny before a composite level settles the broader case.

A separate public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA or SAF tripwires found that 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. That does not make the regulatory lens superior to the funding lens, or vice versa. Filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that limitation.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat an overconfident thesis. CP reliance of 29% may have been a visible financing choice rather than evidence of imminent impairment. The funding index was 23.7 and stable. The 27-month historical interval is long enough for an institution’s funding mix, liquidity, and counterparties to change materially. Because the availability clock is partly proxied, the replay cannot prove the precise contemporaneous information set.

The sample further limits any generalisation. Only 10 of 15 failed institutions disclosed usable liabilities, and only 4 had the funding signal fire first. The temporal model missed its stated gate; the heuristic outperformed the hazard measure on the reported held-out rows. Nothing here shows that CP reliance outperformed every alternative warning method, or that it distinguished Altico from every comparable lender.

The defensible thesis is therefore conditional: the disclosure made Altico a stronger candidate for rollover-capacity diligence. It did not show failure was inevitable, determine timing, or provide a complete explanation of the default.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an Altico replay. As of 2026-09-20, it reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions, with 21 excluded as stale. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange with a 2025-03-31 as-of date and age of 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 2026-03-31 and 6 months; ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 2025-09-30 and 12 months.

These are published screens, not ratings or predictions. The rule can assign yellow for a funding flag among other conditions. But the market layer lacks tier authority: records are fresh and clocked, yet display and tier use are not approved for every expected canonical record. Its market evidence interface identifies Yahoo Finance daily closes as source, but the dossier does not permit market-derived display to support a published tier conclusion.

The next falsifiable test

This account would weaken if a prospective dataset, timed to actual publication, found that disclosed CP reliance did not precede measurable funding stress more often than comparable balance-sheet indicators after controlling for disclosure availability. It would weaken further if flagged institutions repeatedly renewed funding without observable pressure while other usable lenses consistently gave earlier warnings.

The test must retain actual availability times and preserve absent liability disclosure as missing rather than benign. It should compare the funding signal with independently observed subsequent stress outcomes. Until then, this construction-period replay is a hypothesis generator, not a validated trading rule, default model, or substitute for institution-specific diligence.

Follow the pressure chain

The products have distinct remits. LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk: funding mix, disclosure quality, and lender-specific pressure points. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; its overview offers system context. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity; its board reports incomplete segment coverage rather than a universal all-clear.

A system-funding divergence is a warning to investigate, not proof of a squeeze. A lender funding flag does not prove an exit problem, and partial market coverage cannot be read as normality. The diagnostic handoff is to locate pressure: institutional liabilities, system funding capacity, or executable exit capacity.

Sources, method, and limits

Core materials are the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, and Altico replay. Further desk material appears in LiquiLens research and investigations.

The limits are substantive: filing-availability-proxied construction, a 60-day fallback lag, optimistic lead times, no bitemporal contract, selective liability disclosures, and no inference of calm from missing data. The replay identifies a historical balance-sheet mechanism worth testing. It does not convert that mechanism into a repeatable forecast.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Before the event: what Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank's filings did and did not reveal
entry.summary: A construction-PIT replay of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
entry.content:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It opens the public Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is 2023-11-24. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated 2021-03-31, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of 2021-05-30. Its status is saf_triggered, its breached fields are NNPA, and its recorded lead is 29 months.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: True. Its first signal is dated not observed, with knowledge-time proxy not available, index unavailable, band not observed, flags none published, and lead unavailable months.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

What the lenses saw

The public replay page preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains 15 failed institutions and 5 first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of 41 months. The funding replay contains 10 institutions with liability disclosures and 4 first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is ****. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

What today's board shares

Today's board contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes 21 stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

Follow the pressure chain

Seiche asks whether system funding capacity is tightening. LiquiLens asks which institution balance sheet would transmit that pressure. Undertow asks whether the risk can be exited in traded markets. The three layers may disagree, and that disagreement is often the finding.

Readers who need the rule tested on their own counterparties can use the six-week proof pilot. The public replay, including this case's misses and voids, stays open.

Sources, method, and limits

  • - LiquiLens historical validation record, the structured source for every case value quoted above.
  • - The Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank replay, a human-readable case file generated from that record.
  • - Three-market evidence index, which states why India, US and Europe evidence has different status.
  • - Current Failure Radar board, used only for today's tier counts and coverage boundary.
  • - Seiche overview and Undertow public board, sibling layers not used to score this case.
  • - LiquiLens research record and reviewed investigations.

entry.title: Before the event: what United Western Bank's filings did and did not reveal
entry.summary: A construction-PIT replay of United Western Bank: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
entry.content:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It opens the public United Western Bank record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is 2006-09-02. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated 2001-03-31, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of 2001-05-30. Its status is threshold_2, its breached fields are NNPA, and its recorded lead is 63 months.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: True. Its first signal is dated not observed, with knowledge-time proxy not available, index unavailable, band not observed, flags none published, and lead unavailable months.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

What the lenses saw

The public replay page preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains 15 failed institutions and 5 first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of 41 months. The funding replay contains 10 institutions with liability disclosures and 4 first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For United Western Bank, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is ****. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

What today's board shares

Today's board contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next United Western Bank.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes 21 stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

Follow the pressure chain

Seiche asks whether system funding capacity is tightening. LiquiLens asks which institution balance sheet would transmit that pressure. Undertow asks whether the risk can be exited in traded markets. The three layers may disagree, and that disagreement is often the finding.

Readers who need the rule tested on their own counterparties can use the six-week proof pilot. The public replay, including this case's misses and voids, stays open.

entry.title: Sambandh Finserve’s early stress signal was funding, not a forecast
entry.summary: A historical replay places a fragile wholesale-liability signal before Sambandh Finserve’s default. The lesson is a balance-sheet mechanism to investigate, not a validated prediction or a market verdict.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines information associated with Sambandh Finserve before its 2020-10-13 default. Publication date: 2026-09-17. The relevant filing period ended 2016-03-31, with a knowledge-time proxy of 2016-05-30. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

The narrow thesis is that Sambandh Finserve’s balance sheet should have felt stress first through funding. Wholesale leverage could leave refinancing capacity exposed to a change in lenders’ willingness to roll liabilities. That is not a claim that a ratio forecast the default, that the outcome was fully knowable, or that the screen measured a probability of failure. It is a claim about where disclosed balance-sheet pressure appeared earliest and where diligence should have concentrated.

A filing-period signal is an observation in disclosed accounts. A market-price signal is a contemporaneous repricing measure. A model derivation combines inputs under stated rules. They are not interchangeable evidence. Sambandh’s signal is a filing-period observation replayed with an availability proxy. This article makes no market-derived institutional conclusion.

The record before the event

Sambandh was scoreable in the funding lens. Its first signal was attached to 2016-03-31: an index of 78.7, in the fragile band, with wholesale leverage of 8.51x against a 7x threshold. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the historical record uses period end plus 60 days. That produces the knowledge-time proxy of 2016-05-30 and a stated lead of 52 months before default.

There are material absences. No first PCA action-zone event is recorded, and neither an action-zone date nor a PCA lead is available. The institution is fraud-masked. That is not cosmetic: filings later shown to have been falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. The dossier assigns that failure mode to a forensic screen. A liability ratio can flag a disclosed vulnerability without establishing that the disclosure was reliable.

The historical status is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. The input contract is not bitemporal. The replay is not eligible as a validated backtest or as real-money evidence, and its lead times are explicitly described as optimistic. The dated sequence is available in the Sambandh replay and the wider replay archive. It cannot prove that an analyst possessed every relevant input at the apparent lead date.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a liability-side warning. The PCA replay did not record an initial action-zone event for Sambandh. That supports a limited statement: in this supplied record, the earliest disclosed concern came through funding rather than an RBI PCA/SAF tripwire. It does not show that funding is generally earlier, more accurate, or more useful for every institution.

Across the failed-institution summaries, PCA covers 15 institutions, with 5 entering an action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. Funding also covers 15 failed institutions, but only 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Coverage is decisive. A funding lens cannot identify a liability condition when the necessary series is not disclosed.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it has the same filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT status, no bitemporal input contract, and no validated-backtest or real-money eligibility. This is diagnostic evidence, not demonstrated deployable performance. Readers can inspect the Failure Radar board, historical validation, and research archive.

Why the warning mattered

Wholesale leverage matters as a possible transmission channel, not as a complete explanation. A liability-heavy funding structure can leave balance-sheet flexibility sensitive to refinancing appetite and terms. The disclosed ratio therefore raised a question: could the liability base withstand less accommodating lender behaviour?

The 8.51x observation does not answer that question. It does not identify counterparties, maturity concentrations, management actions, the timing of crystallisation, or the cause of the eventual default. It identifies where further evidence would have been most valuable.

Calling this a funding signal rather than a forecast preserves the evidentiary order. The ratio was observed under a published rule. The 60-day clock is a construction assumption when publication timing is absent. The 52-month lead is a model-derived interval, not proof of a tradable or actionable advance warning.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. This may be retrospective coincidence amplified by an assumed availability clock. Because the lead begins at period end and uses a 60-day proxy where necessary, the apparent 52 months may overstate what a contemporaneous analyst could have known. The dossier calls these leads optimistic.

The statistical record is not a clean endorsement. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC is 0.752, with an interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The disclosure heuristic recorded 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reported 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and failed it; it remains diagnostic only.

Fraud masking sharpens the challenge. If accounts can be unreliable, an early ratio flag cannot be credited with seeing the whole case. Equally, an absent flag cannot be read as safety. The fair conclusion is only that funding fragility was an early disclosed concern for Sambandh, not that the model validated a prediction of default.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this historical replay. As of 2026-09-17, it contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale institutions are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with an 18-month-old row as of 2025-03-31. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with a 6-month-old row as of 2026-03-31. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, with a 12-month-old row as of 2025-09-30. The supplied rows show no fired signals and no market drawdown. Those blanks do not establish calm.

The market layer is fresh and clocked, dated 2026-09-16, but has no admission, publication, or tier authority. Admitted canonical records are 0/25, and display rights are not approved for every expected record. It cannot supply a market-price conclusion here. See market evidence for that authority boundary.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if properly clocked prospective disclosures show that high wholesale leverage does not precede measurable refinancing pressure, lending restraint, or liability-side deterioration more often than comparable institutions without the flag. It also fails if a bitemporal dataset using actual publication availability loses useful discrimination once the construction-PIT proxy is removed.

A credible test requires fresh vetted public dossiers, explicit publication clocks, disclosed liability series, and a pre-specified rule applied before outcomes. Fraud-masked cases must remain separate. Until then, this is diagnostic scrutiny, not confidence.

Follow the pressure chain

Follow the disclosed sequence from 2016-03-31, through the 2016-05-30 knowledge proxy, to the fragile funding flag and the 2020-10-13 default. At each point, ask whether evidence is disclosed, timely, and independently reliable. The purpose is to test a path from funding structure to balance-sheet flexibility, not to manufacture certainty.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are separate products and evidence domains, not interchangeable verdicts. See LiquiLens investigations, Seiche, and Undertow.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the supplied evidence record, including the Failure Radar board, validation record, market evidence index, and Sambandh replay. The tier is a published rule over published components. The conformal alarm has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority.

The essential limit is simple: a dated disclosure, an assumed availability date, and a model rule do not become a contemporaneous market signal or a proven forecast merely because a later default occurred. This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: New India Co-operative Bank: a disclosed NNPA warning preceded the event, but fraud limits the replay
entry.summary: The reconstructed record places an NNPA action-zone breach before New India Co-operative Bank’s recorded event. That is a filing-period observation, not market-price confirmation or a model-derived failure forecast, and fraud masking limits what the case can establish.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

This historical replay is not current news, a forecast, a credit rating, or investment advice. New India Co-operative Bank has a recorded default date of 2025-02-13. Its first PCA/SAF action-zone observation belongs to the 2021-03-31 reporting period, labelled FY2021, with a knowledge-time proxy of 2021-05-30.

Those dates have separate meanings. The reporting period describes when the underlying filing-period measure was recorded. The knowledge-time proxy estimates when the information could have become available under the replay’s construction rule. The default date is the recorded outcome.
