Conflating them would turn a historical reconstruction into a claim about contemporaneous knowledge or tradable timing that the dossier does not support.

The narrow finding is that the reconstructed public record contains an NNPA breach before the recorded event. The dossier records no first funding signal. Neither finding establishes causation, and the fraud-masked status means a ratio-based reconstruction cannot be treated as a complete account of the institution’s condition.

The record before the event

The Failure Radar board identifies New India Co-operative Bank’s first action-zone signal in FY2021. The named breach is NNPA, with a stated lead of 44 months to the recorded event.

This is a filing-period signal. It means a disclosed measure crossed a PCA/SAF-style tripwire in the reconstructed record. It does not show when management understood the underlying condition, when a supervisor acted, when depositors altered behaviour, or when any market incorporated information. Nor does it establish that the NNPA breach caused the event.

The 2021-05-30 date requires particular care. The availability rule uses an explicit publication clock when one is present; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. For this case, the date is a knowledge-time proxy generated by that rule, not a verified case-specific publication timestamp. Treating 2021-03-31 as the moment an investor could have acted would overstate the evidence.

Fraud masking is not a footnote. The dossier states that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine, while the forensic screen addresses that problem. A detected breach therefore does not prove that the engine observed the whole condition, or that the disclosed series captured the decisive source of stress. It is the earliest recorded action-zone breach in this replay.

What the lenses saw

The PCA/SAF lens saw NNPA. The funding lens records no first signal. That is non-firing or unavailable evidence, not affirmative evidence that liabilities were stable. The funding lens only sees institutions that disclose a liability series; lack of a recorded funding signal cannot be converted into a finding of benign funding.

The historical summaries retain that eligibility distinction. Of 15 failed institutions, 5 first entered an action zone, with a median stated lead of 41 months. Of the same 15 failures, 10 had liability disclosures; 4 had a funding signal fire first, with a median stated lead of 38 months. These describe different eligible subsets. They are not probabilities for this bank and do not determine which lens must lead in every failure.

A market-price signal is not part of the case thesis. The current market layer is sourced from Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, but no market-price reading is presented for this institution. More importantly, the pack has no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. A fresh retrieval clock does not authorize market-derived institutional conclusions. The market evidence index cannot remove that boundary.

A model derivation is different again. A board tier is a published rule over published components, rather than an independently observed balance-sheet fact. The dossier says the Merton PD is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. It also says the conformal alarm is diagnostic and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Those constructions do not change the case-level observation: the disclosed NNPA lens fired, while the funding lens did not record a first signal.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it located visible, disclosed asset-quality pressure before the recorded event. Under the quadrant rule, any RBI action-zone breach can place an institution in red. That is an operational classification rule, not a declaration that failure was inevitable.

The absence of a recorded funding signal cannot negate the observed impairment evidence. Doing so would mistake a disclosure and eligibility limitation for a positive balance-sheet judgement. The dossier supplies no basis for that inference.

The defensible conclusion is therefore limited: the replay found an early disclosed impairment warning in a fraud-masked case. It did not establish complete detection. Fraud masking explains why the reconstruction can be informative and inadequate at once: it may identify a visible fragment without showing that the disclosure record faithfully represented the full condition.

The wider India diagnostic cannot be used to inflate this single case. It covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it is a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic, is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Its stated lead times are optimistic.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case defeats a stronger thesis. NNPA may be a broad marker of disclosed deterioration rather than a specific explanation for this institution’s outcome. The supplied evidence contains no causal decomposition, liability-run chronology, supervisory narrative, or complete forensic account. It can show only that NNPA was the first recorded PCA/SAF signal, not that it was the first underlying stress.

Fraud intensifies that objection. If disclosures were falsified, the apparent 44-month lead could be an early visible fragment, a delayed representation of deeper stress, or a measure distorted by the condition under examination. The dossier does not allow a choice among these explanations.

Model diagnostics provide no escape from that uncertainty. The hazard panel has 205 rows and 9 events, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only. The leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with an interval from 0.338 to 1.0; the same held-out comparison gives the heuristic an AUC of 0.799. These results argue against prospective promotion, not for a failure forecast. See the historical validation record.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate comparison object, not a continuation of this replay. As of 2026-09-16, it shows 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green; 21 are excluded as stale. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with filings as of 2025-03-31 and age of 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow as of 2026-03-31 and aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow as of 2025-09-30 and aged 12 months.

Those are dossier-screen outcomes, not a ranking of imminent distress. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory. Missing, stale, future-dated, unclocked, or unauthorized information is not evidence of calm.

The market layer is available and fresh as of 2026-09-15, but rights and display approvals remain incomplete. It has no publication or tier authority. A market-price reading must be observed and authorized for the claimed use before it can support a current institutional conclusion. That condition is not met.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis would weaken if prospectively clocked filings showed that action-zone NNPA breaches did not precede independently documented stress after fraud-masked cases were separated and liability disclosures were consistently available. It would also weaken if a comparable prospective sample showed the funding lens firing earlier and more reliably than the impairment lens.

The needed test is not another period-end reconstruction. It requires fixed eligibility rules, a bitemporal input contract, verified publication times, and no retrospective substitution of amended or later-known facts. Until then, this remains a bounded historical diagnostic rather than an investable signal.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with the filing-period observation: NNPA crossed the action-zone screen in FY2021. Then identify what is not observed: no first funding signal is recorded, but funding strength is not established. Next separate market evidence: no authorized market-price signal is used. Finally separate model output: a tier or PD is a derivation subject to authority and eligibility rules, not a replacement for the underlying record.

The pressure chain breaks at record trustworthiness. In this fraud-masked case, a ratio engine can assess only the information it receives. The case replay is useful as evidence of that constraint, not as proof that disclosed metrics can see through compromised information.

LiquiLens: institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche: system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow: market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct research boundaries and must not be fused into a single institutional verdict. See Seiche and Undertow.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the Failure Radar board, validation record, market evidence index, and New India Co-operative Bank replay. Related desk work is available through LiquiLens research.

Material limits are construction-PIT history, the 60-day proxy where no explicit publication clock exists, optimistic stated lead times, incomplete liability visibility, and fraud masking. The current market pack is fresh on its own clock but lacks admission, publication, and tier authority. No missing evidence is treated as reassuring.

Research, not investment advice. This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Nedungadi Bank’s capital breach was the first visible warning in the disclosed record
entry.summary: A historical replay places Nedungadi Bank’s first RBI capital action-zone breach before default. That is a bounded filing-period signal, not a market-price signal, a live forecast, or proof that capital caused the failure.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast. It uses a construction-PIT record that is not eligible for validated-backtest or real-money use. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.

Nedungadi Bank offers a narrow answer to LiquiLens’s question: which balance sheet should appear stressed first, and why? In the available record, the first observable warning was regulatory capital. CRAR crossed the first RBI action-zone threshold in the period ending 1999-03-31, identified as FY1999. The replay assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 1999-05-30. Default followed on 2002-11-02, with a stated lead of 41 months.

That chronology supports a limited proposition only. Capital was the first visible pressure point among the lenses eligible in this replay. It does not establish that capital caused the default, that funding was sound, or that public observers had a complete contemporaneous record. A filing-period signal reports what a disclosed balance-sheet measure showed at a reporting date. A market-price signal is a market repricing observation. A model derivation is an output produced by data, assumptions, and rules. None can be substituted for another.

The record before the event

The historical record puts Nedungadi Bank into its first action-zone status at the first threshold and identifies CRAR as the breach. The institution is not marked fraud-masked. That makes the capital observation usable within this replay; it does not make the disclosed record complete.

The funding lens is explicitly unscoreable. It records no first signal and no funding lead time. This is a missing-data and eligibility disclosure, not evidence of stable liabilities. The funding lens needs a liability series, and the record does not provide the scoreable disclosure necessary for Nedungadi Bank. An unavailable funding result cannot be recast as evidence that funding pressure was absent.

Timing is conditional as well. The reporting period ended on 1999-03-31. Where no explicit publication clock is present, the replay uses period end plus 60 days, producing 1999-05-30 here. The dossier says lead times are optimistic and that the record lacks a bitemporal input contract. The stated 41 months is therefore a construction-PIT chronology, not proof of the precise moment at which an investor, depositor, creditor, or supervisor could have acted.

Read the Nedungadi Bank replay alongside the Failure Radar board and the historical validation record. They document a period-end-proxy construction-PIT exercise: a means of examining disclosed warning sequences, not a validated backtest or a real-money tool.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw a CRAR breach. The funding lens did not produce an eligible result. The first is a filing-period threshold signal; the second is a data-availability status. Neither is a market-price observation.

The wider PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions. 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. It is a public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA and SAF tripwires. The funding summary covers a narrower eligible set: 10 of 15 failed institutions had liability disclosures, 4 had a funding signal fire first, and the median lead was 38 months. The denominators matter. The lenses do not observe the same universe, so their apparent ordering is not a clean contest between capital and funding.

The dossier also says institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that limitation. Nedungadi Bank is not marked fraud-masked, but the wider constraint remains: a disclosed ratio cannot demonstrate that every underlying disclosure was complete or accurate.

Model evidence needs a third, separate reading. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The disclosure heuristic is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only. These are model derivations from a limited construction record, not observed default probabilities for Nedungadi Bank.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because an RBI action-zone breach identifies a disclosed regulatory-capital constraint. That is more precise than saying the bank was destined to fail. It directs further investigation toward the capital buffer, the reporting that supports it, and whether subsequent evidence confirms or contradicts pressure elsewhere on the balance sheet.

The interval before default means the breach was not merely a final datapoint in this replay. But a long measured lead does not become a tradable rule, a causal explanation, or a forecast. Historical lead times are explicitly described as optimistic. Because the funding series was not scoreable, this case cannot show that capital beat funding for Nedungadi Bank rather than being the only eligible early lens.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. A capital threshold may be a lagging, coarse regulatory disclosure rather than the first economically meaningful indication of strain. Risks may exist before a period-end ratio captures them. A capital ratio does not resolve funding durability, asset liquidity, external support, or information unavailable in public filings.

More fundamentally, capital may seem first because competing lenses could not score the institution. The missing funding result prevents this record from establishing that capital was uniquely earlier than funding. The period-end-plus-60-day clock may also make the apparent warning interval look more actionable than it was. Without a bitemporal input contract, that is a material limitation rather than a technical footnote.

The proposition should fail if prospectively timestamped, eligibility-matched evidence shows that action-zone breaches add no useful information beyond funding and forensic signals. It should also fail if actual publication clocks erase the apparent lead. This historical sequence cannot settle either question.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate current diagnostic, not an extension of the Nedungadi conclusion. As of 2026-09-15, it contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale names are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 dossier aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow on a 2026-03-31 dossier aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow on a 2025-09-30 dossier aged 12 months. Their signals-fired fields are empty, and no market drawdown is supplied for them.

The board tier is a published rule over published components, not a replayed failure outcome. Its market layer is fresh as of 2026-09-11 and was retrieved on 2026-09-15, but market-derived display, admission, and tier authority are absent for the expected aggregate. Admitted canonical records are 0/25. The source is Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, but rights and expected-record approvals are incomplete. No market-price conclusion follows from that layer.

The next falsifiable test

A credible test would use vetted public dossiers, explicit publication clocks, and matched eligibility across capital, funding, and forensic lenses. It would preserve absent liability-series disclosures as missing rather than treating them as calm. It would separate fraud-masked institutions and test whether an action-zone breach adds information after the other eligible lenses are known.

The Nedungadi proposition fails if capital does not lead subsequent deterioration more usefully than eligible alternatives, or if measured lead disappears when proxy clocks are replaced by observed publication times. Until then, construction-PIT diagnostics cannot be promoted into a live failure forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

The supported chain is deliberately short. A disclosed capital-threshold breach identifies where balance-sheet investigation should start; other evidence must then confirm, weaken, or contradict the case. Nedungadi Bank supports the middle observation: CRAR breached an action-zone threshold before default. It does not establish every upstream cause or downstream transmission.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are distinct diagnostics. Their outputs should not be fused into one assertion of stress.

Sources, method, and limits

Relevant materials include the Failure Radar board, validation file, market evidence index, Nedungadi replay, research archive, and investigations archive.

The historical period end is 1999-03-31; the knowledge proxy is 1999-05-30; the board date is 2026-09-15; and the market-layer date is 2026-09-11. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings can remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. The conformal alarm has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Nedungadi’s bounded lesson is not that every capital breach ends alike. It is that this disclosed record first pointed investigation toward capital, while the counter-case remains strong enough to require corroboration.

Research and market data, not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: First Leasing replay draws the line between disclosed stress and forensic risk
entry.summary: First Leasing Company Of India’s fraud-masked default produced no recorded first action-zone or funding signal in this construction replay. That is a limit on reported-balance-sheet surveillance, not evidence of calm.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. The default examined here occurred on 2013-12-02. It is not investment advice and not a credit rating.*

Which institution balance sheet should feel financial stress first, and why? First Leasing Company Of India supplies an uncomfortable answer: sometimes a screen built from public disclosures cannot establish that it did.

The case is an NBFC recorded as fraud-masked. Its PCA-style record contains no recorded first action-zone entry or lead time. Its funding record is scoreable, but contains no recorded first funding signal or lead time. Those absences do not show that reported capital, asset quality, or funding conditions were sound. They show that this replay did not document a qualifying disclosed threshold signal before default.

That distinction is the point of the case. A filing-period signal arises from reported information becoming available under the replay’s publication-clock rule. A market-price signal comes from market data, with separate authority and display constraints. A model derivation can arrange available inputs, but cannot make missing or falsified disclosures reliable. First Leasing is therefore a boundary test, not an early-warning victory.

The record before the event

First Leasing Company Of India is identified as fraud-masked, with default dated 2013-12-02. The PCA lens records neither a first action-zone date nor lead months. The funding lens is scoreable, yet records neither a first signal nor lead months. In this construction, those are missing findings, not affirmative resilience findings.

The historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not eligible as a validated backtest or a real-money test, and it does not have a bitemporal input contract. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, information availability is proxied as period end plus 60 days. The dossier says resulting lead times are optimistic. The historical validation record should therefore be read as a public-disclosure replay using a conservative timing proxy, rather than proof of a participant’s real-time information set.

The narrow proposition is that disclosed deterioration can register in an action-zone, deterioration, or funding lens before a failure. But threshold engines only receive reported disclosure. If filings were later shown falsified, apparent compliance may describe the inputs rather than the institution’s condition.

What the lenses saw

Across the failed-institution record, the PCA-style lens entered an action zone first for 5 of 15 failed institutions, with median lead of 41 months. The funding lens had liability disclosures for 10 of 15 failed institutions, fired first for 4, and had median lead of 38 months. These are summaries of disclosed historical cases. They do not establish that either lens covers every failure route.

First Leasing supplies no such sequence. The fraud-masked designation controls the interpretation. The validation note says institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine, while the forensic screen owns those cases. That is a stated limitation. It is not grounds to reconstruct an unobserved warning from evidence outside this dossier.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. But it has the same filing-availability-proxied construction and optimistic-lead limitation. The market evidence index identifies it as a construction-PIT diagnostic, not prospective validation.

Why the warning mattered

A useful warning identifies a pressure channel that can be inspected. An action-zone or deterioration signal concerns disclosed balance-sheet conditions. A funding flag concerns disclosed liability information. A forensic indicator concerns whether the disclosed information can be trusted.

First Leasing shows why those categories cannot be merged. The absence of recorded PCA and funding leads does not exonerate the institution. Conversely, the fraud-masked label does not establish a concealed capital path or liability sequence; the dossier provides neither. What it does establish is an evidentiary handoff. Reported thresholds assess reported conditions. Questions about disclosure integrity require forensic work.

Model diagnostics require the same restraint. The leave-one-institution-out hazard AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic AUC is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote. These measures can frame questions; they cannot turn this replay into a calibrated failure forecast.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. If fraud-masked failures sit outside threshold surveillance whenever the thresholds miss them, the framework may be weakest precisely where users need protection most. A system that cannot distinguish truly reassuring reported disclosures from false reassurance has a material blind spot.

This case supports that criticism. The dossier does not show that fraud masking caused the default. It does not identify a hidden funding sequence. It does not establish that forensic review would have produced an earlier public warning. Calling this a forensic handoff honestly describes the boundary, but does not prove that the handoff succeeds.

The narrower defence is not that the framework caught First Leasing. It did not document a qualifying filing-based lead. The defence is that relabelling the missing findings as stability would be worse. The framework preserves both the missing findings and the fraud-masked designation. Its useful claim is limited to a division of labour: disclosure-driven lenses can surface disclosure-driven pressure, but cannot authenticate every disclosure.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a replay result for First Leasing and must not inherit its outcome. As of 2026-09-14, it shows 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale cases are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with filings as of 2025-03-31 and an age of 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with filings as of 2026-03-31 and an age of 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, with filings as of 2025-09-30 and an age of 12 months.

Their displayed signal lists are empty, and their market drawdown fields are not recorded. The Failure Radar board is consequently a filing-based comparison view, not a First Leasing analogue.

The market layer is available as of 2026-09-11 and was retrieved on 2026-09-14. Yet market-derived display, model, tier, and publication use are not approved for every expected canonical record. Admitted canonical records are 0/25, and the layer has no tier authority. A market-price signal must not be inserted into a filing-period tier merely because prices were retrieved.

The next falsifiable test

The proposed division of labour is testable. Future fresh vetted public dossiers should preserve explicit publication time when present and otherwise retain the period-end-plus-60-days proxy. Before outcomes are known, the record can test whether action-zone, deterioration, or funding signals precede usable forensic findings, and whether public inconsistencies in fraud-masked cases can be identified before default.

The thesis fails if a properly time-stamped prospective record finds that filing-based thresholds do not lead useful investigative evidence. It also fails if purported forensic findings do not survive review, or if missing disclosed signals are repeatedly treated as comfort despite later contrary evidence. Until that record exists, historical leads remain optimistic construction-PIT diagnostics.

Follow the pressure chain

Begin with the reported balance sheet: is a qualifying action-zone, deterioration, or funding condition actually disclosed? Then ask whether the observation is fresh and eligible under the published rule. Finally ask whether the disclosure deserves trust. First Leasing warns against skipping that final question.

The product boundaries are explicit. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. The Seiche overview and Undertow board can add system or exit context, but neither supplies a missing forensic fact for this institution replay.

For the underlying case record, see the First Leasing replay. The appropriate response is investigation of the pressure chain, not a mechanical verdict from a colour label.

Sources, method, and limits

Primary dossier outputs are the Failure Radar board, historical validation, and market evidence index. Related material is available through the LiquiLens replay archive and LiquiLens research.

The method presents one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design, and nothing is scored from memory. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. The conformal alarm remains a diagnostic, while its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

First Leasing is useful because it refuses false resolution. It records no documented filing-based threshold lead, preserves the fraud-masked limitation, separates filing authority from market authority, and leaves the forensic question open where the evidence remains open.

entry.title: Madhavpura’s replay shows where a balance-sheet radar can go blind
entry.summary: Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank produced no recorded conventional early funding or action-zone warning. Fraud masking means that silence cannot be treated as resilience: a disclosure-driven screen cannot verify a balance sheet when reported evidence may be false.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank defaulted on 2012-06-04. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at any institution today.*

The conclusion from this replay is narrow. The institution that should feel stress first is not always the institution that a public-data balance-sheet engine can identify first. Madhavpura is fraud-masked. Its funding lens was not scoreable, and the replay records no first action-zone entry. Those absences do not establish calm before the event. They establish that the disclosed record did not yield a conventional warning through these lenses.

A filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and a model derivation are different objects. A filing-period signal describes what a dated public disclosure permits a screen to observe. A market-price signal is a repricing observation only when its inputs are authorized for that use. A model derivation turns specified inputs into a score or tier; it cannot repair falsified or missing inputs. Madhavpura is a test of that boundary, not proof that hidden stress was visible in advance.

The record before the event

Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank is classified as a UCB. The historical record gives its default date as 2012-06-04 and explicitly marks the case fraud-masked. It provides no first RBI action-zone breach, no PCA lead time, no scoreable funding series, no first funding signal, and no funding lead time.

The permitted inference is limited: these lenses contain no recorded conventional early warning to narrate. The record does not permit an inference that liquidity, capital, asset quality, depositor behaviour, or management conduct was sound. Missing, unusable, or falsified evidence is not evidence of calm.

The replay must also remain separate from current dashboard clocks. The Failure Radar board is as of 2026-09-13; its market layer is as of 2026-09-11 and was retrieved on 2026-09-13. Those dates do not turn a replayed failure into live evidence about Madhavpura. The dedicated historical replay and the Failure Radar board are the relevant records.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens replays public-disclosure versions of RBI action-zone tripwires. Among failed institutions in its summary, 5 of 15 entered the action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. The funding lens is narrower: it can operate only where an institution discloses a liability series. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had those disclosures; 4 produced a funding signal first, with median lead of 38 months.

Madhavpura is not evidence for either summary result. Its funding evidence was not scoreable and its PCA replay records no first action-zone entry. The dossier’s limitation is direct: filings later shown to be falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that problem.

That is not a semantic distinction. A conventional balance-sheet model begins with reported assets, liabilities, capital, and funding behaviour. If reports misrepresent the relevant condition, a model can calculate faithfully from filings while describing the institution poorly. A benign-looking ratio would then be a property of the reported input, not a verified property of the balance sheet.

The broader India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. But it is labelled a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic, not validated backtest evidence. Madhavpura sits at the fraud-masked boundary rather than within the non-fraud headline result. The validation record and market-evidence index preserve that qualification.

Why the warning mattered

The warning is methodological: fraud masking must remain a forensic limitation, not become an unflagged balance-sheet verdict. Calling an institution safe because a disclosed threshold did not fire would confuse an information failure with a credit conclusion.

The wider validation does not erase this constraint. Its hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, with 179 censored or unusable rows excluded. Leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0; the comparable heuristic AUC is 0.799. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below its 0.65 gate. That diagnostic cannot promote because construction-PIT evidence cannot promote.

These are diagnostic results, not a claim that a warning was investable or available in real time. Historical evidence uses an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise a period-end plus 60-days proxy. It lacks a bitemporal input contract, is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, and its lead times are optimistic.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case defeats an overextended thesis. The replay is too sparse to establish that Madhavpura’s balance sheet visibly deteriorated in a particular sequence before default. Neither conventional lens records a first signal, and the dossier supplies no line-item chronology from which to reconstruct one. “Unknown” is more defensible than a claim that hidden stress was demonstrably present at a specific earlier point.

Fraud masking explains why silence cannot be reassurance; it does not prove that a public balance-sheet screen could have identified fraud earlier. The counter-case should prevail unless independently auditable forensic evidence supplies that missing bridge.

Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory. The conformal alarm is diagnostic only, with historical tier wiring suspended and no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Those rules stop a plausible narrative from becoming unsupported evidence.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a live analogue of Madhavpura. As of 2026-09-13, it shows 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow on a 2026-03-31 filing aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow on a 2025-09-30 filing aged 12 months. A further 21 institutions are excluded as stale.

Those entries are filing-based screen outputs, not declarations of failure. The market layer has fresh readings but no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0 of 25. It cannot add market-price confirmation to these tiers.

Seiche’s composite reads 44, EROSION, with guarded confidence because slow-moving or modelled structure leads while market plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. Seiche’s overview concerns system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow’s board concerns market liquidity and executable exit capacity. LiquiLens concerns institution and lender balance-sheet risk. These are product boundaries, not interchangeable stress labels.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis would weaken if a prospectively assembled, genuinely bitemporal record of fraud-masked cases showed that disclosed PCA, funding, or other public balance-sheet measures repeatedly gave timely, independently verified warnings before forensic evidence emerged. It would strengthen if such cases repeatedly appeared compliant on published thresholds while later evidence showed that reported inputs masked the relevant risk.

The test must preserve actual filing availability rather than substitute a period-end proxy where publication time is unknown. It must distinguish missing liability disclosure from stable funding, assess forensic evidence separately from threshold performance, and refuse to treat a model derivation as either a market-price signal or proof of a reported balance sheet.

Follow the pressure chain

For a normally disclosed institution, the pressure chain runs from reported balance-sheet condition to capital or action-zone pressure, then to liabilities and disclosed funding behaviour, and only then to authorized market repricing. Every link requires a dated, vetted input. A disclosure break is a limitation, not evidence that pressure stopped.

For a fraud-masked institution, the prior question is whether the public record can be trusted to represent assets, liabilities, and capital. If that remains unresolved, ratios may accurately summarize filings while failing to summarize the institution. That is the usable lesson from Madhavpura, and no broader one is warranted.

For related work, see the LiquiLens research archive, investigations archive, and replay archive. None substitutes for contemporaneous, auditable evidence.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied dossier, including the Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, Madhavpura replay, Seiche overview, and Undertow board.

Historical evidence is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. The filing proxy can make lead times optimistic. Funding coverage depends on liability disclosure. Fraud masking is an explicit boundary: falsified filings can look compliant, and the absence of an alert must not be recast as proof of calm.

Research and market data, not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: IL&FS replay: a funding watch arrived first, but the record cannot certify a forecast
entry.summary: The IL&FS reconstruction places a funding watch before the recorded default while finding no first PCA action-zone entry. That is a filing-period signal under an optimistic availability proxy—not a market confirmation, a causal account, or a validated prediction.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. IL&FS has a recorded default date of 2018-08-28. The historical record is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, is not eligible as a validated backtest or real-money record, lacks a bitemporal input contract, and explicitly treats lead times as optimistic. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not establish the same outcome at another institution.*

The narrow thesis is that IL&FS’s disclosed funding condition appeared before a formal PCA action-zone signal in this reconstruction. The first funding reading was 45.4, in the watch band, for the period ended 2015-03-31; its knowledge-time proxy was 2015-05-30. The stated distance to the recorded default is 38 months. PCA has no first action zone and no lead time in the supplied record.

That ordering deserves attention, but it cannot carry more weight than the record permits. It is a filing-period signal: an indicator assigned to a reporting period and placed on an estimated information clock. It is not a market-price signal. Nor is it a model derivation proving that funding weakness caused the event. IL&FS is also marked fraud-masked, a designation that sharply limits what an engine based on reported disclosures can infer.

The record before the event

IL&FS was scoreable on the funding lens. Its first disclosed funding signal is attached to 2015-03-31, has index 45.4, sits in the watch band, and has no listed flags. The replay uses explicit publication time where available; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. The 2015-05-30 knowledge proxy is therefore an availability convention, not evidence that every market participant possessed or acted on the information at period end.

Measured from that proxy to 2018-08-28, the dossier reports 38 months. The PCA replay, by contrast, records no first action-zone entry. The defensible conclusion is limited: under the reconstruction’s rules, the funding lens registered before a PCA action-zone event. It does not show that the funding measure was uniquely informative, that it identified a specific liability instrument, or that it would have produced a usable decision in real time.

The construction has a material missing-data boundary. The funding lens only observes institutions disclosing a liability series. Institutions without that series are not silently treated as healthy. The IL&FS replay record and Failure Radar board should be read as diagnostic records, not credit verdicts.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens supplied the positive historical observation: watch first. The PCA lens supplied a contrasting observation: no first action zone. These are separate filing-based lenses, and neither should be recast as a live market verdict.

A balance-sheet interpretation is possible but remains a model derivation. If liabilities must be renewed while assets are difficult to turn into cash or depend on continuing finance, worsening funding resilience can create pressure before a disclosed solvency or action-zone threshold is crossed. That is a plausible pressure-chain hypothesis, not a fact established for every link at IL&FS. The replay establishes signal ordering and an event date; it does not reconstruct causation.

The aggregate evidence is similarly constrained. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures, and the funding signal fired first for 4, with median lead of 38 months. The PCA/SAF replay reports 5 of 15 entering an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. These figures describe public-disclosure replays, not prospective performance certification. The underlying availability clock can be explicit publication time or the conservative-looking but still proxy-based 60-day convention.

Why the warning mattered

A funding watch can matter as an investigation-order signal. It says an analyst should examine disclosed liability resilience rather than wait for a formal threshold to settle the question. But it does not say the institution was mechanically destined to fail, and it does not create a calibrated failure probability.

The fraud-masked flag is central rather than incidental. Filings later shown to be falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine. The dossier assigns that problem to the forensic screen; an ordinary disclosure threshold cannot manufacture information absent from the reported record. Missing or misleading disclosure is therefore not evidence of calm.

This distinction also prevents a category error. A filing-period watch is not a market-price signal, because the market layer is separately governed by freshness, identity, rights, display, admission and tier-authority checks. It is not a model derivation, because the proposed liability-to-stress chain is an interpretation rather than an observed causal result.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. This may be hindsight dressed as an early warning: one named replay, a period-end proxy, no bitemporal contract, and an explicitly optimistic lead-time label. A watch index of 45.4 is not a demonstrated probability of default. The first signal has no listed flags. And fraud masking means the apparent disclosure trail may not faithfully represent the underlying institution.

The aggregate diagnostics do not cure those defects. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, which it fails. The leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0; the heuristic AUC is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Those results are too uncertain, and too construction-dependent, to promote this replay into a forecast engine.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an extension of IL&FS’s outcome. As of 2026-09-12, it contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with filings as of 2025-03-31, age 18 months and score 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, as of 2026-03-31, age 6 months and score 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, as of 2025-09-30, age 12 months and score 66.0.

Those are published risk tiers, not credit ratings or failure predictions. The board excludes 21 stale institutions and presents nothing older than 24 months as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design.

Its market layer is dated 2026-09-11 and retrieved on 2026-09-12, but has no admission, publication or tier authority. Rights approval, display approval, model-gate approval and tier-use approval are absent; admitted canonical records are 0/25. Consequently, no market-derived ranking or confirmation may be inferred from it. See the board record and market evidence index.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis fails if prospective, genuinely time-stamped disclosures show that funding watches do not precede independently observed stress, or if PCA and forensic indicators arrive earlier with stronger out-of-sample performance. It also fails operationally where liability data are unavailable, stale or contradicted by verified later information. No signal in those circumstances means no measured signal, not safety.

A proper test needs a bitemporal input contract, actual publication times, pre-specified thresholds and a prospective outcome window. It should report separately on institutions with and without liability disclosures, retain fraud-masking cases rather than converting them into clean negatives, and publish the unavailable population. Until then, IL&FS remains historically suggestive ordering, not a tradable forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

Use LiquiLens for institution and lender balance-sheet risk: disclosed funding conditions, deterioration, forensic boundaries and tiers. Use Seiche for system dollar-funding capacity. Use Undertow for market liquidity and executable exit capacity. These are different products, inputs and claims; they should not be fused into a single stress assertion.

Seiche, generated on 2026-09-12, reports 44.2, EROSION, with guarded confidence. Its editorial account says the calendar is carrying the strain call while overnight-cash pricing still signals abundance; slow-moving or modelled structure leads and current market plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. That is neither IL&FS evidence nor market confirmation of an institution-level funding watch. Undertow reports NORMAL only for IG; several other segments are PARTIAL, with observations ranging from 2026-06-30 to 2026-09-12. Partial coverage is not a clean exit-capacity verdict.

Sources, method, and limits

Sources are the IL&FS replay, Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, Seiche overview, Undertow board, and US non-depository funding watch.

All claims here come from the supplied dossier. Historical evidence uses a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT record, not validated-backtest or real-money eligibility. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic only and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Fraud masking, unavailable liability disclosures, stale exclusions and unapproved market display data are limitations, not inconveniences to be averaged away.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Religare Finvest’s earliest visible strain was funding — but fraud masks the balance-sheet story
entry.summary: The historical replay records a watch-band funding signal before Religare Finvest’s default. That makes disclosed liabilities an early pressure channel to investigate, not a causal explanation or a forecast.
entry.content:
*This is not current news and is not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Religare Finvest, whose default date in this record is 2018-01-18. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome. The filing-based record is construction-PIT, uses a period-end availability proxy where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, and can make lead times optimistic.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is Religare Finvest’s funding side. Its disclosed liability series generated the first recorded signal in the available replay. But that answer must not be inflated into a claim that funding caused the default, that the signal was known on the reporting date, or that a historical watch reading can predict another institution’s outcome.

The case is explicitly fraud-masked. That is not a footnote. It means a threshold engine working from public disclosures can appear to see a balance sheet that later proved incomplete or false. The useful finding is therefore limited: funding weakness was the earliest *visible* pressure channel in this record. The full failure mechanism remains unresolved by this dossier.

The record before the event

Religare Finvest is an NBFC. Its funding lens was scoreable and first entered the watch band at the 2016-03-31 period end, with an index of 44.3 and no listed flags. The record assigns a knowledge-time proxy of 2016-05-30, rather than assuming that the information was available at period end. Against the recorded default date, the replay assigns a 19-month lead.

That apparent lead is a filing-period construction, not a market-price observation and not a tradable timestamp. The historical record is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock where present; otherwise it uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier expressly says lead times are optimistic.

The PCA record has no first action-zone entry for Religare Finvest. This cannot be read as evidence of safety. Fraud-masked institutions can look compliant to a threshold engine when the underlying filings do not faithfully represent the condition being measured. The relevant case file is the Religare Finvest replay; the broader framework is available through the Failure Radar board.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a watch-band condition first. That fact is meaningful only within its disclosure constraint: the lens can operate where an institution provides a liability series. Of 15 failed institutions in the funding summary, 10 had liability disclosures. Funding fired first in 4 of those cases, with a stated median lead of 38 months. That is evidence that disclosed funding can be an early investigative prompt, not evidence that it is universally the earliest signal.

PCA did not register a first action-zone breach in this case. Across the failed-institution summary, 5 of 15 entered the action zone first, with a stated median lead of 41 months. This is a replay of public-disclosure PCA/SAF tripwires, not proof that regulatory thresholds encompass every route to distress. Its method and eligibility limits are set out in the historical validation record.

The wider India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and says 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. Yet it retains the same filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT status, lack of a bitemporal contract, and exclusion from validated backtesting and real-money use. Fraud-masked cases are precisely where an attractive aggregate hit rate can offer the wrong comfort. The market evidence index should be read as diagnostic evidence, not a performance claim.

Why the warning mattered

Liabilities are the channel through which a lender keeps financing assets and meeting obligations. A deterioration in disclosed funding can therefore matter before a formal action-zone threshold appears in public data. In this replay, the funding signal came before the default while PCA has no recorded first action-zone entry.

That sequence supports only a conditional statement: funding was the most plausible first visible pressure channel in the data supplied. It does not establish the mechanics of a creditor withdrawal, a maturity problem, asset deterioration, a transaction, or a management decision. None of those particulars appears in the dossier. Nor does a funding index of 44.3 identify a failure probability.

The distinction matters because this is a model derivation from disclosed information. It is not a market-price signal. It is also not an assertion about the institution’s complete economic condition, especially where fraud masking applies. The responsible conclusion is that the signal merited hard questions about the dependability and resilience of liabilities, not that it supplied a complete causal account.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. The first reading was a watch-band signal with no listed flags, derived under a proxy availability clock. It may have been non-specific noise rather than the earliest economically decisive stress. Because the record uses period end plus 60 days when no explicit publication time exists, even its stated 19-month lead may overstate what was actionable.

Fraud masking is the sharper objection. If disclosures were later shown falsified, public balance-sheet data may have failed to represent the relevant liabilities, assets, conduct, or connected pressures. A seemingly early funding warning could then be incidental. PCA’s absence of a recorded first action-zone entry does not rescue the thesis; it illustrates that threshold-based public evidence was incomplete.

The model diagnostics do not overcome that objection. The leave-one-institution-out hazard result reports row AUC of 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. Its heuristic comparator is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reports AUC of 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and fails that gate. The dossier gives that failure no promotion effect. These are construction-PIT diagnostics, not validation of a predictive failure model.

What today's board shares

As of 2026-09-11, the board shows 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Its dates are not interchangeable with the publication date: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank’s orange row is as of 2025-03-31 and 18 months old; Belstar Microfinance Limited’s yellow row is as of 2026-03-31 and 6 months old; ESAF Small Finance Bank’s yellow row is as of 2025-09-30 and 12 months old. A further 21 institutions are excluded as stale.

Those tiers are published rules over published components, not credit ratings or forecasts. The current market layer is fresh as of 2026-09-10, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. Market-derived display is not approved for every expected canonical record. A fresh retrieval clock is not authorization to use market prices in a tier, and missing or unauthorized market evidence is not calm.

The products also have distinct scopes: Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk; Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. See the Seiche overview, the Undertow board, and LiquiLens research. None supplies a current verdict on Religare Finvest’s historical outcome.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis should fail if a prospective, publication-time-verified sample finds that funding-watch readings do not precede independently documented stress more often than comparable institutions without those readings. It should also fail if forensic findings consistently explain the cases in which funding appears early.

The required test must preserve original filing and publication timestamps, avoid amended or later-known inputs, separate fraud-masked cases, and observe outcomes only after information was genuinely available. The present record cannot satisfy that standard by assertion because it lacks a bitemporal input contract.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with the liability disclosure and ask whether funding is scoreable. Then ask when that disclosure became knowable, rather than treating a period end as a knowledge date. Check whether the funding signal aligns with other published deterioration, a forensic indicator, or an action-zone breach. Only then consider market evidence—and only when it is fresh, clocked, admitted, and authorized.

For Religare Finvest, the chain begins with a watch-band funding reading and ends at a fraud-masked default. The middle is materially unknowable from this dossier. Preserving that gap is the principal discipline of the replay.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies on the Failure Radar board, historical validation record, market evidence index, and Religare Finvest replay. Further desk material is available through LiquiLens investigations.

The historical method uses explicit publication time when present and otherwise period end plus 60 days. It is construction-PIT, not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and subject to optimistic lead times. The conformal alarm is diagnostic only and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Institutions without vetted public dossiers are absent by design, not scored from memory. This is not investment advice.

This is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Global Trust Bank’s first disclosed warning was capital and asset quality, not funding
entry.summary: The historical replay places Global Trust Bank’s first recorded action-zone breach in FY2002, before its default. But falsified filings, unscoreable funding data and optimistic construction-PIT timing mean this is an investigative signal, not a validated forecast.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Global Trust Bank before its default date of 2004-07-24. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere. This is not investment advice, and the screen is not a credit rating.*

Global Trust Bank is the narrow answer to the desk question only in one specific sense: its disclosed capital and asset-quality measures entered the first recorded RBI action zone before the event. The replay records threshold_2 breaches in CRAR and NNPA. That is a filing-period signal: reported balance-sheet weakness at a stated reporting date, made usable at a stated or proxied knowledge time. It is not a market-price signal, because no authorised market reading is used to establish this historical conclusion. And it is not a model derivation masquerading as an observed fact: the lead time follows a construction rule and carries explicit timing limits.

The thesis is therefore modest. On the public record represented here, Global Trust Bank’s first observable fault line was loss-absorption capacity exposed to impaired assets, rather than a disclosed funding alarm. It does not follow that funding was sound, that the reported ratios captured underlying reality, or that this sequence explains every part of the default.

The record before the event

The first PCA action-zone entry is recorded at the period ending 2002-03-31, labelled FY2002. The first-action-zone record identifies CRAR and NNPA breaches, and gives 2002-05-30 as the knowledge-time proxy. The default date is 2004-07-24; the stated lead is 25 months.

Those dates answer different questions. The period end tells us when the reported condition was measured. The knowledge-time proxy estimates when an outside observer could have used it. The default date tells us when the subsequent event occurred. The replay uses an explicit publication clock when one is present and otherwise applies period end plus 60 days. That convention is a modelled availability rule, not proof of what every investor, creditor or supervisor knew on a particular day.

Global Trust Bank is fraud-masked. That disclosure is central rather than decorative: filings later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine, while a reported breach may also understate or misdate real weakness. The full case record is available on the Global Trust Bank replay.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens replays public-disclosure versions of RBI action-zone tripwires. In the historical PCA summary, 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. Global Trust Bank’s stated 25-month lead is below that median, but it still establishes the sequencing claim: disclosed CRAR and NNPA weakness appeared before the event.

The funding lens cannot confirm or contest that sequence for this bank. Global Trust Bank’s funding series was not scoreable; it has no first funding signal and no funding lead time. Among the failed-institution summary, liability disclosures existed for 10 of 15 institutions, the funding signal fired first for 4, and median lead was 38 months. Global Trust Bank is outside that scoreable group.

Missing funding data are an unknown, not a clean bill of health. The lens only sees institutions that disclose a liability series. It cannot infer durable deposits, stable refinancing or the absence of a concealed run-risk where that disclosure is unavailable.

The hazard work supplies another distinction. Its leave-one-institution-out diagnostic reports AUC of 0.752 on 205 rows and 9 events; the disclosure-score heuristic reports 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reports 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and is diagnostic only. These are model results, not observed bank facts, and they do not turn the replay into a tradable or validated failure forecast. The Failure Radar board and historical validation file set out those records.

Why the warning mattered

CRAR and NNPA point to a plausible balance-sheet pressure chain. A capital-adequacy breach indicates less buffer against risk-weighted exposures. A net non-performing-assets breach indicates impaired assets that may require recognition, provisions or losses. If losses consume capital, a thinner buffer can reduce room for further deterioration and make confidence more fragile.

That is a mechanism, not an assertion that the ratios supplied a complete causal account. The filing-period signal says reported capital and reported asset quality crossed the relevant tripwires. It does not demonstrate a contemporaneous liability run. Nor can the absence of a scoreable funding signal establish that funding pressure arrived later.

A market-price signal would be a separately authorised reading of investor repricing. None is required for this historical finding. The current market layer is fresh in clock terms but has no admission, publication or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. It cannot be used to retrospectively validate Global Trust Bank’s warning or to reinforce a current named-institution conclusion.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any broad early-warning thesis. First, the historical evidence is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It lacks a bitemporal input contract, is not validated-backtest eligible and is not real-money eligible. The availability proxy can make measured lead times optimistic.

Second, fraud masking attacks the premise that disclosed ratios approximate economic condition. A threshold engine cannot discover facts hidden by falsified filings. It may flag disclosed deterioration, but it cannot certify the absence of worse deterioration, establish the true timing of losses, or distinguish a reliable report from a misleading one.

Third, no scoreable funding sequence exists for Global Trust Bank. Without it, the proposed progression from impaired assets to capital compression to creditor or depositor sensitivity remains a plausible chain, not a demonstrated chain. The counter-case is not that the PCA record is irrelevant; it is that this evidence cannot prove that public ratios alone would have produced a dependable supervisory verdict, investment decision or generalisable prediction.

The correct use is an alert for investigation. It is not evidence that every CRAR-and-NNPA breach ends in default, and it is not evidence that institutions without a funding flag are safe.

What today's board shares

As of 2026-09-10, the board contains 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green institutions, while 21 stale institutions are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, using a filing as of 2025-03-31 aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, using 2026-03-31 aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, using 2025-09-30 aged 12 months.

These are current screening observations, not analogies to Global Trust Bank and not claims of failure. The market evidence index does not authorise market-derived display or tier use for every expected canonical record. A fresh market pack is therefore not interchangeable with a permitted market-price signal.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity through its overview. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity through its board. These research boundaries are complementary, not licences to fuse unauthorised inputs into a single institutional verdict.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if authentic, time-stamped pre-event disclosures show that Global Trust Bank had not breached the relevant CRAR and NNPA action-zone conditions by the stated knowledge time, or show that the recorded breach derives solely from later reconstruction rather than then-available information.

It strengthens if independently time-stamped liability disclosures show subsequent funding pressure consistent with the proposed chain. Either test must preserve original publication timing and identify falsified filings. Otherwise, apparent lead time remains potentially optimistic.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with impaired assets and reported loss recognition. Ask whether those pressures compress capital. Then ask whether a reduced buffer affects confidence and whether liability pressure is independently observable. Do not reverse the sequence merely because funding distress is easier to narrate after a failure.

For current work, require fresh vetted public dossiers, remove stale, future-dated and unclocked readings from signal or tier authority, and treat absent liability disclosure as unknown. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory.

Sources, method, and limits

The principal records are the Global Trust Bank replay, Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, and LiquiLens research. The US NDFI diagnostic is separate context, not evidence about this institution.

Historical evidence remains PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT; it is not validated-backtest eligible or real-money eligible; lead times may be optimistic; and fraud masking can make reported compliance misleading. The conclusion is limited to the earliest disclosed warning represented in this dossier: capital and asset quality, not a proven funding sequence.

entry.title: Altico’s replay: a stable funding band can still contain a refinancing warning
entry.summary: Altico’s disclosed commercial-paper reliance was a filing-period signal of rollover-freeze exposure well before default. It is a useful historical clue, but the construction-PIT record cannot establish a validated predictive advantage.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Altico before its default date of 2019-09-12. The relevant filing period ended 2017-03-31, with a knowledge-time proxy of 2017-05-30. Current board and market material discussed below is separately as of 2026-09-08.*

The question is not whether Altico’s funding flag predicted its default. The dossier cannot support that claim. It can support a narrower observation: Altico’s first funding signal identified commercial-paper reliance of 29% and explicitly described rollover-freeze exposure, even though the funding index sat in a stable band. That contrast makes Altico a useful replay of a balance-sheet question: which institution should be investigated first when reported broad measures look calm but liabilities require recurring refinancing?

This is a screen for inquiry, not a conclusion about creditworthiness. It is not a credit rating, not investment advice, and not a prediction of institutional failure.

The record before the event

Altico defaulted on 2019-09-12. Its recorded first funding signal belongs to the period ending 2017-03-31, with 2017-05-30 used as the knowledge-time proxy. The recorded lead was 27 months. The funding index was 23.7, its band was stable, and the disclosed flag was CP reliance of 29% with rollover-freeze exposure.

Those items are different kinds of evidence. The period-end balance-sheet observation is a filing-period signal. The knowledge-time proxy is an attempted estimate of when that signal could have been available, not proof of an exact public-information clock. The stable band is an output of a funding index. The rollover flag is a component-level warning. None is a market-price signal, and none is a calibrated probability that Altico would fail.

The Altico replay and Failure Radar board preserve this distinction. A stable aggregate band did not erase the disclosed funding feature; it meant that the broad index did not register a more severe state. The replay therefore argues against reading a single band as a clean bill of health.

What the lenses saw

Altico’s funding lens was scoreable and fired first, with the recorded 27-month lead. The historical funding summary covers 15 failed institutions. Liability disclosures were available for 10, the funding signal fired first for 4, and the median lead was 38 months. These are descriptive replay results, not a validated backtest or a real-money record.

A separate regulatory-action lens gives a different picture. In the public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA or SAF tripwires, 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. The India diagnostic describes 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with a median lead of 21.5 months. These figures do not show that a funding flag dominates a supervisory threshold. They show that different disclosed lenses may register at different points in a failure sequence.

The historical record is explicitly PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Where an explicit publication clock was unavailable, the availability basis was period end plus 60 days. The dossier says lead times are optimistic. A filing-period value may therefore have been treated as knowable earlier than a user could have verified it.

The historical validation record adds a further restraint. Its temporal diagnostic AUC was 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and did not pass. The held-out comparison also reported a heuristic AUC of 0.799 against hazard AUC of 0.752 on the same rows. The model derivation is consequently diagnostic only; it cannot promote the construction-PIT evidence into a settled forecasting claim.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered as a question about liability structure, not as proof of causation. The dossier’s own wording identifies rollover-freeze exposure. Commercial paper is therefore the specific disclosed channel worth examining in this replay: refinancing dependence can be important even when a wider funding index remains stable.

That conclusion should be kept at the level the evidence permits. Altico’s flag did not establish that refinancing pressure caused the default. The dossier does not provide an event-by-event account of funding withdrawals, asset sales, liquidity use, hidden losses, or misconduct. It does show a disclosed feature, a later default date, and a recorded lead under a proxy availability convention.

The more defensible lesson is about aggregation. A composite can summarize multiple inputs while a discrete component identifies a vulnerability the composite does not elevate. The filing-period signal is therefore a reason to inspect refinancing sensitivity; it is not a market verdict and not a model-derived failure frequency.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat an overconfident thesis. Altico may be an anecdote selected after the event. Its funding band was stable. Among failed institutions with the stated historical coverage, only 4 funding signals fired first, and only 10 of 15 had usable liability disclosures. The lens is conditioned by disclosure availability. Institutions without a liability series are not demonstrated to be safe; they are simply not observable through that particular lens.

Timing may also flatter the result. The dossier warns that period-end-plus-60-day availability can make lead times optimistic. Its hazard panel excluded 179 censored or unusable rows, while the temporal diagnostic did not clear its stated gate. Filings later shown to be falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the dossier assigns that limitation to a forensic screen. Altico is not fraud-masked, but the broader masking risk remains.

A serious reader can therefore reject the proposition that CP reliance reliably identifies the next failure. The evidence supports only a conditional investigative rule: where the disclosure exists, a rollover flag may deserve attention alongside, rather than instead of, other lenses.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not evidence about Altico’s past and must not be fused with the replay. As of 2026-09-08, the board reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale institutions are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, based on 2025-03-31 material aged 18 months, with a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow from 2026-03-31, aged 6 months, with a score of 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow from 2025-09-30, aged 12 months, with a score of 66.0.

These are published screen tiers, not ratings or forecasts. The stated rule can use levels, deterioration, funding flags, forensic indicators and, only when authoritative, market drawdown inputs. The market evidence endpoint is fresh by its pack clock, but has no publication, admission, knowledge, or tier authority. Rights and display approval were not granted for every expected canonical record. Freshness is not authorization, and this market layer cannot validate or rank a current institution here.

The next falsifiable test

The Altico inference should fail if prospectively collected disclosures of short-term rollover dependence do not identify earlier subsequent funding strain than comparable disclosed balance sheets. It should also fail if actual publication timestamps remove the apparent lead created under the period-end-plus-60-day proxy.

A credible test would fix the funding definition before outcomes, use vetted public dossiers, record actual availability, and preserve the rule before observing subsequent events. It would need to improve on the disclosed heuristic in a future temporal sample. Until then, the replay remains a historical mechanism test, not a deployable prediction engine.

Follow the pressure chain

The pressure chain begins with the liability mix and its refinancing requirement. Altico’s disclosed CP-reliance flag places attention on that requirement, but does not establish its later path. LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; its composite was 44.9, EROSION, with guarded confidence because modelled or slow-moving structure led current market-plumbing confirmation. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity and reports several segments as PARTIAL.

These are separate layers. They are not confirmation that Altico’s historical mechanism is active now, and no layer substitutes for another.

Sources, method, and limits

Key dossier-linked materials include the Failure Radar board, validation record, market evidence, Altico replay, and LiquiLens research.

Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current on the board; failed institutions are presented through replay evidence instead. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design and are not scored from memory. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. Missing liability disclosure is not safety, missing system context is not calm, and a historical replay is not a forecast.

entry.title: Abhyudaya’s earliest replay signal was asset quality, not funding
entry.summary: The historical record places an NNPA action-zone breach ahead of any recorded funding signal at Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank. That ordering warrants scrutiny, not a claim that a screen foresaw or caused the eventual event.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines information associated with Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank before its 2023-11-24 default date. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution.*

The central finding is narrow. In this replay, Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank first entered the recorded action zone at 2021-03-31, in FY2021, on NNPA. Its funding lens was scoreable but recorded no first signal. The balance-sheet pressure visible first in the disclosed record was therefore asset quality, not a liability-side alarm.

That is a filing-period signal, not proof that market participants acted on it at that moment, and not a model-derived probability of failure. The difference is decisive. A period end identifies when a reported condition existed; a publication clock identifies when it could have been known from the available public record; a model combines inputs under rules that may be useful for presentation but cannot establish causation. This replay has a knowledge-time proxy of 2021-05-30, based on period end plus 60 days where no explicit publication clock is present.

The record before the event

The case record identifies an NNPA breach as Abhyudaya’s first recorded supervisory action-zone signal. It reports a 29-month lead to the default date and marks the institution as not fraud-masked. The proper conclusion is not that NNPA alone determined the outcome.
