It is that the disclosed asset-quality condition was the first recorded trigger demanding closer work on loss absorption, funding disclosures, and the path between them.

The replay is classified as PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and does not have a bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it uses the period-end-plus-60-days proxy. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic.

That limitation bars a stronger claim about real-time foresight. A threshold may have become public later than the proxy assumes. Equally, a measured lead is not an investable lead. The relevant evidence is available in the Abhyudaya replay and the wider LiquiLens replay archive.

What the lenses saw

The PCA/SAF lens recorded the NNPA breach first. In the PCA summary, 15 institutions failed, 5 entered the action zone first, and median lead was 41 months. The funding summary describes a different and materially constrained lens: of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures, 4 fired a funding signal first, and median lead was 38 months.

Those summaries do not show that either lens predicts an individual outcome. They show that different public disclosures can reveal different parts of a pressure chain. The funding lens can only assess institutions with a disclosed liability series. No fired funding signal is therefore not evidence of stable funding; it can be an observation boundary.

The broader India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports that 88.9% of non-fraud failures were flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. It carries the same construction-PIT status and optimistic-lead warning. Readers should treat the Failure Radar board and historical validation record as diagnostics, not as a promoted failure model.

The hazard work reinforces that restraint. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The comparison heuristic reached 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Its temporal AUC was 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is explicitly diagnostic only. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote.

Why the warning mattered

An NNPA action-zone breach matters because it directs attention to the asset side before a funding alarm is recorded. If impaired assets weaken, the questions become whether loss recognition, provisions, earnings capacity, capital resilience, and liability disclosures can withstand the strain. The dossier supports that investigative sequence; it does not supply evidence for a deposit run, a liquidity event, or a single causal mechanism at Abhyudaya.

The absence of a first funding signal is useful precisely because it prevents the article from asserting one. It leaves a limited proposition: asset quality was the earlier recorded pressure point in this replay. A supervisory-relevant tripwire is more informative than an isolated ratio, but it still cannot reveal all information held by management or supervisors, or decide whether a breach would be cured.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. An NNPA breach may be lagging, manageable, or shaped by recognition timing. The decisive pressure could instead have been governance, operations, funding, or another unobserved channel. The funding lens’s silence cannot distinguish calm from insufficient liability disclosure. Nor does the replay establish that an asset-quality signal was the first condition known to all relevant actors.

The timing limitation sharpens that objection. Without a bitemporal input contract, and with a fallback publication proxy, the apparent ordering can change when a true filing-availability archive is available. The dossier also warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. Abhyudaya is not fraud-masked, but that boundary still prevents a clean screen history from becoming proof of safety.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from the Abhyudaya replay. As of 2026-09-07, it has 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, using a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months, with a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, using a 2026-03-31 filing aged 6 months, with a score of 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, using a 2025-09-30 filing aged 12 months, with a score of 66.0.

No market drawdown is supplied for those rows. Market data are fresh, but they have no publication, admission, model-gate, or tier authority because rights and display use are not approved for every expected canonical record. They cannot validate names or tiers. The board also excludes 21 stale institutions. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory.

The next falsifiable test

The asset-quality-first reading fails if properly time-stamped disclosures show that the NNPA breach was cured without material deterioration in loss-absorption capacity, while an independently documented funding or other channel appeared earlier and proved more consequential. It also fails if a true publication-time archive materially reverses the ordering.

The practical test is therefore prospective and archival: preserve original availability times, separate filing conditions from public knowledge, and observe whether an asset-quality trigger precedes a demonstrable balance-sheet constraint. Until that standard is met, the replay supports scrutiny rather than certainty.

Follow the pressure chain

Begin with the disclosed action-zone condition. Then examine the transmission through loss absorption and liability disclosures, without treating missing series as reassuring. Only after that should an analyst ask whether market pricing or executable exit conditions independently confirm stress.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity; its overview reads 44.9, EROSION, with guarded confidence as of 2026-09-07. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity; its board has multiple PARTIAL segments. Those are distinct product boundaries, not interchangeable confirmations of Abhyudaya’s historical mechanism.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses the dossier’s market evidence index, US NDFI watch, LiquiLens research, and cited replay and validation materials. Components are replayed independently on the 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic; its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. Fresh readings here still lack the approvals required for per-name publication and tier use. The conclusion is bounded: Abhyudaya’s NNPA breach was the earliest recorded screen signal in this replay. It identifies an asset-quality question worth investigating, not inevitability, complete causation, a present judgment on another institution, or investment advice.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: United Western Bank’s first recorded warning was on the balance sheet, not in funding
entry.summary: The historical replay places an NNPA action-zone breach before default, while the available funding lens records no first signal. That ordering is meaningful, but it is a construction-PIT diagnostic rather than a prediction rule.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines United Western Bank through a construction-PIT public-disclosure record; similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

United Western Bank’s earliest recorded pressure in this file was a disclosed balance-sheet signal. The bank entered an RBI action-zone threshold in the period ended 2001-03-31, on an NNPA breach. The replay assigns that observation a knowledge-time proxy of 2001-05-30. Default followed on 2006-09-02, producing a 63-month lead in the record.

The claim needs to remain narrow. The PCA screen fired before the event; the funding lens, though scoreable for the bank, records no first signal. That is an ordering of available disclosures, not proof that funding was sound, that the NNPA breach caused default, or that every comparable breach will lead to distress. It distinguishes a filing-period signal from a model derivation and from a market-price signal that this case does not supply.

The record before the event

The core chronology is short. The period ended 2001-03-31 is the first action-zone observation, classified as threshold_2; NNPA is the listed breach. The knowledge-time proxy is 2001-05-30. The recorded default date is 2006-09-02. The United Western Bank replay and the historical validation record are the relevant source records.

This is a public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA/SAF tripwires. Where an explicit publication clock is present, the construction uses it. Otherwise, it uses period end plus 60 days. That convention is a proxy for availability, not evidence of what every decision-maker knew. The dossier explicitly says the resulting lead times are optimistic, that the record lacks a bitemporal input contract, and that it is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible.

The broader PCA summary provides context but cannot establish this bank’s causal history. It covers 15 failed institutions, with five entering an action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. United Western Bank is one file inside that limited record, not confirmation that action-zone entry is a universal precursor.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw an NNPA threshold breach. The funding lens had no first signal. Read literally, that is the result: the disclosed asset-quality and supervisory-threshold screen appeared first in this replay.

A non-signal from funding is not a positive finding about deposits, liquidity, or liability resilience. The funding lens only sees institutions with usable liability disclosures. In the historical set, liability disclosures exist for 10 of 15 failed institutions; a funding signal fired first for four, with a median lead of 38 months. Limited visibility makes absence especially unsuitable as reassurance.

The model layer is a separate matter. Its hazard panel contains 205 rows, nine events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic scored 0.799 on the same held-out rows. A temporal diagnostic returned 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and did not pass. It remains diagnostic only and cannot promote the construction-PIT result.

Nor is there a usable market-price confirmation here. The market layer is fresh and clocked, but has no admission, tier, or publication authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. It therefore cannot confirm, soften, or rank the institutional conclusion. The market evidence index documents that boundary.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it identified a concrete disclosed condition before default and before any recorded funding signal. It changed the appropriate question from whether the bank looked broadly normal to whether the deterioration would reverse, persist, or deepen.

That is not a complete pressure chain. The dossier provides no intervening liability-run chronology, market repricing sequence, or decomposition that would establish why default followed. A threshold is a filing-period screen, not a calibrated failure probability. The hazard model is a model derivation with its own weak promotion status; a Merton measure, where available elsewhere, is a market repricing signal rather than a calibrated failure frequency. These categories should not be fused into certainty.

The replay marks United Western Bank as fraud_masked: false. That does not guarantee perfect disclosure. The method note cautions that filings later shown falsified can appear compliant to threshold engines; the forensic screen owns that limitation. Missing evidence must not be translated into calm.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any stronger version of the thesis. The apparent 63-month lead may partly reflect construction rather than an actionable contemporaneous advantage. The period-end-plus-60-days convention is conservative only relative to a period-end assumption; it is not a complete historical publication archive. Without a bitemporal input contract, amended data, timing gaps, and incomplete disclosure remain live threats to inference.

Further, an action-zone breach can identify stress without identifying a terminal outcome. The PCA cohort itself does not show that every failure was first captured by that lens. Funding may also have been stressed in ways that the disclosed-liability series did not measure. Therefore the defensible conclusion is limited to the available record: the PCA observation came first, while the funding lens did not record a first signal.

This is not a credit rating. It is also not evidence that a similar institution should fail, or that an investor could have converted the replay’s lead into a reliable trade or exit decision.

What today's board shares

Today’s Failure Radar board is separate from this historical clock. As of 2026-09-06, it shows zero red, one orange, three yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 are excluded as stale. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, while Belstar Microfinance Limited and ESAF Small Finance Bank are yellow.

Those tiers are published rules over published components, not predictions of failure. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory. Current market observations cannot supply authority where display rights and canonical-record approvals are absent.

The next falsifiable test

The thesis would fail if a prospective bitemporal dataset, using actual publication times and complete liability disclosures, found that action-zone breaches did not precede adverse outcomes more usefully than funding signals. It would also fail in an individual case if a disclosed breach reversed without a later adverse event while funding consistently supplied the earlier dependable warning.

That test must preserve the distinction between a filing-period observation, a market-price signal, and a model output. Construction-PIT diagnostics are useful prompts for investigation, not tradable timing rules.

Follow the pressure chain

For this bank, the observable chain is deliberately sparse: period ended 2001-03-31; NNPA breach; threshold_2; knowledge-time proxy of 2001-05-30; no first funding signal; default on 2006-09-02. Each arrow describes ordering, not unobserved causation.

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche covers system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. The Seiche overview reports EROSION with guarded confidence; the Undertow board includes PARTIAL and NORMAL segment readings. Neither is institution-level confirmation for this replay.

Sources, method, and limits

Primary references are the Failure Radar board, validation record, market evidence index, and United Western Bank replay. Additional desk context is available through LiquiLens research and LiquiLens investigations.

The historical evidence is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated for backtesting or real-money use, lacks a bitemporal input contract, and may overstate lead times. Missing funding or market evidence is not evidence of calm. This article is not investment advice.

entry.title: Sambandh Finserve’s disclosed funding flag was the earliest visible pressure point
entry.summary: This historical replay identifies wholesale leverage as the first disclosed funding signal before Sambandh Finserve’s recorded default. It is not a market-price call, a causal finding, or evidence that a threshold model could see through fraud-masked filings.
entry.content:
*This is not current news and not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Sambandh Finserve using a construction-PIT record. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

Sambandh Finserve is the clearest answer this replay can offer to the question of which institution balance sheet should have felt financial stress first. Its funding record turned fragile at the filing period ending 2016-03-31, when disclosed wholesale leverage was 8.51x against a 7x threshold. The replay assigns that observation a knowledge-time proxy of 2016-05-30 and records a 52-month lead to the default date of 2020-10-13.

That is a filing-period signal, not a contemporaneous market-price signal and not a model-derived probability of failure. It says disclosed liabilities warranted investigation before the event. It does not establish that the ratio caused default, that creditors withdrew funding, or that the underlying disclosures were economically complete. The fraud-masked designation is decisive: a threshold engine can be reassured by filings later shown to be falsified.

The record before the event

The first scoreable funding signal is attached to the 2016-03-31 period end. Where no explicit publication clock is present, the reconstruction uses period end plus a 60-day filing lag, producing the 2016-05-30 knowledge-time proxy. That convention avoids pretending the information was known on the period-end date. It does not prove that a lender, investor, or supervisor actually possessed every relevant input then.

The funding index was 78.7, in the fragile band, with the explicit flag of wholesale leverage 8.51x >= 7x. The recorded default followed on 2020-10-13. This is the full supported sequence. The dossier does not provide a loan-book chronology, liquidity-buffer data, lender concentration, refinancing negotiations, creditor actions, or a Sambandh market-price series. It cannot support a complete causal account.

The underlying historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, lacks a bitemporal input contract, and may make lead times optimistic. The Failure Radar board, historical validation record, and Sambandh replay are research materials, not proof of live decision-time knowledge.

What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a disclosed liability-side vulnerability. Wholesale leverage crossed its stated threshold, producing the fragile classification. That makes the funding structure an investigative priority because liabilities can impose a timetable: funding may need to be refinanced, repriced, or replaced while asset cash flows may arrive later or prove less dependable. This is a mechanism implied by the category of signal, not a claim about an unobserved Sambandh refinancing event.

The PCA record did not provide a competing early warning. It has no first action-zone entry and no PCA lead time. That is an absence of a qualifying PCA result in this replay, not evidence that the institution was sound. In a fraud-masked case, apparently compliant public data are especially weak grounds for reassurance.

Across the historical failed-institution sample, the funding lens had liability disclosures for 10 of 15 failed institutions, fired first for 4, and had a median lead of 38 months. The PCA/SAF replay covered 15 failed institutions; 5 entered the action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. These are descriptive construction-PIT results. They do not validate a supervisory rule, establish an investable strategy, or turn a funding threshold into a forecast.

Why the warning mattered

A single leverage ratio cannot diagnose insolvency. Its importance is narrower: liabilities are often the balance-sheet side capable of forcing a timetable. A fragile funding classification should prompt questions about maturity, refinancing terms, cash generation, and disclosure quality. It should not settle those questions.

Sambandh’s fraud-masked status prevents the stronger conclusion. The dossier says that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. The funding lens neither solved the case nor became irrelevant. It identified a disclosed fragility, while the record warns that disclosed fragility may understate or misstate economic reality.

This distinction also separates a filing signal from a model derivation. The funding flag is a published threshold outcome over disclosed data. The historical hazard work is a separate diagnostic exercise: its leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, while the heuristic was 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Neither result changes what Sambandh’s disclosed filing did or did not reveal. The model result is not an observation of Sambandh’s market price, and it is not a calibrated claim about its failure frequency.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat the thesis. Wholesale leverage above 7x may be an imperfect screening convention rather than a durable measure of financial stress. A 52-month interval leaves ample room for conditions to change. The period-end-plus-60-day proxy may overstate usable lead. Most importantly, fraud masking means the public inputs may not have represented the institution’s actual condition.

The model diagnostics reinforce rather than resolve that objection. The temporal test AUC was 0.645 against a 0.65 diagnostic gate and did not pass. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic only: its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. A skeptic can reasonably treat Sambandh as an investigative case study, not evidence of a generally deployable failure model.

The absence of a Sambandh market-price series is also material. No price-based confirmation is available in this record. Therefore the thesis cannot be that markets recognized the vulnerability first, or even that markets confirmed it at all. The replay identifies the earliest visible disclosed funding flag among the supplied lenses, not the earliest economically real stress signal.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is separate from this failed-institution replay. As of 2026-09-05, it has 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions, and excludes 21 stale names. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange at 74.9 on a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8 on a 2026-03-31 filing aged 6 months; ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 66.0 on a 2025-09-30 filing aged 12 months. None has listed fired signals in those comparison rows.

Those placements are not Sambandh analogues, credit ratings, or failure predictions. The market layer is fresh by its clock, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority: rights and expected-record approvals are incomplete. Its readings cannot convert current board positions into market-confirmed calls. See the market evidence index for that restriction.

The next falsifiable test

A prospective test would record future funding flags at actual publication time rather than a period-end proxy, then compare them with later independently observable refinancing stress, liquidity pressure, or deterioration. If flagged institutions do not show earlier or more frequent subsequent pressure than comparable unflagged institutions, the claim that this lens identifies the balance sheet that feels stress first fails.

That test must preserve negative evidence. No liability disclosure is not a clean bill of health; no market reading is not reassurance. A credible prospective record needs publication clocks, underlying disclosures, and explicit handling of fraud-masking risk before a diagnostic can be promoted. It must also keep filing observations, market observations, and model outputs separate rather than treating them as interchangeable confirmation.

Follow the pressure chain

Start with disclosed wholesale leverage and the threshold. Then ask whether funding could impose a timetable. Next test disclosure completeness and reliability, because fraud masking can sever the link between reported ratios and economic reality. Finally, separate the institution’s condition from the market’s capacity to absorb an exit.

This is a product boundary, not a combined verdict. LiquiLens research addresses institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche’s overview addresses system dollar-funding capacity. Undertow’s board addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity. They answer different questions.

The distinction matters here. A funding flag belongs to the balance-sheet inquiry. A usable market-derived reading would concern repricing or exit conditions, but the current market layer lacks publication and tier authority. A hazard statistic is a model diagnostic over its own construction record. None can repair the missing evidence in either of the others.

Sources, method, and limits

The relevant sources are the Sambandh Finserve replay, Failure Radar board, validation file, and market evidence index. Current presentation uses one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier; failed institutions are replayed instead. Nothing is scored from memory.

The conclusion is deliberately narrow: disclosed wholesale leverage supplied the earliest visible reason to investigate Sambandh’s funding side. It does not show causation, predict default, validate the model for real-money use, or imply safety where signals are absent.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: New India Co-operative Bank showed a disclosed stress signal first — but the replay cannot explain the whole event
entry.summary: The record places an NNPA action-zone breach before the later event. That is a filing-period warning, not a market-price confirmation or a model-derived failure forecast — and the fraud-masked designation sharply limits what the screen could know.
entry.content:
This historical replay is not current news and not a forecast.

*This is a historical replay, not current news, a forecast, or investment advice. It uses a public-disclosure construction-PIT record. Similar signals do not imply the same outcome.*

The narrow answer to LiquiLens’s question is New India Co-operative Bank. Its disclosed balance sheet entered an RBI action zone before its later event. That does not establish that a screen foresaw the failure, detected fraud, or supplied a complete causal account. The institution is marked fraud-masked. A filing can therefore contain a valid warning while remaining an incomplete, and potentially unreliable, picture of the underlying condition.

The lesson is about escalation rather than prophecy. A disclosed NNPA breach warranted investigation. It was not proof that all reported measures were accurate, a market confirmation of distress, or a calibrated probability of failure.

The record before the event

New India Co-operative Bank’s first recorded PCA/SAF action-zone signal was an NNPA breach for the period ended 2021-03-31, identified as FY2021. The replay assigns 2021-05-30 as its knowledge-time proxy. Where no explicit publication time is present, the method uses period end plus 60 days. The recorded lead from that proxy to the default date of 2025-02-13 is 44 months.

Those are distinct clocks. The period end is the accounting date of the disclosed condition. The knowledge-time proxy estimates when a reader could have encountered it. The default date marks the event used in the replay. None is a market-price timestamp, and treating them as interchangeable would exaggerate what the evidence establishes.

The case appears in the New India Co-operative Bank replay and within the Failure Radar board. Both are retrospective evidence interfaces. They do not show that an investor, depositor, supervisor, or counterparty acted on the signal at the proxy date.

Fraud masking is the central qualification. The dossier states that institutions whose filings were later shown to have been falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine. The NNPA breach remains a disclosed warning. But apparent compliance elsewhere cannot become reassurance, and the replay cannot claim access to facts not faithfully represented in public disclosure.

What the lenses saw

The PCA/SAF lens recorded a specific filing-period signal: NNPA crossed its action-zone rule in FY2021. This is the clearest finding. It says a disclosed asset-quality measure met a published tripwire. It does not say why the institution later reached its event, nor does it determine the timing of every pressure that followed.

The funding lens did not provide a first signal for this institution. That is a missing-data disclosure, not a favourable finding. The funding lens only sees institutions with a disclosed liability series, and the supplied record provides no funding signal here.

Across the PCA summary, 15 failed institutions are included, 5 entered the action zone first, and median lead was 41 months. In the funding summary, 10 of the 15 had liability disclosures, 4 had funding signals that fired first, and median lead was 38 months. These are descriptions of a replay, not prospective performance claims.

The historical evidence is labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. Availability uses an explicit publication clock when present, otherwise period end plus 60 days. The dossier explicitly says lead times are optimistic. The historical validation record retains those constraints.

A separate hazard diagnostic does not rescue a stronger claim. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a 0.338 to 1.0 confidence interval. The disclosure heuristic records 0.799 on the same held-out rows. Temporal AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote, so this remains diagnostic only.

Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because a disclosed action-zone condition appeared before the event. The dossier does not prove a full transmission mechanism. The defensible inference is limited: the public record supplied an asset-quality escalation point. It does not establish how much subsequent pressure travelled through earnings, capital, funding, governance, fraud, or another channel.

That restraint separates claims often collapsed into one. The NNPA breach is a filing-period signal. The supplied material contains no admitted market-price signal for this name. Scores, PDs, and tiers are model derivations governed by stated rules; they are not observations that a failure was already known to the market.

The method note says components are replayed independently and fused only for presentation. PD levels are corpus-fitted and prior-corrected to a 0.25% annual population base rate. The Merton PD is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. Neither construction converts the disclosed NNPA breach into proof that the model identified the later outcome in full.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case defeats a claim of prescience. A period-end proxy can place a warning earlier than the point at which a particular user could have accessed, interpreted, and trusted the relevant information. The dossier calls the resulting lead times optimistic. Without a bitemporal input contract, historical availability and amended values remain material limitations.

More fundamentally, one NNPA breach is not a complete failure narrative. The funding lens did not fire first. The bank is fraud-masked. The supplied evidence does not establish continuous deterioration from the FY2021 filing to the later event, and it does not show that a threshold can reliably separate a recoverable institution from one that will fail.

Fraud intensifies the objection. A threshold engine can identify an adverse disclosed condition while missing material facts outside reliable disclosure. The strongest conclusion is therefore not that the model caught the event. It is that the disclosed record gave a reason to investigate earlier and more deeply.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an extension of this replay. As of 2026-09-04, it contains 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. It excludes 21 stale institutions. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current, while institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design. Absence is not calm; it is an evidence boundary.

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 record aged 18 months, with a 74.9 score. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow on a 2026-03-31 record aged 6 months, with a 77.8 score. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow on a 2025-09-30 record aged 12 months, with a 66.0 score. The listed comparison rows show no fired signals and no market drawdown field.

The market pack is fresh as of 2026-09-04, but it has no admission, publication, signal, or tier authority. Rights and display approvals are incomplete for every expected canonical record. The market evidence endpoint documents this restriction. A fresh retrieval clock is not, by itself, an authorized market-price signal for board tiering.

The next falsifiable test

This thesis would weaken if prospective, bitemporal evidence showed that action-zone breaches added no useful lead after actual publication availability was established, or if fraud-masked institutions made disclosed triggers indistinguishable from benign cases. It would strengthen only if eligible dossiers were frozen at authoritative publication times, later-amended values were excluded, and outcomes followed the signals.

The practical test is to preserve each eligible public dossier at its actual publication time and compare action-zone information with the disclosure heuristic prospectively. Until that exists, this remains a historical diagnostic, not a production failure forecast.

Follow the pressure chain

LiquiLens covers institution and lender balance-sheet risk. That is the relevant boundary for filing disclosures, action-zone conditions, and missing-dossier limits. Seiche’s overview covers system dollar-funding capacity. Its composite reads 44.8, EROSION, with guarded confidence because modelled or slow-moving structure leads current market plumbing.

Undertow’s board covers market liquidity and executable exit capacity. IG is NORMAL, while several segments are PARTIAL. These are complementary contexts, not confirmation of a claim about New India Co-operative Bank. They use different objects, clocks, and authority conditions.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies on the Failure Radar board, the validation dataset, the market evidence record, the New India replay, Seiche’s overview, Undertow’s board, and the replay archive.

Missing, stale, future-dated, and unclocked market readings may remain visible but cannot create a signal or tier. The conformal alarm remains diagnostic and has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. This is the research boundary: a public-disclosure replay can identify a disclosed warning, but it cannot validate historical tradability, reconstruct hidden facts, or turn a model derivation into an observed market verdict.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Nedungadi Bank’s first recorded pressure point was capital, not a market call
entry.summary: The historical replay identifies a CRAR action-zone breach before Nedungadi Bank’s default, but its timing is a filing-availability proxy and its evidence cannot support a forecast, a credit verdict, or a claim of causation.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Nedungadi Bank through a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT record. The default date is 2002-11-02; the first action-zone period-end is 1999-03-31, with a knowledge-time proxy of 1999-05-30. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is Nedungadi Bank’s disclosed capital position. The first recorded qualifying signal was a CRAR breach in the RBI action zone, attached to FY1999. That is a filing-period signal: a reconstruction of when a disclosed condition could have become available under the dossier’s publication convention. It is not a market-price signal, because no market-derived measure establishes the case. Nor is it a model derivation that can convert the breach into a failure probability.

The distinction is decisive. The replay measures a lead of 41 months from its availability proxy to the recorded default. It does not show that every relevant observer possessed, interpreted, or acted on the information at that time. It does not prove that the capital breach caused the default. It says only that, among the available lenses, capital was the first recorded action-zone pressure point.

The record before the event

Nedungadi Bank entered the first RBI PCA/SAF action zone at the 1999-03-31 period-end, designated FY1999, because of CRAR. Where no explicit publication clock is present, the record uses period-end plus 60 days. That yields the 1999-05-30 knowledge-time proxy. The institution’s default is recorded on 2002-11-02.

This is explicitly labelled PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. It is not eligible for validated backtesting or real-money use; it has no bitemporal input contract; and the dossier says its lead times are optimistic. A reporting date, a proxy availability date, and the moment at which a depositor, investor, supervisor, or counterparty understands a filing are different events. The 41-month interval must therefore be read as a construction result, not as a contemporaneous trading or supervisory record.

The case file is available in the Nedungadi Bank replay. The wider rule set and roster are on the Failure Radar board. Neither source makes the historical replay a present-tense finding.

Nedungadi carries no fraud-masked flag. That is not a general assurance about disclosure quality. The validation record warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that failure mode. Missing, unusable, or misleading disclosure is not evidence of calm.

What the lenses saw

The PCA lens recorded CRAR as Nedungadi’s first action-zone breach. The funding lens was not scoreable: it has no first signal and no lead time for this institution. That absence is a missing-data disclosure, not a favorable funding conclusion. The funding lens can only observe institutions that disclose a liability series.

The historical summaries illustrate why the two lenses should not be collapsed into one story. Of 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. Of the same 15 failures, 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures show that funding and action-zone signals can arrive separately. They do not establish that one lens universally leads the other, and they cannot resolve Nedungadi’s funding condition without the missing liability series.

The hazard work is also diagnostic rather than promotable evidence. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal test AUC is 0.645, below its 0.65 gate. The panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows are excluded. The historical validation record is a limit disclosure, not a performance certificate.

Why the warning mattered

An RBI action-zone breach matters because it identifies a regulatory threshold tied, in this case, to capital. The defensible inference is not that the threshold supplied a default clock. It is that a breach can identify a balance-sheet constraint before a recorded failure, and that this constraint deserves investigation alongside asset quality, earnings, funding, management response, and disclosure reliability.

For Nedungadi, the warning mattered because it was concrete and independently specified: CRAR, not an after-the-event composite score and not a price-based alarm. The record supports a pressure-chain hypothesis in which constrained loss-absorption capacity may make adverse developments harder to accommodate. But the dossier does not supply the intervening causal history needed to prove that sequence. It provides no scoreable funding confirmation and no market-price evidence for the institution.

That restraint is the point. A filing-period breach can be useful without being a forecast. A market-price signal would instead describe repricing in traded prices; none is established here. A model output would be a derivation from its inputs and assumptions; it cannot repair unavailable funding evidence or turn proxy timing into observed knowledge.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any inflated version of the thesis. A capital threshold breach can be an early, noisy regulatory classification rather than a reliable marker of eventual failure. A lender may restore capital, reduce risk, improve earnings, obtain support, or otherwise leave the pressure zone. The 41-month lead leaves substantial room for paths other than default.

The construction itself could overstate the apparent advance warning. The 60-day filing convention is a proxy when an explicit publication clock is absent. The dossier says lead times are optimistic and denies validated-backtest and real-money eligibility. Its temporal diagnostic does not clear its stated gate. Its PCA summary is a public-disclosure replay of RBI tripwires, not a causal account of each institution’s failure.

The missing funding series is equally damaging to an overconfident thesis. The record cannot demonstrate a deposit or wholesale-funding event for Nedungadi, cannot rank capital against funding for this case, and cannot establish that capital was the only important vulnerability. The correct conclusion remains narrower: CRAR was the first recorded qualifying lens, not the sole explanation.

What today's board shares

The current board is separate from the Nedungadi replay. As of 2026-09-03, it shows 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a score of 74.9 and an as-of date of 2025-03-31. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8, as of 2026-03-31. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 66.0, as of 2025-09-30.

Those tiers are screens over published components, not credit ratings or failure predictions. The board excludes 21 stale institutions. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current.

The market layer was retrieved on 2026-09-03 but has no publication, admission, signal, or tier authority. Rights and display approvals are not in place for every expected canonical record. The market evidence index therefore cannot supply a market confirmation for the board or for the Nedungadi replay.

The next falsifiable test

The capital-first interpretation would weaken if prospectively timestamped disclosures showed that the CRAR breach was not available by the assumed proxy date. It would weaken further if comparable action-zone breaches regularly resolved without subsequent deterioration, while institutions without such breaches displayed equal or greater recorded distress.

A stronger test requires actual publication clocks, preserved amended-file vintages, distinct capital and liability series, and outcomes observed without retrofitting the rule. Until then, the 41-month figure is an investigative clue. It is not a calibrated probability, a trade signal, or investment advice.

Follow the pressure chain

For historical institution work, begin with the LiquiLens replay archive and LiquiLens research. LiquiLens concerns institution and lender balance-sheet risk; it is the appropriate lens for a disclosed capital breach and for gaps in institution-level evidence.

The products should not be merged into a single stress verdict. Seiche addresses system dollar-funding capacity, as described in the Seiche overview. Undertow addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity, as described in the Undertow board. Their different coverage, clocks, and authority gates prevent any of them from substituting for Nedungadi’s unavailable funding evidence.

Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied Failure Radar board, historical validation, market evidence, and Nedungadi replay. Historical components were replayed independently on a 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation.

The conformal alarm remains diagnostic; its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Where present in the broader framework, Merton PD is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. These limits are not footnotes to the conclusion; they define what the conclusion can mean.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

entry.title: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank’s first visible pressure point is asset quality, not a confirmed funding event
entry.summary: Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is the sole orange institution in the current monitored set, but the designation rests on an aged filing-period signal: GNPA of 9.4%. Market confirmation is unavailable for publication, and key funding lenses are dark.
entry.content:
The finding

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is the balance sheet in this monitored set most likely to register visible financial pressure first. That is a conditional filing-based finding, not a claim that failure is imminent. The current orange tier rests on disclosed asset quality and a modelled monitoring probability, while the evidence needed to establish a funding event or a market repricing is unavailable or inadmissible.

The key disclosed burden is GNPA of 9.4%. The subject dossier is as of 2025-03-31 and is aged 18 months at publication. Its monitored PD_12m is 0.0031, compared with 0.0016 at the FY2024 reference point; delta_pd_12m is 0.0015. Those are model derivations from the filing record, not observed market prices and not a credit rating. The model basis explicitly identifies GNPA 9.4%.

That distinction is central. A filing-period signal says what the reported balance sheet showed at a stated reporting date. A market-price signal would say how tradable claims were priced at an admissible observation time. A model derivation transforms disclosed inputs into a monitoring estimate under stated assumptions. None of those is interchangeable. The orange tier is a prioritisation device for investigation, not an investment recommendation or an assertion of default.

The mechanism

The proposed mechanism begins with impaired assets. A high GNPA ratio can become an earnings and capital problem if provisioning, recoveries, and operating earnings do not offset the credit burden. Capital then has less capacity to support lending, absorb later shocks, or reassure funding providers. The pressure chain is plausible, but the dossier does not supply a future loss path, recovery path, or provisioning trajectory. It therefore supports a vulnerability thesis, not a completed causal diagnosis.

Reported CRAR was 20.93, with 5.93 percentage points of headroom over the 15.0 licensing CRAR floor used in this assessment. That is meaningful reported capacity. It is not evidence that capital cannot erode, nor does it identify the speed at which losses might consume the buffer. Utkarsh is outside the 2021 bank-PCA framework, so the dossier does not allege a PCA breach. Treating licensing-floor headroom as a PCA all-clear would be a category error.

The narrower call is that credit-cost and capital pressure are the first visible route because they are the route the filing discloses. It does not say funding is safe. Funding is not scored, and the relevant lenses are dark.

What the filings say

The filing-based screen assigns a score of 74.9 and grade A, alongside the adverse GNPA observation. These labels can coexist because they answer different questions. The score is within a corpus-monitoring probability framework and is explicitly not a credit rating. A relatively low modelled probability does not negate a material asset-quality burden; equally, GNPA alone does not establish near-term incapacity.

The historical record carries a major limitation. It is PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT, with no complete bitemporal public-availability and revision archive. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the process uses period end plus a conservative 60-day filing lag. That reduces quarter-end lookahead but cannot reconstruct overwritten amendments. Lead times are therefore optimistic. The subject is not eligible for validated backtesting or real-money use.

The published Failure Radar board defines orange as a PD level at or above 1.00%, deterioration from at least 0.25%, or a fresh authoritative market DD below 1. Utkarsh’s designation should be read through the dossier’s actual components and constraints, rather than as a generic statement about any institution with impaired loans.

What the market says

The publication cannot responsibly say that the market confirms or rejects the filing thesis. The supplied market observation is dated 2026-09-02 and is fresh by age, but retrieval preceded the asserted exchange-session close. Display-use and display-rights approvals are absent. Model-gate, tier-use, and same-session market-cap-clock approvals are also absent. The market-derived display has no publication or tier authority.

This is not a benign absence. An inadmissible market reading cannot be translated into confidence that equity holders, creditors, or depositors see no strain. Nor can it strengthen the orange tier. The market layer is visible as a coverage record, but no per-name market signal is authorised for this call. The market-evidence index should therefore be consulted as a methodology and admissibility record, not as proof of a current Utkarsh price signal.

The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. Utkarsh reported substantial CRAR headroom, no PCA action-zone breach is alleged, and the filing is aged 18 months. The modelled PD_12m remains below the orange rule’s 1.00% level criterion. On that view, the orange designation may be an appropriately cautious reaction to a historical asset-quality burden, rather than evidence that the bank is now approaching balance-sheet incapacity.

The conformal diagnostic also did not alarm: distress was 25.1 against a threshold_distress of 26.799999999999997. But that result cannot exonerate the bank. Its wiring status is SUSPENDED_REVALIDATION_REQUIRED, its gate is CLOSED_REVALIDATION_REQUIRED, and it has no score or tier authority. A suspended diagnostic cannot be used to intensify the thesis or dismiss it.

The counter-case would become materially stronger with a newer vetted filing showing improving GNPA and preserved or increased capital headroom. Admissible liability evidence showing stable funding would strengthen it further. Neither is supplied here.

The evidence that is dark

The deposit-run lens is dark because there are no consecutive deposit disclosures. Wholesale reliance, CD strain, and LCR headroom are also dark. Those gaps block a full assessment of funding pressure. They do not demonstrate an absence of funding risk.

Forensics are ineligible. There is no forensic verdict and no forensic indicator. That is a missing-data disclosure, not evidence of clean accounts. The dossier itself notes that filings later shown to be falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that problem when it is eligible.

The radar excludes 21 stale institutions rather than presenting them as current. Its current comparison rows include Belstar Microfinance Limited, ESAF Small Finance Bank, and IndusInd Bank Ltd in yellow; Utkarsh is the single orange name, with no red names. This is selective monitored coverage of institutions with fresh vetted public dossiers, not a universal ranking of lenders.

What would change the call

A newer vetted filing could weaken or overturn this view if it showed sustained improvement in GNPA while CRAR remained resilient. The pressure chain would be broken if impaired assets improved, credit costs ceased absorbing capital capacity, and reliable liability disclosures showed no associated funding deterioration.

The thesis would strengthen if GNPA deteriorated, CRAR moved toward the licensing floor, or newly eligible evidence revealed deposit, wholesale, CD, or LCR strain. Future market evidence should enter only after rights, identity, timing, model, and tier-use gates are satisfied. A price observation without those authorities is not a substitute for evidence.

Follow the pressure chain

Follow the chain from GNPA to provisioning and earnings, from earnings to capital absorption, and from capital capacity to lending flexibility and creditor confidence. Funding is the next link, but it is unlit rather than benign. The relevant research boundary is institution and lender balance-sheet risk: that is LiquiLens’s remit.

System conditions belong elsewhere. Seiche addresses system dollar-funding capacity, while Undertow addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity. The Seiche overview reports an EROSION regime with guarded confidence, led by modelled or slow-moving structure rather than broad current market-plumbing confirmation. The Undertow board reports partial coverage across several segments. Neither product supplies an authorised Utkarsh market-price verdict.

Sources, method, and limits

This article relies only on the supplied Failure Radar board, validation record, and market-evidence index. Readers can inspect related LiquiLens research, replay material, and investigations. The US NDFI watch is separate context and is not evidence about Utkarsh.

Historical validation is diagnostic only. The hazard panel has 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions; its temporal AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 diagnostic gate. The India replay covers 48 institutions and reports a 21.5-month median lead, but it is filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT and its lead times are explicitly optimistic. Similar historical mechanisms do not establish the same outcome here. This is a current filing-based analysis, not investment advice, and the orange tier is not a credit rating.

entry.title: Rupee Co-operative Bank replay: the signal was an evidence boundary, not a clean warning
entry.summary: This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Rupee Co-operative Bank’s record shows why a balance-sheet screen must separate a filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and an absence of scoreable evidence.
entry.content:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome.* Rupee Co-operative Bank defaulted on 2022-09-22. The supplied record does not identify a balance sheet that should have felt stress first through a usable public signal. Its central lesson is narrower, but important: an unscoreable record is an evidence boundary, not a benign result.

That conclusion is not a retrospective claim that the institution was healthy before the event. It is also not a claim that a model detected what the available inputs did not show. A filing-period signal depends on published, scoreable institutional disclosures. A market-price signal depends on an observable market repricing measure. A model derivation is an output constructed from its inputs and assumptions. These are different evidentiary objects, and none can be substituted for another when the record is missing.

A Failure Radar tier is a published rule over published components, not a solvency verdict, a failure prediction, or not a credit rating. Rupee Co-operative Bank is a useful hard case precisely because a failed institution need not leave a neat, timely trail for every public screen.

The record before the event

The replay records Rupee Co-operative Bank as an urban co-operative bank, with the event date of 2022-09-22. Fraud masking is marked false. That means this case is not tagged as one in which later-discovered falsification made apparently compliant filings misleading. It does not establish capital strength, asset quality, liquidity, funding resilience, or prior safety.

The institution-specific PCA record contains no first action-zone observation and no lead time. The funding record is explicitly unscoreable, with no first signal and no lead time. The dossier supplies no historical filing as-of date for the institution. That date cannot be inferred from the default date, the publication date, or a later board timestamp.

The relevant record is therefore the Rupee Co-operative Bank replay, not a current institutional dossier. The Failure Radar board is dated 2026-09-01 and its market layer is dated 2026-08-11. Those dates describe later analytical material, not information demonstrably available before Rupee Co-operative Bank’s event.

What the lenses saw

Read literally, neither named balance-sheet lens supplies a usable lead in this case. The PCA lens does not show a first action-zone breach. The funding lens cannot operate without a scoreable liability series. Neither result says that pressure was absent. It says the supplied replay cannot establish that either lens observed it first.

That distinction becomes sharper under the historical construction label: PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT. The record is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and has no bitemporal input contract. Where an explicit publication clock is absent, availability is proxied by period end plus 60 days. The dossier also states that lead times are optimistic. A period-end proxy may impose a conservative delay convention, but it still does not prove the actual information set available to a lender, depositor, investor, or supervisor at that time.

The broader replay gives context but cannot fill this institution’s gaps. Across failed institutions, the PCA summary reports 15 cases, with 5 entering the action zone first and a median lead of 41 months. The funding summary also reports 15 failed institutions, but only 10 have liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first in 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those are cohort descriptions, not proof that Rupee Co-operative Bank travelled either path. The validation record preserves those limits.

Why the warning mattered

The warning here was epistemic. A desk seeking to rank balance-sheet stress needed evidence on supervisory-threshold inputs or liabilities, with a credible availability date. The replay does not provide a scoreable funding series and does not provide a first PCA action-zone observation. The proper result is an unresolved institution-specific record.

That matters because absence is easily misread. “No signal” can mean that a threshold did not fire on available inputs. “No score” can mean that the needed inputs were unavailable or unusable. “No market-price signal” would mean something else again: that a market-based measure was absent, unavailable, or did not cross its own rule. These states cannot honestly be collapsed into “no risk.”

The methodology says components are replayed independently on a 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation. It also says the conformal alarm is diagnostic, with no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Those constraints are not footnotes. They prevent a model derivation from being presented as a contemporaneous observation.

The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any stronger thesis: this replay may be too incomplete to say which balance sheet would have felt stress first, or whether either disclosed lens would have given a useful warning before the event. Pressure may have emerged outside the captured series, moved more quickly than the filing proxy, or remained outside the supplied public record.

The validation statistics reinforce caution. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a CI95 range of 0.338 to 1.0. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and failed that gate. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC is 0.799.

Those figures do not establish that the screen is useless. They do establish that historical discrimination is uncertain and that construction-PIT diagnostics cannot be promoted into a tradable or decision-ready backtest. The counter-case therefore defeats any assertion that Rupee Co-operative Bank was cleanly flagged. It does not defeat the narrower thesis that the honest output is a documented blind spot rather than reassurance.

What today's board shares

Today’s board is a separate comparison, not historical evidence about this institution. As of 2026-09-01, it reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a score of 74.9 and a dossier as of 2025-03-31 that is 18 months old. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8, as of 2026-03-31 and 6 months old. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 66.0, as of 2025-09-30 and 12 months old, with market distance-to-default of 1.927 and the market_dd_below_2 signal.

These are current screen states, not forecasts. The board excludes 21 stale institutions, and nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Its market layer uses daily auto-adjusted Yahoo Finance closes through 2026-08-11, documented in the market evidence index. An absent institution is not thereby green; Rupee Co-operative Bank’s replay shows why.

The next falsifiable test

This account can be disproved with a genuinely bitemporal, pre-event public record. It would need dated filings or disclosures, a verified publication clock, and scoreable PCA or liability-series inputs. If that record showed a timely action-zone breach or funding signal, the replay should identify the first lens and its lead time.

If it instead showed neither signal before the event despite verified timely availability, the claim that the key warning was an evidence boundary would be weakened. Either result would be more informative than retrospective reconstruction from later dates. Until then, the missing data must remain visible rather than being converted into a signal.

Follow the pressure chain

For a risk committee, the sequence is procedural: establish the filing or publication date; test whether supervisory-threshold inputs are scoreable; test whether liability disclosures exist; then separate any market repricing observation from the filing-based evidence. A missing link stops the inference chain. It does not complete it.

LiquiLens addresses institution and lender balance-sheet risk. Seiche addresses system dollar-funding capacity, as described in the Seiche overview. Undertow addresses market liquidity and executable exit capacity, as shown on the Undertow board. The questions can be related, but system funding, an institution balance sheet, and executable market exit are not interchangeable measurements.

Sources, method, and limits

The core materials are the Rupee Co-operative Bank replay, the Failure Radar board, the historical validation file, and the market evidence index. Additional desk material is available through LiquiLens research and the investigations archive.

This is a public-disclosure replay with period-end proxy construction timing, not a validated backtest or a real-money test. Lead times are optimistic. Fraud-masked filings can appear compliant to threshold engines; this case is not fraud-masked, but that general limitation remains. This is not investment advice.
